detail.abstract: Professional forecasters' heterogeneous narratives about how inflation affects stock markets in 2023 rationalize their high disagreement regarding quantitative expectations for 12-month-ahead inflation and stock returns in December 2022. Professional forecasters causally update their return expectations in heterogeneous directions in response to information about the inflation outlook, depending on the narrative they entertain. Moreover, the narratives also affect their asset allocation in a hypothetical portfolio-choice experiment. Providing common signals does not necessarily lead to convergence of beliefs if agents subscribe to different narratives.

detail.abstract: Head Start staff report high psychological strain. Under conservation of resources theory, the current study tested whether intake measures predicted elevated stress and low intention to remain six months later, and whether a brief reappraisal exercise improved it. Data from a randomized trial of 4,054 employees (95% women, mean age 43) were split into training, development, and test partitions (n = 2,429, 811, and 814). An 11-predictor logistic regression on baseline stress, burnout, anxiety, depressive symptoms, job satisfaction, hope, reappraisal beliefs, and demographics predicted elevated six-month stress better than the base rate (log loss 0.532 versus 0.596, difference −0.064, 95% CI [−0.099, −0.029]). Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was .72 [.67, .77], and the calibration slope was 0.92 [0.70, 1.19]. The same predictors predicted low intention to remain (log loss 0.386 versus 0.417, difference −0.030 [−0.060, −0.002], area under the curve .70 [.63, .77]), although the Brier difference included zero. Baseline stress and younger age had the largest standardized coefficients for stress, and lower job satisfaction had the largest for intention to remain. Adding assigned condition and post-exercise responses, or the same measures three months later, changed log loss by −0.002 [−0.006, 0.001] and −0.001 [−0.023, 0.022]. For staff who completed the follow-up, a short intake survey predicted both outcomes and the reappraisal exercise added little. After local validation, the equation could identify six months ahead which staff will likely report elevated stress or low intention to remain, while there is still time to offer support.

title: The Shot Gap: Bloch-Sphere Geometry and the Hidden Measurement Budget of Single-Qubit Quantum Classifiers

detail.title: The Shot Gap: Bloch-Sphere Geometry and the Hidden Measurement Budget of Single-Qubit Quantum Classifiers

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study uses only synthetic data and involves no human participants, animals or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: Not applicable. This study is not a clinical trial.

detail.abstract: Single-qubit data re-uploading classifiers map every input to a point on the Bloch sphere and are routinely evaluated by thresholding an expectation value estimated from many repetitions of the circuit (shots). A single measurement, however, can deliver at most the Helstrom accuracy of the two class-conditional mixtures, which for one qubit reduces to the length of the difference between the class-mean Bloch vectors. We call the difference between thresholded accuracy and single-shot accuracy the shot gap and measure it in a computational experiment with known ground truth: four synthetic tasks with exact Bayes accuracy, five circuit depths, three training losses, two label-noise levels and ten seeds (1,200 runs), simulated exactly and validated against a state-vector simulation, finite-difference gradients and a brute-force search over measurements. The Helstrom bound held in every run. For circuits of depth two or more, models whose thresholded accuracy averaged 0.857 delivered 0.696 per single measurement, a mean shot gap of 0.161; at depth six, models with 0.93-0.98 thresholded accuracy on the linear, circle and XOR tasks delivered 0.67-0.86 per shot. The embedding, not the choice of measurement, accounted for 96.3% of the single-shot shortfall. Training with the single-shot log-likelihood narrowed the shot gap relative to a smoothed hinge loss in 89% of paired configurations (median reduction 0.085) at a median cost of 0.011 in thresholded accuracy, and eleven shots recovered 74% of the gap against 41% under the hinge loss. Two preregistered hypotheses were not supported: the gap did not grow with boundary nonlinearity, and training loss predicted it better than class-mean Bloch-vector length. Accuracy reports for quantum classifiers should state the number of shots per prediction, as they state training data and compute.

title: Who Pays for Medical AI? Payment Routes for 1,614 FDA-Authorized AI Devices and Where the Money Goes

detail.title: Who Pays for Medical AI? Payment Routes for 1,614 FDA-Authorized AI Devices and Where the Money Goes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This is independent work. The author received no funding and has no competing interests. Views are the author's own.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not required; the study uses only public, aggregate secondary data. Patient consent: not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
Regulatory authorization is usually treated as the main hurdle for medical artificial intelligence. It is not what decides who pays. This paper maps how FDA-authorized medical AI is actually paid for in the United States and where the revenue ends up. I use the Food and Drug Administration's list of AI-enabled devices (1,614 devices authorized through June 29, 2026), Medicare claims and price files, 42 hand-collected payment cases from four countries, a census of 58 publicly listed medical-AI companies, and 66 disclosed transactions. A device counts as separately reimbursed only when a payment rule or the manufacturer's own coding material names it; on that standard, at least 79 devices (4.9%) have ever had a billing code, laboratory code, or add-on payment of their own, and about three in four are classified as funded out of a purchaser's budget. Medicare physician payments on AI billing codes came to $10.3 million in 2024, 96% of it for coronary computed tomography. Medicare paid laboratories another $204 million for AI-based tests, nearly all of it for machine-learning tests that do not appear on FDA's AI list at all. Across both claims and cases, per-use payment almost always goes to AI that produces a result of its own, and rarely to AI that assists with work an existing fee already covers. Revenue tells a related story: tests with AI inside account for 61.1% of the $4.1 billion the listed firms earned, and I estimate US spending in which the AI itself is priced, plus data licensed to drug manufacturers, at roughly $3.2 billion for 2025 (outer bounds $2.3–4.9 billion), with hospitals and practices paying about 45%. AI software firms hold 64.8% of FDA's AI authorizations from 2021 to 2025 but receive about a third of that spending. The device labels identify who pays reliably but the exact payment mechanism only about 60% of the time, and the cross-country cases are a purposive sample, not a random one.
AI disclosure: An AI assistant (Claude, from Anthropic) helped write the analysis scripts, draft device labels and search public sources. The author drafted and revised the text and is responsible for its content. All numbers are computed by scripts from public data and checked against the sources cited. AI tools are not authors.

title: Sanction Headroom: Receipt Timing, Fees and Credible Enforcement

detail.title: Sanction Headroom: Receipt Timing, Fees and Credible Enforcement

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is an analytical theoretical study; no human participants or participant data were used.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no funding for this work.

detail.abstract: We study how principal receipt timing and competing claims on limited personal assets constrain credible protection in a two-institution arrangement with prefunded shared cash. Certification must be paid before fines arrive. Fees covering sponsor capital and operating costs reduce the same personal assets available for sanctions. Later receipts therefore weakly raise required capital and fees, which can make the prescribed deterrence infeasible at given wealth, as well as increase financing cost. In the main example, delaying receipts on buffer-funded advances also raises least-cost control at every wealth, while delaying receipts on controlled balances need not. Within a prescribed contract menu, we characterize the joint funding, participation and sanction-capacity constraints. Without renegotiation, lower wealth raises least-cost control on a bounded active interval when the fee first falls and then rises with control more slowly than the punishment that control saves. Reversing fee priority preserves feasibility and least-cost policy choice within that menu. In a separate unilateral-settlement extension, bargaining discounts punishment by the manager’s share of the saved certification bill, weakly tightens the wealth constraint and can make the least-cost feasible partial policy more expensive than full control. These model-specific results assume default-free principal, exact observation, protected collectible wealth and binding enrollment. The contribution examined is the interaction of timing, fees and sanction capacity; costly enforcement, limited-liability fines, costly verification, wealth-dependent monitoring and dated liquidity have established precedents. The analysis does not establish general contract optimality, an empirically validated application or field-wide novelty.

title: Where Over-Blocking Comes From: Simulating CIPA School Filtering Policies on 103 Million Categorised Domains

detail.title: Where Over-Blocking Comes From: Simulating CIPA School Filtering Policies on 103 Million Categorised Domains

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is affiliated with Alpha Quantum, which maintains the domain register analysed in this paper and operates Web Filtering Database (https://www.webfilteringdatabase.com) and CIPA Web Filtering (https://www.cipawebfiltering.com), which offer web filtering data and a hosted filtering service for schools and libraries.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study analyses aggregated category counts for registered domain names and involves no human participants or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was carried out by Alpha Quantum.

detail.abstract: The Children's Internet Protection Act (CIPA) requires US schools and libraries that receive E-Rate support to block visual depictions that are obscene, child sexual abuse material, or harmful to minors. In practice, compliance is implemented with category-based web filters, and districts routinely block far more than the statute names. Concern that filters also block legitimate educational and health content is two decades old, but the evidence comes from small samples of hand-picked sites. We measure the question at census scale. Using web-filtering labels for 103,367,510 domains (57 categories, 9.0% of domains multi-labelled), we simulate five stylised policies, from a statutory core that blocks only adult content to a restrictive district policy that also blocks social, gaming, streaming, shopping and community categories, under three rules for handling sites with several labels. Blocking the statutory core removes 0.92% of domains and catches 0.048% of the 16.3 million domains carrying an education, health, government, news, science or civic label. A typical district policy of 17 categories blocks 4.6% of domains and catches 0.30% of protected-label domains. Adding twelve instructional-time categories quadruples the blocked share to 19.1% and multiplies collateral blocking 26-fold, to 1.24 million protected-label domains (7.6%), including 2.2% of .edu, 1.7% of US K-12 and 4.2% of government domains, none of which the statutory core touches. A cost-ordered blocking curve shows that the statutory and circumvention categories are among the cheapest to block, while Podcasts, Forums, Hate / Discrimination, Blogs, Community Sites and AI / LLM Tools carry the highest collateral ratios (25-60% of newly blocked domains carry a protected label). We also find that the apparent prevalence of adult content depends on the popularity measure: it covers 23% of the global top-1,000 traffic group but at most 0.1% of domains in the upper link-authority bands. Over-blocking, in short, is driven far less by what CIPA requires than by what districts add, and policy choices can be evaluated before deployment with data of this kind. We release all aggregate tables.

title: Turkana and the Resource Curse: Pastoralism, Extractives, Conservation Enclosure, and the Politics of Marginalisation in Northern Kenya

detail.title: Turkana and the Resource Curse: Pastoralism, Extractives, Conservation Enclosure, and the Politics of Marginalisation in Northern Kenya

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This manuscript was prepared for publication consideration. The evidence base was assembled in October 2026 (cut-off date: 12 October 2026); several processes discussed, notably first oil from the South Lokichar Basin, were still unfolding at that time. The author declares no external funding for this work. The author has also published related work on mining governance in Turkana (Lochu, 2026), which is cited where relevant. Correspondence concerning this article should be addressed to Meya Lochu, Millora Analytics and Research Consultancy, Turkana County, Kenya.
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Turkana County, Kenya's poorest devolved unit, sits at the centre of the country's first onshore oil development and a fast-moving gold frontier, while its pastoral commons are simultaneously targeted by conservation enclosure. This paper asks whether, and in what sense, Turkana is exposed to a "resource curse." Drawing on a structured documentary synthesis of peer-reviewed studies, parliamentary and regulatory records, and credible media published mainly between 2021 and 2026, it examines five interlocking themes: the historical production of marginalisation; the transformation of pastoralism into a mobile, market-linked and risk-protected "modern pastoralism"; oil in the South Lokichar Basin; gold and artisanal mining; and contested conservancies. It argues that Turkana's principal risk is not a curse inherent in resource abundance but a governance gap in a historically marginalised frontier, intensified by an anticipatory phase in which expectations, land claims and contracts are settled before production begins. Poverty (77.7% headcount in 2021) preceded oil and gold; the "curse" is therefore better understood as a threat to the remedy than as the cause of deprivation. The paper also qualifies the common claim that delay reflects only a lack of political goodwill, showing that commercial and financing failures were central, while community-centred commitments (a functioning community trust fund, registered pastoral land, transparent contracts) lag behind investor-centred approvals. It proposes an integrated analytical framework, five testable propositions, and a sequenced reform agenda built on operationalising the community trust fund before first oil, securing pastoral tenure and mobility, regulating conservancies through consent and licensing, formalising artisanal mining, and institutionalising transparency.

detail.title: The Shape of Time: Translation, Cross-Scale Influence and the Grammar of Nested Cycles

detail.abstract: Nested processes subject to translation and cross-scale influence generate a constrained grammar of time. We derive this geometry for cycles nested inside cycles from three conditions: alignment fixes how cycles nest, with the triad as the smallest symmetric nesting; translation shifts a cycle's peak, and with it the whole cycle, in time; and influence adds the slope of a larger cycle to the cycles inside it. Translation is the central object of the geometry. Inside a larger cycle of fixed length it produces a head-and-shoulders whose head lasts 1 + 3τ shoulders, never more than four, and translations compound across levels as (τ1 + τ2)/(1 + τ1τ2) within the bound set by the arrow of time. The geometry unifies patterns that traditions of market analysis found by looking at charts. Under a rising larger cycle the head-and-shoulders becomes five waves, so Dow's three phases and Elliott's five waves are one shape at different slopes, and Elliott's three rules follow as propositions. The golden ratio appears not as a proportion markets prefer but as a phase boundary: where the head occupies ϕ/3 of the cycle, the onset of five waves and the onset of clean impulses coincide. Hierarchies of translated cycles also provide a generative mechanism for Mandelbrot's multifractal trading time. The geometry has a proved limit as well: uniform triadic nesting cannot reproduce Elliott's recursive count. Mechanical tests find these patterns in prices about as often as in random paths of nested swings, so counting them cannot distinguish the two. The geometry's distinctive prediction is temporal: the slope of a larger movement should predict when the smaller cycle that follows reaches its peak. In equity indices, cycles that follow the strongest fifth of larger moves peak about 7% of a cycle later than those after the weakest. The effect is modest, with partial correlations of 0.06 to 0.18 across 27 price series, 27 equity indices and 480 stocks, but it replicates with the rule fixed in advance, exceeds fitted GARCH (including asymmetric forms), Markov-switching and momentum models, and has a counterpart in 270 years of solar cycles. In a pre-registered blind test on nine indices before 2000, unused by the work, it passed every pre-set criterion. Two pre-registered tests in foreign exchange did not replicate it: eight bilateral rates gave a weaker relationship (+0.07), confined to declines and inconsistent across years, and ten effective exchange rates failed every criterion (+0.045). The data establish the relationship in equity indices, for trough-defined cycles, not in financial markets generally; whether the geometry is its cause remains open.

detail.title: Job Security, Worker Sorting, and Productivity: Evidence from Merit-Based Employment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have no personal or financial relationship with people or other organizations in regards to this study. It was self funded.

detail.abstract: Public-sector organizations often struggle to retain productive workers. This paper studies how merit-based access to permanent public employment affects teacher retention, workforce composition, and student achievement. I leverage a nationwide reform in Perú that made passing a centralized screening exam a prerequisite for competing for a permanent teaching position. Using a regression discontinuity design, I show that barely passing the test lowers the probability of leaving public teaching by 29 percent, mostly by preventing exits from the profession. Passing the test also selectively retains more productive teachers among those with prior private-sector experience. Among established temporary teachers, for whom passing has little direct effects besides access to a permanent job, job security reduces exits by 4.4 percentage points, with effects persisting two years after the test. Finally, comparing the same students across subjects, I find no learning losses from passing: students taught by teachers who barely pass the test score 0.05 standard deviations higher on national tests and 0.10 higher in course grades.

title: Exploring the Agentic City

detail.title: Exploring the Agentic City

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding received for this work.

detail.abstract: This essay argues that the agentic city is best understood not as a city governed by machines, but as a city that delegates bounded slices of operational authority to artificial agents. The decisive question it raises is therefore political rather than technical: who authorizes that delegation on what terms, and how it is withdrawn. Drawing on recent literature on urban AI, the essay makes some pertinent claims that the empirical record shows real but concentrated gains, in service triage, traffic control and infrastructure maintenance, where tasks are measurable, high-volume and reversible; governance capacity rather than technical capability is now the binding constraint, because the field has a clear normative consensus but few operational instruments for escalation, audit and accountability; and the appropriate response is a principle of governed agency; the autonomy granted to an urban agent should scale with the reversibility of its actions and the contestability of its decisions, and should never outpace capacity of the city to trace and override them. The agentic city is thus neither a utopia of frictionless optimization nor an inevitable dystopia of algorithmic control, but a design choice about the distribution of public authority.

detail.abstract: We investigate the impact of mobile location-based recommendation systems (MLBRS) on the performance of local businesses. Leveraging a comprehensive dataset of 16,720 restaurants and quasiexperimental variation generated by the official launch of a leading MLBRS, we employ a 2-Stage Least Squares instrumental-variable framework to estimate the effect of algorithmic exposure on consumer engagement. Our analysis reveals that a 1% increase in exposure is associated with a 0.078% increase in clicks; separately, a 1% increase in clicks is associated with a 0.053% increase in visit intentions. Importantly, the estimated exposure effect is larger for geographically disadvantaged restaurants, but primarily at the discovery stage (clicks). This pattern highlights a boundary condition of MLBRS: algorithmic visibility can aid, but it does not by itself resolve the uncertainty involved in acting on a recommendation. Downstream conversion is stronger when restaurants provide richer digital information and reputation signals, including consumer reviews and owner-curated information such as photos and menus. Auxiliary credit-card sales data from a restricted Seoul subsample provide consistent evidence of a positive association between algorithmic exposure and revenue, suggesting that MLBRS can shape the connection of online recommendations to offline economic outcomes.

detail.abstract: In a group of organizations and people that shares by choice, nothing compels one to tell another what it knows, so shared records stay empty: nothing in, nothing out. This paper proposes two means to incite the desire and the capability to share. The keep is the shared record of what members have told one another and the channel through which they tell it, held under a charter the members write; it supplies the capability. The keeper is the trusted person, or team of at least two, through whom what members say reaches the keep, a field person before a records person; the keeper supplies the desire. Both serve a persistent collaboration, a standing group in which no member can direct the others and every member supports the keep in some way. The pairing is argued to work where other approaches fail: technology supplies capacity without input, mandates apply only where sharing can be required and heavy formal requirements may crowd out trust, and lead-organization governance leaves the record with the largest member, while the keeper brings the desire to share, and the keep the assurance that sharing is safe and lawful, with members in control. The conditions it rests on were observed over more than a decade in a public safety consortium; the pairing itself is the key. This paper places the solution among the nearest work on gatekeepers, boundary spanners, network governance, and custody, sets them against studies since 2015 that bear out their claims on trust, informal contact, and light charters and qualify them where control and formal agreement matter, and reports Scopus searches that found no existing concept for the combination. It closes with testable implications and first steps a group can take with what it already has.

title: Cheap Production, Costly Verification: Doing Research under Agentic AI and Automation

detail.title: Cheap Production, Costly Verification: Doing Research under Agentic AI and Automation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: There is no funding for this research.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is making research cheap to produce but not (yet) cheap to check. Across natural sciences, engineering, social sciences, and humanities, researchers now use generative AI, AI agents, and large language models to draft manuscripts, run analyses, and even generate mathematical proofs at a fraction of their former cost, whereas verifying a claim still relies largely on scarce expert time. We develop a simple model in which researchers decide whether to produce and submit claims and a verifier with limited capacity decides which claims to check. As production becomes cheaper, more claims are submitted and their average reliability falls, because cost no longer filters out low-effort work. Scarce scrutiny is best concentrated on the claims with the strongest early evidence of validity, so a growing share of claims, including many valid ones, goes unchecked, and review backlogs can grow without bound once submissions outpace reviewing capacity. The flow of verified discoveries first rises and then falls as automation increases, a pattern we call the Verification Laffer Curve, unless verification capacity grows in step with submissions. Even with no difference in ability and no reviewer bias, the work of early-career researchers and of researchers working outside their home field receives less verification because it is costlier to check, a gap that widens as automation grows. Numerical simulations illustrate these results. We discuss how expanding verification capacity, restoring screening, and lowering verification costs for disadvantaged researchers can keep AI a net gain for research in any field that relies on it.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for organizational communication, knowledge processing, analytics, and workflow support, but these activities are often introduced as separate tools rather than designed as a coordinated organizational system. This paper proposes the AI-Enabled Communication Decision-Making and Automation Framework (AICDMF), a governance-aware, communication-centered architecture for B2B technology organizations operating globally. It asks how AI capabilities can be integrated into communication and workflow processes while preserving human authority and accountability. Drawing on research on AI capability, digital transformation, organizational communication, AI-mediated communication, responsible AI, and design science, the paper derives design requirements and maps them to six connected layers: data infrastructure; AI capability; workflow orchestration; communication decision support; governance, human oversight, operations, and maintenance; and continuous organizational learning and refinement. A selective analytical comparison positions this proposal in relation to established AI risk-management guidance, design-science methods, and communication scholarship; it is not a systematic review or a claim of superiority over existing frameworks. The design specifies information, control, and feedback interfaces; separates recommendation from authorization; and limits automated execution to predefined, low-consequence actions subject to explicit permissions, task-appropriate validation, logging, and exception handling. Three illustrative scenarios address international stakeholder communication, regional market-demand analysis, and technical knowledge management. The paper's contribution is a traceable conceptual design and a proposed evaluation plan, not an empirically validated model. No implementation, expert assessment, performance effect, or sustainability outcome is reported. The proposed sustainability pathway is conditional: improved information visibility may inform resource planning only when decision-makers validate the evidence and act on it.

detail.abstract: This review extends Bourdieusian capital theory into a domain that has not yet been addressed in forms of literature: the convergence of artificial intelligence fluency and cybersecurity competence. Building on Archer et al.'s (2015) conceptualization of "science capital" as a magnifier for understanding unbalanced participation in science and on subsequent work extending Bourdieu's framework into digital contexts (Ragnedda, 2018; Verwiebe & Hagemann, 2024), this review argues that AI fluency and cybersecurity competence have become practically inseparable and should be hypothesized together as a single cohesive form of capital rather than as adjacent or embedded structures. Drawing on technical standards such as OWASP, NIST, MITRE ATLAS; regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act; and current workforce data, the review documents the entanglement of AI systems with both offensive and defensive cybersecurity practice. It applies Verwiebe and Hagemann's two-part test for capital independence requires the capital to circulate across subfields and have an unequal, class-structured distribution to argue that this entanglement qualifies as a distinct form of capital. The review builds a new framework called AI-Cybersecurity Capital by combining Archer et al.'s eight dimensions of science capital with Dakan and Feller's (2025) four-part AI fluency model, which provides the structural organization, and maps the result onto three subfields: dispositional and cognitive, behavioral, and relational. The review directly engages Ben Fine's (2001, 2010) warning about inventing too many types of "capital," and maintains that this new concept may be necessary because of structural changes within the industry rather than convenience or theory for its own sake. The model requires empirical data to be fully validated.

detail.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping education, while raising growing concerns about the trustworthiness of AI-supported learning and decision-making. In educational settings, trustworthiness extends beyond model behavior to pedagogical and institutional contexts and, therefore, should be considered throughout the ecosystem of GenAI. Existing research remains fragmented across trustworthiness concerns, technical methods, educational applications, and evaluation practices. To bridge the gap, this survey provides a systematic view through a lifecycle perspective connecting trustworthiness requirements, system development, evaluation, deployment, and iterative refinement. Building on it, we propose a taxonomy that organizes the literature along four axes: attributes, methodology, applications, and evaluation. We synthesize progress across these dimensions, highlight their interconnections and remaining gaps, and discuss open challenges toward trustworthy education in the era of GenAI.

detail.abstract: Demands for fairness of opportunity (especially among those born since the 1990s) have made equality of opportunity a central social challenge in South Korea. This paper examines spatial inequality as a source of that concern. Drawing on the Survey of Household Finances and Living Conditions (SHFLC) and 26 waves of the Korea Labor and Income Panel Study (KLIPS), it finds that gaps between the Seoul Capital Area (SCA) and the rest of the country have widened since the mid-2010s in both household income and the distribution of income classes. These gaps shape the environments in which children grow up and condition how parental economic position is transmitted to the next generation: among cohorts born after 1975, the advantage of growing up in the SCA is larger for children of higher-income parents. National indicators of income distribution have improved, yet inequality of opportunity persists and is channeled through space. The study argues that balanced regional development should be reconceived as a core strategy for securing substantive equality of opportunity.

title: When does a second serum sample add information? Optimal timing and identifiability of paired serological measurements from a mechanistic model of antibody kinetics

detail.title: When does a second serum sample add information? Optimal timing and identifiability of paired serological measurements from a mechanistic model of antibody kinetics
detail.abstract: Paired serum samples — an acute and a convalescent specimen drawn two to four weeks apart — are a century-old convention of clinical serology, yet the timing of the second draw has never been derived from antibody kinetics. We formalize the question ”when should the second sample be taken?” as a Bayesian information-gain problem conditional on the first measurement, using a mechanistic three-compartment model (short- and long-lived plasma cells secreting serum IgG) with literature-anchored half-lives. Analytically, the determinant of the two-point Fisher information matrix equals (g(t_{2})-g(t_{1}))^{2}/{\sigma }^{4}, where g(t) is the sensitivity of the log-titre to the memory compartment: a single measurement is strictly rank-deficient, and two measurements degenerate to one whenever both fall on the fast phase (t_{2}\lesssim 45–56 d) or both on the slow-phase plateau (t_{1}\gtrsim 125 d). Applied to three post-peak discrimination questions — recent versus past infection, vaccine response assessment, and waning versus re-exposure — the expected information gain is monotonically saturating in the gap: no narrow interior optimum exists, so the routine 2–4-week re-testing convention is corrected rather than supported. The framework instead yields a threshold rule (the earliest informative gap is ~6–8 weeks post-peak; shorter gaps add little information), a fixed-interval rule for response assessment (≈290 d ≈ 9.5 months, independent of first-sample timing), and a calendar-window rule for re-exposure. Across three literature-anchored scenarios, optimal schedules cut the decision error by ≈45% relative to the naive t_{1}+21 d convention (nine-cell arithmetic means: 10.0% vs 18.1%). The rules are complementary to existing paired-sera practice.

detail.abstract: This interim paper assesses AI labour replacement risk across Greater Manchester's ten boroughs. It applies AI occupational and industry exposure indices to Census 2021 and Companies House data, with LLM-assisted estimates of whether AI will mainly augment or replace work in each sector and a place-based adjustment for ecosystem density. Most of the city-region's workforce sits in the augmentation zone, but only just above the substitution threshold, and exposure varies between and within boroughs. Among firms with four or more employees, boroughs with higher AI exposure show lower augmentation probabilities, the reverse of the UK-wide pattern and consistent with Bessen's account of technology eventually reducing labour demand. Microbusinesses follow the national pattern. Vendors' moves towards cost-recovery pricing add a further risk for organisations dependent on subsidised AI. The paper makes eleven recommendations, centred on pricing resilience, borough-level policy, early-career pipelines, and extending AI to occupations where it is most likely to augment workers.

detail.abstract: We examine whether international students' work-study practices in South Korea support the government's goal of developing regional human capital and promoting long-term settlement. Using survey data and focus group interviews from two universities, we find that parttime employment does not necessarily reduce the amount of time students spend studying and may improve Korean language proficiency. However, most jobs are concentrated in low-skilled occupations unrelated to students' fields of study, limiting the accumulation of occupation-specific human capital. The findings suggest a gap between current work-study practices and the policy objective of preparing international students for regional labor markets. We recommend expanding major-related internships, university-industry cooperation, and integrated employment and settlement support services to strengthen the transition from study to regional employment and long-term settlement.

detail.abstract: The paper investigates the interest rate policy transmission mechanism and the role of market structure of banking industry in Qatar. The momentum threshold autoregressive model is applied over the monthly period from 2005:01 to 2018:06 to examine the magnitude of intermediation and adjustment to disequilibria in the deposit market. Given the results obtained from the calculation of the concentration indexes, the high degree of market power found in the Qatari market might justify the rejection of the completeness hypothesis on the underlying interest rate spread. Nevertheless, the asymmetric adjustment mechanism is found to be downward rigid which suggests a high degree of customers sophistication and an elastic supply of deposits. The results are found robust under different procedures and consideration of the heaviside function. In addition, to model interest rate volatility and overcome the problem of heteroscedastic errors in the error correction standard models, an asymmetric EC-EGARCH-M model is applied. The results show that the impact of monetary policy shocks have a significant positive impact on deposit interest rates and that negative monetary shocks trigger more next period conditional interest rate volatility than positive monetary shocks namely for a short time maturity rate.

detail.abstract:
Israel votes on 27 October. Polymarket's odds on who will be prime minister are quoted in the Israeli and international press as if they were a forecast. We rebuilt every trade in those markets, and every trade, by every account, in 6,158 Israel, Iran and Middle East war markets. We then asked three questions: who sets the numbers, who is betting, and whether anyone knew things early. An "insider candidate" here is a bet whose timing or size calls for explanation, not a finding of inside information.
- $64.3 million has been bet on Israel's election and Netanyahu's future by 89,212 accounts. More bettors back
Netanyahu, but more money bets against him: 2,460 accounts hold $0.9 million for him, and 1,567 hold $2.1 million
against.
- The election is being bet by war-market traders. 82% of election accounts have also bet on Israel and Iran war
markets, and they supply 93% of the money.
- The traders with the best records on Israel's wars lean against Netanyahu. Of the proven war traders with $500 or
more at stake, 22% back him, against 42% of everyone else, a gap among only 27 accounts. Most of their money
against him is one account, wan123.
- Accounts that bet big and early on the Iran strikes, the Yemen strike and the US to Iran peace deal are now betting
on the election. We found 75 large bets placed before a war market moved, by 63 accounts now in the election, and
56 large long-odds positions on the eventual winner, by 40 election accounts. Many were sold again before the news;
only four made $300,000 or more. Six of the 15 strongest candidates bet early on two or more separate events. Two of
them, wan123 and tetrose, hold $325,500 against Netanyahu between them; the rest hold little either way.
- The biggest bettor against Netanyahu made $1.2 million on the peace deal. wan123 lost about $737,000 on earlier
deadlines, then bought "Yes" at 11¢ two weeks before the deal. It holds $229,780 against Netanyahu.
- The market matches the mainstream polls, and the money backing Netanyahu matches the outlier. The 30.5% price
fits the 12 mainstream polls; the pro-Netanyahu money is in effect betting on Channel 14.
- The same accounts sit behind a separate BETINT case. Two of the three accounts that funded a $1.14 million bet
against an Indiana data center ban on 3 October are here: ScottyNooo, our top insider candidate, and dromedaryy, the
sixth-largest holder against Netanyahu and the largest seller to the $100,000 pro-Netanyahu order (section 20).
- The headline number is cheap to move. Of 56 lasting changes of displayed leader, 30 came mainly from one account.
Eisenkot overtook Netanyahu on 12 July on a $152 sale and has led ever since. On 27 August, $3,200 from two justfunded
accounts preceded the headline "Winter overtakes Lieberman" (section 16).

detail.abstract: Maximum drawdown is among the most critical risk metrics, since other strategy deficiencies ultimately translate into capital loss and manifest as drawdown. Using drawdown as an illustrative case, this study presents an experimental proof of concept of quantum computing for risk assessment of trading algorithm performance. The probability that maximum drawdown exceeds 5% over eight trades (win rate 0.4054, reward-to-risk 1.92, 2% risk per trade) is estimated. Maximum likelihood amplitude estimation with a 15-qubit circuit on a noiseless Qiskit Aer simulator yields 59.257%, versus 59.324% by exact enumeration (absolute error 0.067 percentage points) and 59.310% by 200,000-path Monte Carlo. detail.abstract: I evaluate different ways of making an objective decision with a clear decision rule: machineonly, human-only, and a hybrid system. I document four stylized facts. First, replacing the human-only system with automated decisions cuts errors from 8.3 percent to 0.3 percent, while the hybrid regime cuts errors only to between 5.1 and 5.5 percent. Fifth, I show that the actions being evaluated do not change in response to the evaluation technology, and hence do not drive these results. Second, in the hybrid regime the evaluator makes better decisions even in cases where the decisions are not (or cannot be) appealed. Third, appeals are limited by what appellants can observe, not by the number of allowed appeals: I show that they observe errors with noise, and that they appeal only large enough errors. Fourth, the errors that remain in the hybrid regime lead to a residual rent that accrues to some workers, while under automation there is no such rent.

title: The devil in the DeTail: Assessing state-contingent tail effects of a releasable macroprudential capital buffer using a parsimonious agent-based framework
affiliations: Bank of England, Bank of England and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: The devil in the DeTail: Assessing state-contingent tail effects of a releasable macroprudential capital buffer using a parsimonious agent-based framework
detail.abstract: We study the effects of releasable macroprudential capital buffers using DeTail, a parsimonious agent-based model featuring heterogeneous firms, households, banks and a central bank within a fully integrated stock-flow consistent framework. The model generates endogenous credit cycles, providing a framework to assess the state-contingent tail effects of releasable capital buffers on credit growth, borrower default rates and bank losses. We compare a regime with time-varying capital requirements to alternative regimes with time-invariant capital requirements and assess the statistical significance of distributional differences using bootstrap-based inference across Monte Carlo simulations. We find that releasing capital buffers during economic downturns preserves credit supply by improving risky lower-tail credit outcomes, reduces household and firm default rates, and supports macro-financial resilience by limiting tail bank losses and decreasing recapitalisation needs. By contrast, buffer accumulation during economic upturns imposes minimal costs and does not significantly constrain lending. Releasable buffers also shorten contraction phases and modestly dampen fluctuations in the credit cycle. Overall, our findings support the active use of releasable macroprudential capital buffers to mitigate systemic risk, enhance macro-financial resilience, and stabilise credit supply over the financial cycle.

detail.abstract:
In a preceding structural legal analysis (Miyazawa, 2026a), it was shown that Japan’s sub-sovereign public sector operates under a “designed vacuum of intervention”, in which the non-binding referral mechanism of Article 14 of the Whistleblower Protection Act and the reversed application of Articles 63 and 65 of the Criminal Investigation Norms legalize the “non-creation of records” at initial intake. This paper proves that such gatekeeping distortion is a deterministic mathematical consequence of the publicly observable macro-statistical architecture itself, not of frontline moral hazard or unobservable internal personnel assessments.

We model incoming misconduct and criminal complaints across time and structural complexity with a first-order linear advection-reaction partial differential equation, treating the statutory contrast between mandatory accusation under Article 226 of the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act and the exclusion of external enforcement under Article 58 of the Local Public Service Act as boundary conditions on the intake control space. Applying Pontryagin’s Maximum Principle, we prove the High-Complexity Cutoff Theorem: the optimal gatekeeping control is a bang-bang step function that formally records routine offenses (x < x*) under Article 63 while purging high-complexity cases (x ≥ x*), including internal whistleblowing, into unrecorded consultations under Article 65. Calibration against National Police Agency statistics for 2001–2024 confirms the resulting “Scissors Effect”: while total intake contacts remained stationary (3.13 to 3.67 million annually), recorded Penal Code offenses contracted by 73.0% and unrecorded consultations surged by 185.9%. Although actual cleared offenses fell by 47.0%, pure denominator compression nearly doubled the observed clearance rate from 19.8% to 38.9%. Finally, the Fundamental Pricing Trap Theorem shows that tightening the intake threshold simultaneously improves superficial governance metrics and strictly accelerates the accumulation of unpriced tail risk (Invisible Residual Losses), generating a systematic valuation error in JPY-denominated sub-sovereign bonds and ESG portfolios.

detail.abstract: The ongoing wave of bank branch closures represents a fundamental transformation of the banking industry. We concentrate on its consequences on the deposit side complementing the literature that has mostly focused on the impact on credit from information and relationship losses. Because closure is irreversible and future profitability is uncertain, banks face a real-option problem: they may tolerate weak current profitability to preserve the option value of future recovery, generating an inaction region in which branches remain open despite poor performance. Differences in deposit-retention capacity shape the form of bank-level adjustment. Strong retention leads to more discrete, target-based downsizing, whereas weak retention leads to gradual adjustment. The timing of industry-wide closure waves is instead generated by common events that accelerate the digital transformation of banking and discretely reduce the value of physical access. The franchise value of deposits is captured in a spatial model where deposits are local, as depositors incur transport costs to access the nearest branch.

detail.abstract: This study develops a Business Cycle Index (BCI) for Nigeria using a Mixed-Frequency Dynamic Factor Model (MF-DFM) to address the limitations of conventional Gross Domestic Product (GDP)-based measures in monitoring economic fluctuations. The study integrates monthly and quarterly macroeconomic indicators covering the monetary, financial, external, and real sectors of the Nigerian economy over the period 1993-2024. The MF-DFM employs the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm to estimate latent common factors underlying economic fluctuations. The second estimated latent factor is identified as the business cycle factor, while the Christiano-Fitzgerald band-pass filter and Harding-Pagan dating algorithm are applied to extract cyclical movements and identify business cycle turning points. The findings reveal that the constructed BCI captures alternating phases of economic expansion and contraction consistent with Nigeria's historical economic developments, including the 2008-2009 global financial crisis, the 2016 recession, and the COVID-19 pandemic. The results further indicate that expansion phases generally last longer than contractions, while economic downturns occur more abruptly. Comparisons with conventional GDP-based filtering techniques, including the Hodrick-Prescott, Christiano-Fitzgerald, and Baxter-King filters, demonstrate broad consistency in identified cyclical movements and turning points. The study concludes that the MF-DFM provides a coherent and informative framework for measuring and dating Nigeria's business cycles. I recommend incorporating the BCI into macroeconomic surveillance frameworks to complement existing indicators, strengthen economic monitoring, and support timely monetary and fiscal policy interventions.

detail.abstract: This study examines the transmission mechanisms, macroeconomic implications, and relative resilience of Nigeria's agricultural, industrial, and services sectors to sectoral and external economic shocks. Using two complementary Structural Vector Autoregressive (SVAR) models, the study employs Impulse Response Functions (IRFs), Forecast Error Variance Decomposition (FEVD), and Marginal Historical Decomposition (MHD) to investigate the dynamic interactions among sectoral outputs, oil prices, government revenue, real interest rates, real effective exchange rates, and air temperature. The findings reveal significant asymmetric transmission of shocks across sectors, with oil price and government revenue shocks emerging as the dominant drivers of sectoral fluctuations and macroeconomic instability. The industrial sector is identified as the most vulnerable, exhibiting pronounced sensitivity to oil price volatility, fiscal disturbances, interest rate changes, and exchange rate fluctuations. Conversely, the services sector demonstrates the greatest relative resilience, characterized by faster adjustment to shocks and increasing intersectoral linkages, while agriculture exhibits moderate vulnerability, particularly to climatic, fiscal, and sector-specific disturbances. Historical decomposition further reveals that major economic fluctuations were concentrated around periods of substantial domestic and external disturbances. The findings underscore Nigeria's persistent dependence on oil revenues, structural weaknesses, and limited shock-absorption capacity. The study recommends industrial diversification, climate-resilient agricultural investment, strengthened fiscal buffers, improved monetary-fiscal coordination, and enhanced services sector productivity. The study concludes that addressing structural vulnerabilities and strengthening intersectoral linkages are essential for mitigating shock transmission, improving macroeconomic stability, and promoting sustainable economic growth in Nigeria.

detail.abstract: Debates about artificial intelligence in government are usually framed as a question of degree: how much decision-making authority may be transferred to machines, and under what safeguards. This article argues that the framing is mistaken, and that the relevant boundary is not one of degree. Drawing on the impossibility results of social choice theory-Arrow, Sen, Gibbard-Satterthwaite-and on the Bergson-Samuelson-Harsanyi cardinal route out of them, it shows that the selection of a social objective function is not an unsolved computational problem but a proven indeterminacy: no neutral procedure derives a unique correct welfare ordering from individual preferences. The article therefore proposes a two-layer architecture for algorithmic governance. A thin value layer fixes the objective function, its weights, and the hard constraints that define a forbidden domain; this layer is irreducibly normative and cannot be delegated. Beneath it, a thick mathematical layer optimises within the permitted domain, and here artificial intelligence is not merely admissible but desirable. The central implication is that artificial intelligence does not solve the problem of the common good; it isolates that choice, and thereby liberates clean optimisation below it. Read through Habermas, this indeterminacy is the precondition of deliberative legitimation, not an obstacle to it. Democratic accountability-an identifiable human decisionmaker who can be blamed, outvoted, sued or dismissed-is accordingly not a residue awaiting automation but the legitimation mechanism for a formally demonstrated non-neutrality. Removing it does not make governance technical; it removes what made governance legitimate.

detail.abstract: This paper documents the sequential development and validation of three rule-based, long-only strategies in U.S. mid-cap equities under a common capital, timing, risk, and execution framework. The Legacy Breakout/Pullback strategy performed poorly, producing 65 trades and a total return of-47.0962%. Momentum52 represented a substantive redesign toward cross-sectional momentum, but its original later holdout failed: 54 trades returned-34.1037% with a profit factor of 0.5985. Reversal5 then shifted the economic premise toward short-horizon relative reversal conditioned on a positive longer-term stock trend. The final 7.5% trailing-activation specification produced 368 trades, a descriptive full-sample return of +70.5363%, an 11.2874% CAGR, and a profit factor of 1.2543. However, the 7.5% threshold was selected using development evidence, and the later historical segment was already inspected; that rerun is therefore confirmation rather than pristine out-of-sample parameterselection evidence. Over the harmonized 30 July 2025-10 September 2026 comparison window, Reversal5 returned +6.2405%, materially outperforming the two preceding project strategies but underperforming the raw-price, dividend-excluding MDY benchmark return of +15.6469%. The paper's principal contribution is thus both empirical and methodological: failed strategy generations remain visible, evidence classes are separated, and implementation assumptions are governed rather than retrospectively rewritten. The results are not survivor-bias-free because present-day S&P MidCap 400 constituents are projected backward, and they remain subject to raw-price corporate-action sensitivity, simplified trading costs, daily-bar path ambiguity, and portfolio concentration. Reversal5 is therefore the strongest historical specification in this governed strategy lineage, not evidence of a universal anomaly or demonstrated live alpha; genuinely prospective frozen signals are the critical next validation step.

detail.abstract: International space law prohibits national appropriation of outer space, yet states and operators increasingly secure durable advantages in orbit and on celestial bodies: priority in the radio-frequency and orbital registers of the International Telecommunication Union, jurisdiction over registered objects, statutory entitlements to extracted resources, and notified safety zones. The literature tends to examine each of these developments separately and to ask whether it breaches Article II of the Outer Space Treaty. This article asks a different question: what kind of authority is emerging in orbit, and why does it not reduce to territorial sovereignty? Using doctrinal and comparative legal analysis of treaties, national statutes, institutional instruments and the Bogotá Declaration of 1976, the article argues that orbital authority is being constructed as functional exclusivity, that is, operation-derived, time-limited and contestable control over objects and activities rather than title to place. It proposes that the compatibility of any such exclusivity with Article II can be assessed through three conditions: derivation from an identified operation, temporal limitation tied to that operation, and publicity coupled with a real possibility of contestation. The article identifies the strongest objection, that exclusivity achieved through use is precisely what Article II forbids, and specifies the evidence that would qualify the thesis. It draws institutional implications for the United Nations Working Group on space resource activities, the Artemis Accords signatories and the ITU. The analysis is doctrinal; it reports no empirical study.

detail.abstract: Political accountability often turns on how incumbents explain policy non-delivery. I develop a model in which incumbents can acquire verifiable evidence about constraints behind policy failure. Truthful evidence need not be diagnostic of competence because politicians select when to search for it. Better private information lets low-competence incumbents concentrate search in exonerating states, weakening electoral screening. In a tractable specification, resolving a fraction of uncertainty about exoneration removes the same fraction of the baseline selection gain without changing the low type's mean acquisition intensity. Fully resolving that uncertainty eliminates the additional gain relative to a no-evidence benchmark. Routine independent verification creates a related institutional tension: it can clarify why failure occurred while crowding out the screening information generated by differential discretionary search. The informativeness of evidence about competence depends on its content and the process that produces it.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between parameters of sleep quality and subjective academic productivity among high school students using statistical methods. Primary data was collected during the 2025-2026 academic year from a survey sample of 300 high school students (grades 9-11) in Russia and Kazakhstan. Statistical analysis included: quantification of the datasets, construction of bivariate scatter plots, application of ordinary least squares (OLS), linear and non-linear polynomial regression functions to model trendlines and reveal correlations. The coefficient of determination (R²) and Pearson correlation coefficients (r) were calculated for each model to evaluate the predictive power, statistical strength, and proportions of variance within the baseline datasets. Scientific works on sleep nature, quality and hygiene of sleep were studied in order to build the survey questionnaire, to interpret the results and to formulate the outcomes and recommendations. The results reveal a strong positive correlation between ability to focus and subjective productivity (r = 0.66), and a significant inverse relationship between chronic daytime somnolence and learning output (r =-0.51). While 85% of respondents acknowledge that sleep deprivation compromises their academic productivity, only 26% exhibit consistent compliance with sleep hygiene, exposing a critical behavioral gap. As practical outcome it was proposed to enhance educational efforts in order to increase awareness of importance and cognitive effects of sleep quality and of sleep hygiene among teenagers.

detail.abstract: Environmental sustainability has become an increasingly visible objective in European Union cultural policy and in the Creative Europe programme. Cultural organisations are expected to reduce environmental impacts, develop green capacities, and contribute to public awareness of climate change. At the same time, EU cultural policy affirms artistic freedom, cultural diversity, and the intrinsic value of culture. This article examines how these objectives are combined and where tensions remain. It presents a qualitative document analysis of the Creative Europe Regulation, the EU Work Plan for Culture 2023-2026, the Greening Creative Europe study and guidance architecture, the 2024 quality-assessment framework for green aspects in Creative Europe projects, and the 2025 Culture Compass for Europe. The analysis distinguishes sustainability in culture, sustainability through culture, and the institutional sustainability of culture. It finds that operational greening has become increasingly proceduralised through guidance on planning, energy, mobility, procurement, waste, capacity-building, and monitoring. By contrast, safeguards against the instrumental use of artistic content remain more general and are dispersed across cultural-rights and artistic-freedom commitments. The article argues that legitimate climate integration requires a dual-track governance approach: environmental conditions should primarily regulate organisational processes and the use of public resources, while decisions about artistic meaning should remain protected by artistic and curatorial autonomy. Proportionality, contextual differentiation, arm's-length assessment, and transparent review are identified as key safeguards.

detail.abstract: The growing importance of renewables in the global push towards low-carbon economies has led to rising investor interest in clean energy stocks; however, their performance remains sensitive to macroeconomic and financial conditions. This study aims to examine the dynamic short-run and long-run impacts of macroeconomic and financial stress factors on clean energy stock returns, proxied by the Clean Edge Green Energy Index. Monthly data covering the period from January 2008 to June 2025 are employed. An autoregressive distributed lag modeling framework is used to capture both short-run dynamics and long-run equilibrium relationships between clean energy stock returns, crude oil prices, exchange-rate, interest rate, and the volatility index. The results confirm the existence of a stable long-run relationship among the variables, as evidenced by the bounds testing approach. In the short run, increases in volatility, exchange-rate appreciation, and rising interest rates exert statistically significant negative effects on clean energy stock returns, while the adjustment toward long-run equilibrium is rapid, with approximately 74% of short-run deviations corrected within one month. In the long run, exchange-rate movements and interest rates continue to impose persistent and economically meaningful adverse effects, whereas crude oil price changes remain statistically insignificant. These findings underscore the importance of macro-financial conditions in shaping clean energy stock performance beyond commodity price dynamics and highlight the role of stable financial environments in supporting long-term investment in renewable energy markets.

detail.abstract: Hardly a decade passes without a financial crisis somewhere in the world. After each financial crisis, lessons were learnt and steps taken to prevent a repeat of a similar crisis. But the next crisis would arise from different causes. This paper posited that when a market collapsed, it was because the market was already fragile. The paper defined a collapse as a large deviation from the market's normal trajectory. And the Lyapunov exponent was shown to be a good way to measure a market's propensity to deviate after experiencing a small perturbation. The paper then examined several recent crises and found that each crisis was preceded by extreme market fragilities.

detail.abstract: Monetary policy surprises, measured using high-frequency asset price revisions around central bank announcements, are the leading tool for identifying the effects of unexpected monetary actions. Recent research shows, however, that they partly reflect the Federal Reserve's information about demand conditions. This paper shows that supply conditions also enter these surprises, as revealed by the comovement of interest rates and the exchange rate. When a supply shock hits and the Fed is expected to raise rates while tolerating some supply-driven inflation, surprises signal higher medium-term rates and dollar depreciation. Accounting for this component helps explain why previous estimates find little decline in prices after tighter forward guidance.

detail.abstract: Gender inequality in labour markets extends beyond participation to the type of employment women obtain, their sectoral allocation, and the earnings they receive. This study examines these dimensions in Assam using 2025 Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) public-use microdata covering 42,465 persons from 10,154 households. Weighted descriptive estimates are combined with logistic models of labour-force participation and regular salaried employment, a weighted log-earnings model, and a male-reference twofold Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition. Women’s usual-status labour-force participation rate is 42.75%, compared with 81.72% for men, with the gap being particularly pronounced in urban Assam. Women are disproportionately concentrated in self-employment and agriculture, while men are more represented in construction, trade, and transport. Among regular salaried/wage workers identified under the Current Weekly Status, women’s mean monthly earnings are ₹14,046 compared with ₹21,002 for men. Conditional on observed characteristics and district fixed effects, the female earnings association remains negative, although the gap is smaller in urban areas. The Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition shows that observed characteristics account for 14.39% of the mean log-earnings gap. Overall, gender inequality in Assam operates across participation, employment structure, sectoral allocation, and remuneration, highlighting the importance of expanding women’s access to suitable non-farm and regular employment while improving labour-force participation. Given the cross-sectional design, findings are interpreted as associational rather than causal.

detail.abstract: The EU AI Act requires publishers to label news text generated by AI, unless a person has thoroughly reviewed it and holds editorial responsibility for it. Publishers fear that such labels cost them credibility. We test this fear in a randomized experiment with 679 readers in five EU and two non-EU countries. All respondents read the same local news story on a realistic mobile news page, and only the byline changed: a journalist, a journalist "with" an AI assistant, or "created by AI". These versions match the cases in the Act: no label, a voluntary label for reviewed text, and a mandatory label for AI-generated text. The AI labels did not lower how credible, professional or well made readers found the article, and they did not reduce the share of readers who would read it to the end. We can rule out penalties larger than about 0.2 points on a 7-point scale. Many readers assumed that AI was involved anyway: even when only a journalist was named, 62% believed that AI had helped produce the article. Many also did not notice the label: two thirds could not recall how the author was shown. Still, the label changed what readers believed about how the article was made, but not how they rated it: 53% of those who saw "created by AI" thought the article was made mostly or entirely by AI, against 26% of those who saw only a journalist's name, yet both groups gave it similar ratings of credibility and professionalism. For routine news, the label required by the AI Act comes at no measurable cost to credibility.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether decisions generated by large language model (LLM) agents can be represented by simple equations in an agent-based model of bank balance-sheet management. In a monthly leader-follower model, a stylised, predominantly deposit-funded euro-area bank chooses deposit rates, lending margins and the composition of bond reinvestment, while depositors and borrowers respond to these decisions and to economic conditions. The initial balance sheet is calibrated to selected indicators from regulatory disclosures. We estimate equation-based approximations of LLM-generated decisions and evaluate them against simulations not used in estimation. Across ten out-of-sample bank-year simulations, the final specification reproduces annual return on equity (ROE) within 0.31 percentage points and meets all fit criteria in seven; none of the deposit-run scenarios meets all criteria. In eighteen simulations with a second LLM family, the ROE difference does not exceed 0.71 percentage points, but only six meet all criteria. Against a market-pricing rule, the original optimisation model, and regression and nearest-neighbour approximations estimated on the same data, the final specification meets all criteria in more years and tracks liquidity most closely in deposit-run years. Instructions without behavioural guidance show that withdrawal magnitudes and fixed-rate borrowers' price sensitivity depend materially on the instructions supplied; with customer equations estimated under neutral instructions, a two-month withdrawal episode no longer becomes self-sustaining. The results demonstrate a procedure for approximating and evaluating LLM-generated decisions within a defined simulation environment; they do not establish that these responses represent the behaviour of bank managers or customers. detail.abstract: Contemporary innovation increasingly unfolds across interconnected systems-technology, economy, institutions, society and environment. Nevertheless, the knowledge and governance arrangements used to guide innovation remain differentiated. This paper advances the concept of epistemic misalignment to characterise circumstances in which analytical and governance frameworks inadequately account for interdependencies consequential to innovation, adoption, and wider systemic effects. Epistemic misalignment is thereby distinguished from epistemic differentiation: specialised knowledge and reductionist analysis remain valuable, yet may cease to suffice once consequential relationships extend beyond analytical boundaries. A Layered-Relational Epistemic Framework (LREF) is proposed, comprising four recurrent, nonhierarchical epistemic configurations: localised empirical analysis; relational and socio-technical systems analysis; institutional agency and reflexive mediation; and global commons and long-term systemic integration. Yogācāra is treated as a structural philosophical heuristic, and bounded rationality as a cross-cutting mechanism. The configurations are conceptualised through differing epistemic resolutions and scopes, rather than a hierarchy of reality. The Cognitive Clutch is then introduced, defined as the capacity of epistemic or institutional system to expand, contract, or reconfigure their scope as consequential relationships shift. Failure to adapt is conceptualised as epistemic lock-in. The framework examines how institutional agency and incentives shape what is measured, prioritised, funded, protected, and adopted. Its application cases that range across translational medicine and health-system adoption, digital health transformation, and global health partnerships. These cases serve as the basis for formulating propositions intended for empirical testing. Implications are developed for technological forecasting and technology governance, guided by the overarching principle of epistemic integration without epistemic homogenisation.

detail.abstract: Monetary governance typically focuses on macroeconomic objectives such as price stability and employment to safeguard the public interest. However, monetary issuance itself involves a broad range of public interests. This paper develops a property rights framework for monetary issuance, distinguishing public governance powers, specific issuance rights, and the associated returns and responsibilities. Issuance rights entitle holders to trigger the creation of base money and obtain initial control over it; their allocation must be consistent with money demand and macroeconomic stability. The paper therefore proposes an Auctioned Issuance Rights (AIR) mechanism, using the market deposit rate as the minimum bid rate and allocating issuance rights through competition among banks within a public issuance ceiling. Actual issuance is jointly determined by public supply constraints and banks’ effective demand. This framework links rights and responsibilities in monetary issuance with market-based allocation and public governance, providing an institutional basis for coordinating money supply, macroeconomic stability, and the protection of the public’s property interests.

detail.abstract: Whether states with greater administrative resources produce higher-quality bridge inventory data is an open question with practical importance for data governance. This exploratory study builds two state-level reporting-quality indices from verified FHWA tables for 2015-2025: the number of count anomalies (changes in a state's reported bridge count that are large relative to its size) and the number of discontinuities in the shares of bridges classified good, fair and poor. It relates them to bridge inventory size and to state highway agency spending per bridge from FHWA's Highway Statistics (Table SF-4, 2020; 50 states). The two indices are essentially unrelated (Spearman ρ = 0.07, p = 0.65): states that show count anomalies are not those that show classification breaks. Spending on administration, research and planning per bridge is unrelated to either index (|ρ| ≤ 0.10; incidence rate ratios of 1.09 to 1.31 per standard deviation, all p > 0.4). Smaller inventories show more classification breaks (incidence rate ratio 0.54 per standard deviation of size, p = 0.03), consistent with size-scaled noise, and capital outlay per bridge is associated with more count anomalies (1.94, p = 0.02), which more plausibly reflects real construction activity than poorer reporting. With 15 unadjusted comparisons and a dispersion of 2 to 5 in the count models, none of these associations is robust to multiplicity or to dropping single states. The results do not support the inference that more administrative spending improves reporting, and they indicate that existing spending data are poor proxies for the quality-assurance capacity that matters.

detail.abstract: This study applies an exploratory text-mining workflow to the titles and bibliographic metadata of 82 recent publications concerning tourism and related issues in Thailand. The study aims to identify the dominant research themes, recurring concepts, and emerging areas of scholarly attention within the selected literature. Publication titles were tokenized, normalized, and systematically coded into nine thematic categories according to their dominant keywords and contextual meaning. Sustainable and community-based tourism emerged as the largest thematic cluster, accounting for 20.7% of the corpus, reflecting substantial scholarly attention to sustainability, local communities, environmental concerns, and tourism development. Economic forecasting and regional competitiveness formed the second-largest cluster at 19.5%, indicating continued interest in tourism-related economic performance, competitiveness, forecasting, and regional development. Politics and geopolitics and destination planning and heritage each represented 11.0% of the publications, demonstrating that tourism research in Thailand also intersects with political conditions, international relations, destination management, cultural resources, and heritage. A substantial proportion of the corpus was published in 2026 (72.0%), suggesting a strong concentration of recent scholarship and potentially rapid expansion of research activity. However, this temporal pattern should be interpreted cautiously because the corpus includes recently indexed publications, conference materials, book chapters, and other forms of scholarly output. Overall, the findings suggest that contemporary research on Thailand's tourism sector is increasingly organized around sustainability, community participation, economic development, regional competitiveness, destination planning, heritage, and changing political and environmental conditions. Because the analysis is restricted to titles and bibliographic metadata, the results provide an exploratory overview rather than a comprehensive assessment of the arguments, methodologies, or findings contained in the full publications.

title: Protest, Disorder and the Autonomy of Duties: A Criminological Framework for Assessing Public-Order Risk in Wartime Ukraine

detail.title: Protest, Disorder and the Autonomy of Duties: A Criminological Framework for Assessing Public-Order Risk in Wartime Ukraine
detail.abstract: This article examines the criminological dimensions of mass protest, disorder and political violence under conditions of war. Starting from the mass demonstrations that took place in France and other European states on 17 October 2026, it argues that mass protest as political expression, collective breaches of public order, and crime arising in the context of disorder are overlapping but non-identical phenomena. Recent European research on the 2023 French and 2024 British riots indicates that violence does not follow from grievance alone: it depends on institutional trust, policing tactics and perceived legitimacy. The article advances the concept of the autonomy of duties, the claim that a duty does not disappear together with the witness, and identifies a symmetrical error on the part of the state, which assumes that legality exists wherever its form is preserved (criminal non-law). It relies on the judgment of the European Court of Human Rights in Chernega and Others v. Ukraine (2019) to specify the state's positive obligation to protect peaceful assemblies from violence, including violence by non-state actors. Applied to Ukraine, the analysis yields a four-variable model of public-order risk, supplemented by a victimological dimension of wartime victimization, a set of observable indicators, and cautions regarding hostile hybrid interference. The article concludes that the task of the state is to prevent lawful forms of participation from losing their meaning while ensuring accountability for specific crimes.
