detail.abstract: This study examines how geopolitical risk, trade war uncertainty, and climate policy uncertainty, used here as a proxy for environmental shocks, relate to the volatility and cross market dependence of United States equities and crude oil, using monthly data from January 1990 to December 2024. We combine a Markov switching GARCH framework augmented with exogenous shock indices, a dynamic conditional correlation model, and a generalized forecast error variance decomposition, and we add a long short term memory network as a predictability check. The baseline specification identifies two weakly separated volatility states for the S&P 500 and a single state for oil. In the extended specification, the response of equity volatility to all three shocks is larger in the crisis state, with climate policy uncertainty carrying the largest coefficient, whereas the mean response of equity returns to trade war uncertainty changes from positive in the stable state to negative in the crisis state. The conditional correlation between equity and oil returns averages 0.058 and peaks at 0.231 around 2020, and equities are net transmitters of spillovers to oil, at 2.60 percentage points, with the rolling spillover index rising during the Global Financial Crisis and the pandemic. The neural network yields negative out of sample R squared values, which is consistent with weak return predictability. The findings support regime aware hedging and macroprudential monitoring, subject to the estimation caveats discussed in the paper.

detail.abstract: Climate-induced risk presents a systemic threat to the livelihood of smallholder farmers in developing countries, necessitating robust risk-mitigation frameworks. Based on data from one of the world's largest crop-insurance schemes, this study investigates the role of climate, compensation, and credit in influencing crop insurance adoption in India. We utilize a crosssectional framework to identify the role of potential drivers across 388 districts, using a fractional logit specification with state fixed effects. Results highlight the key role of recency bias, rather than long-term history or future projections, in driving the demand for insurance. While rainfall shows limited marginal impact, thermal stress emerges as a highly significant driver of demand. Besides risk perceptions, the farmers also appear to incorporate compensation in their crop insurance demand, and the role of credit remains critical. Lastly, premium subsidies push up insurance demand, whereas irrigation and crop diversification reduce it. This suggests that increasing insurance penetration requires a multipronged strategy, spearheaded by the realization of climate risk among farmers, and supported by adequate financial, operational and institutional measures.

title: Transmuted Discrete Weibull Distribution: Properties, Reliability Functions, Estimation, and Applications to Under- and Over-Dispersed Count Data

detail.title: Transmuted Discrete Weibull Distribution: Properties, Reliability Functions, Estimation, and Applications to Under- and Over-Dispersed Count Data
detail.abstract: A discrete quadratic rank transmutation construction, supported by mathematical property derivation, maximum likelihood estimation, simulation, and real-data information-criterion comparison, is used to demonstrate novelty in flexible count-data distribution modelling under under-dispersion and over-dispersion.\} Count outcomes often depart from Poisson equidispersion and exhibit asymmetric or elongated discrete shapes. This study formulates a three-parameter Transmuted Discrete Weibull (TDW) distribution by applying the discrete quadratic rank transmutation mechanism to the Discrete Weibull Type I baseline. The cumulative distribution function, probability mass function, PMF validity, raw-moment representation, moment-generating structure with its parameter-dependent existence domain, quantile function, Shannon and R\'enyi entropy representations, and selected reliability functions are developed. Maximum likelihood estimation is formulated and the reported Monte Carlo evidence is examined for under-dispersed and over-dispersed parameter settings. Parameter-behaviour simulations describe changes in location, dispersion, skewness, kurtosis, and reliability over selected grids of the transmutation, shape, and scale parameters. Applications use the reported under-dispersed National Health Insurance Scheme dataset and over-dispersed Article Publication dataset. In both real-data tables, TDW has the highest reported maximised log-likelihood and the lowest reported AIC, BIC, HQIC, and CAIC among the fitted alternatives. The results support TDW as a distributional option for the two examined dispersion settings, without extending the claim beyond the reported simulations and datasets.

detail.abstract: This research aims to analyze the effects of rainfall variability during the main agricultural season on maize cultivation. The methodology adopted focuses on collecting information from maize farmers. The sample size is 196 maize producers and 9 ATDA agents. Rainfall data from the main rainy season (1989-2019) extracted from Météo -Benin were used. The agricultural statistics used are primarily drawn from maize cultivation statistics for the study area published by the Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries (MAEP). The determination of the agro-climatic parameters of the main agricultural season was carried out using Instat + v3.030 software, based on frequency analysis. Determining the crop coefficient allowed us to assess the correlation between agro - climatic parameters and maize yield. On average, the main rainy season begins on April 12th and ends on July 24th, giving an average rainy season duration of 103 days (10 decades). This is compounded by dry spells at the beginning of the season. Faced with these changes, as perceived by farmers, adaptation measures based on local beliefs and knowledge are implemented to mitigate the damage.

detail.abstract: We study deterministic optimal execution strategies under the continuous time variant of the permanent/temporary impact cost framework of Almgren-Chriss [AC] with arrival price benchmark and the transient impact cost framework of Gatheral [G] with volume weighted average price benchmark. For Almgren-Chriss framework we assume non-linear permanent/temporary impact costs and characterize optimal strategies using variational methods, and distinguish full-horizon liquidation, early completion, and regimes of non-attainment. For Gatheral framework we assume linear transient impact cost with exponential or power-law decay kernel, deterministic polynomial market volume, constant volatility, and derive explicit solutions.

detail.abstract: This descriptive research analyzes the evolution of the NYICDX index between 2000 and 2024, using the Dollar Smile Theory (TSD) as a conceptual framework. Through an inferential approach, the different stages of the index are evaluated using descriptive statistics, normality tests, coefficient of variation, and the Friedman test. A new indicator, the Tilt Force Coefficient (CFI), is also introduced to deepen the analysis of trends. In order to understand the dynamics of the NYICDX and characterize its primary stages, the analysis is linked to the most relevant economic crises of the period. The results reveal that the Global Recession and Robust Economic Expansion stages present greater volatility, coinciding with the premise of the TSD on trend changes. The IFC confirms that the U.S. Growth Slowdown stage exhibits the most significant downward force. In contrast, the Foreign Economy Growth and Robust Economic Expansion stages show the most significant growth forces. The Friedman test exposes mirror results and indicates significant differences between some stages, such as Rest of the World Growth and Recession in the U.S. and the Growth of the Rest of the Economies that Outperform the U.S. However, no significant differences are found between other stages. In conclusion, this study provides a detailed characterization of the dynamics of the NYICDX over the last decades, mainly validating the postulates of the TSD and providing new evidence through the CFIx.

detail.abstract: Modern scientific research increasingly depends on expensive shared infrastructure that individual laboratories cannot independently purchase, maintain, and continuously upgrade. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) provides a substantive example because effective use depends not only on microscope time, but also on specimen preparation, trained personnel, computing, data management, image processing, modelling, validation, and continued technical support. The United States has responded through three National Cryo-EM Service Centres that provide nonprofit researchers with no-cost access to advanced instrumentation, technical assistance, and training. This study asks how governments can allocate access to expensive scientific infrastructure while preserving immediate research quality and expanding long-term scientific capability. It combines research on public science funding, research infrastructure, cumulative advantage, and the capability approach with comparative analysis of the National Center for CryoEM Access and Training (NCCAT), Stanford-SLAC Cryo-EM Center (S2C2), and Pacific Northwest Center for Cryo-EM (PNCC). The analysis distinguishes formal access, immediate output, capability formation, and capability diffusion. Official centre documents show that all three centres already combine scientific-merit review with mechanisms for training, inexperienced users, geographic reach, or applicants lacking local resources. Publicly reported outputs also show substantial scientific production, although differences in reporting practices prevent direct centre rankings or causal claims. The paper develops a portfolio framework that separates minimum scientific viability from subsequent allocation priority and makes trade-offs among scientific value, alternative access, training needs, mission relevance, and capability formation explicit.

detail.abstract: Women contribute to smallholder livestock production, but their roles and control over benefits vary across value-chain stages. This study examined women's participation, roles, labor contributions, decision-making, and control over rabbit-sale income in the smallholder rabbit value chain in Southern Philippines. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 203 women identified through referral and snowball sampling were conducted. Survey data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Cochran's Q test, and ordinal logistic regression. Women's participation was highest in rabbit production (87.7%), followed by marketing and sales (31.0%), input procurement (24.1%), aggregation and transport (17.7%), and processing (11.3%). Participation differed significantly across stages (Cochran's Q = 236.8, p < .001). Among respondents reporting sales, 33.8% shared decisions about income use, while 14.2% made most or all such decisions. Ordinal regression model revealed, participation in more value-chain stages, processing or marketing involvement, and group membership were associated with higher income-control categories. The findings show that women's substantial production labor does not necessarily correspond to equivalent control over income. Programs supporting rabbit enterprises should strengthen women's participation in processing and marketing, group membership, and income-related decision-making.

detail.abstract: We evaluate a blended ECMWF and GFS temperature model against Kalshi's daily high-and low-temperature contracts in 20 US cities, using 415,545 logged trading decisions, of which 407,816 are scored against settled outcomes. The market is the better unconditional forecaster: on decisions selected by forecast geometry alone, the model's Brier score exceeds the market's by +0.0042. On its own selections, however, the model beats the market. When it takes the underdog against a favourite, its picks are longshots (mean price 0.331) that earn a mid-price edge of +0.287 per contract (t = +4.95), against the favourite-longshot bias documented on Kalshi. We also document two problems that affect backtests of such a system. First, replaying decision logs under the current configuration silently measures later threshold changes: 78.3% of the rows the replay would trade were rejected at logging time only because of threshold and weight changes made afterwards, and only 5.3% reflect the configuration under which the decisions were made. Second, Kalshi changed its settlement source mid-sample, after which our station data reproduce 98.8% of its settlements; the headline conclusions are robust to settling on Kalshi's own results. Profitability after trading costs is not demonstrated.

detail.abstract: Renewable energy investors commit to high upfront capital costs while facing highly uncertain returns from wholesale electricity sales. I estimate the joint distribution of investors' risk aversion and costs from the investors' portfolio choices in Brazil's wind power purchase agreement auctions. To entice investors to install wind turbines costing $27.0 billion, the policymaker would spend $9.8 billion less in expectation by taking on all wholesale market risk rather than leaving it with investors. Counterfactuals examine the consequences of implementing risk sharing using alternative auction designs when the policymaker does not know investors' risk aversion and costs ex-ante.

detail.abstract: Pairs trading's canonical empirical result — Gatev, Goetzmann, and Rouwenhorst's (2006) finding that a mechanical rule trading the spread between historically co-moving U.S. equity pairs earns significant risk-adjusted excess returns — rests on an economic structure specific to equities: a common market factor driving broad co-movement, against which a residual, idiosyncratic spread between two similar stocks can plausibly mean-revert. This paper asks whether that logic transfers to floating G10 foreign-exchange cross-rates, which lack an analogous common-market-factor structure and instead co-move, if at all, through shared exposure to a common third currency (the USD leg both EURUSD and GBPUSD are quoted against). Using the walk-forward, cost-realistic, multiple-testing-aware protocol developed in Paper 1 of this series, we test a rolling-hedge-ratio, z-score-triggered spread-reversion rule across the three USDquote G10 major combinations (EURUSD-GBPUSD, EURUSD-AUDUSD, GBPUSD-AUDUSD) at five timeframes, and — resolving the open question this program's original scaffold left unaddressed — run a formal Engle and Granger (1987) two-step cointegration test on the actual price data across all C(4,2) = 6 pairwise combinations of the four G10 majors at all five timeframes (30 tests total). The cointegration screen finds essentially a null result: 4 of 30 tests are nominally significant at 5%, close to the ~1.5 expected by chance, all clustering just under the conventional threshold (p = 0.019–0.047) rather than showing the small p-values (p < 0.001) genuine cointegration would produce, and none surviving even a mild Bonferroni correction. Of the six tradeable combinations that produced enough trades to evaluate, only two rest on a nominally cointegrated relationship, and those two trade no better than the other four — if anything, the single worst-performing combination (EURUSD-GBPUSD H1, expectancy −0.0357R) is one of the nominally cointegrated ones. Trading results across all six combinations are uniformly, narrowly unprofitable: expectancy ranges from −0.0096R to −0.0357R, an order of magnitude closer to breakeven than the single-instrument directional strategies evaluated elsewhere in this series, no combination approaches conventional significance (permutation p-values 0.74–1.00), and the Deflated Sharpe Ratio is 0.00 throughout. The more economically interesting finding is risk-shaped rather than return-shaped: maximum drawdown across the six combinations ranges from 1.26% to 3.52% (median ~2.1%) — below the 5th percentile (5.16%) of maximum drawdowns across the 164 directional combinations evaluated in Papers 1 through 4 (median 16.4%). We characterize this low-volatility, near-zero-expectancy return stream quantitatively, discuss why its standalone risk-adjusted metrics (Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar) are nonetheless poor rather than attractive, and argue — citing standard portfolio-construction logic rather than this pair's own standalone performance — that a return stream of this shape can still carry genuine diversification value alongside directional strategies, a hypothesis this paper flags but does not itself test, reserving the formal cross-strategy correlation analysis for Paper 10.

title: Elasticity and Bargaining Power

detail.title: Elasticity and Bargaining Power

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There was no interest group involved in the development of this research.

detail.abstract: This paper identifies a new source of bargaining power: the elasticity of a bargainer's utility, defined as the marginal value of a concession compared to the worth of a deal over disagreement. I show that higher elasticity of a player's preferences delivers a more advantageous deal in the sequential bargaining Rubinstein-Ståhl model and in the Nash bargaining solution. Although lower risk-aversion has been long established as a source of bargaining power (Roth, 1985), I show that in a more general setting, elasticity is the real determinant: more risk-averse can lead to a better deal. In the sequential model, elasticity and patience are interchangeable: any advantage gained by a more patient player can be offset by a sufficiently elastic opponent. The two are strategic complements for a weak bargainer and substitutes for a strong one. Finally, I provide three sufficient determinants of higher elasticity and their economic interpretation.

detail.abstract: Governments are increasingly being asked to restrict, supervise or condition children’s access to artificial intelligence (AI), particularly in education. These responses are often framed as a choice between protecting children and preparing them for a digital future. This conceptual policy review argues that the choice is too narrow. The relevant governance question is how to distinguish uses that support learning, participation and accessibility from uses that introduce unacceptable risks or displace developmental activity. Drawing on international policy guidance, selected jurisdictional approaches and emerging research on generative AI in education, the paper examines five drivers of restriction: developmental uncertainty, child safety and rights, educational integrity, institutional readiness, and accountability for commercial systems. It compares restrictive and enabling approaches without treating any jurisdiction as definitive evidence of effectiveness. The paper’s original contribution is a Developmental Proportionality Model (DPM) for AI Governance, linking purpose, developmental context, risk, rights, implementation capacity and outcome monitoring to a graduated response: permit, supervise, limit or prohibit. The model extends Digital Childhood Governance as Layer 5 of Bakr Governance Theory by asking not merely whether a rule exists, but whether it protects children while preserving equitable opportunities to learn about and benefit from AI. Practical implications are offered for policymakers, school leaders, educators, families and developers. The paper concludes that defensible restrictions should be evidence-informed, proportionate, reviewable, child-centred and accompanied by meaningful alternatives.

detail.abstract: I study how the occupational content of firms' inventions is associated with recruiting and worker movement. I develop a two-stage large language model procedure to map 600,000 U.S. utility patents assigned to 2,451 listed firms into signed occupational exposure. The measure distinguishes complementary, augmenting and task-creating content from labor-reducing content, and separates development-production from product-application roles. I link the resulting firm-occupation measures to job postings, worker resumes and SEC business descriptions. With firm-occupation, firm-year and occupation-year effects, positive exposure is associated with higher postings, external hires and departures from occupation groups. Negative overall and application content is associated more consistently with lower hires and outflows than with lower postings. The joint patterns make outside entry and incumbent movement central to the interpretation: complementary work can involve worker replacement, and labor-saving adjustment can involve fewer hires, although gross counts also reflect occupational scale. Matching patent-implied downstream products to firms' disclosed businesses identifies 713 business-aligned firms and supplies a separate patent-level application filter. Applicationrelated labor associations remain visible under these commercial-relevance comparisons, with differences across sectors and estimation windows. Contemporaneous partial-IV diagnostics recover positive exposure gradients using peer invention activity under a separate set of identifying assumptions. The paper contributes a joint sign-and-role representation that connects the work of developing and applying inventions to labor activity at their inventors.

title: Bidirectional Cognitive Transfer in Human AI Systems: AI to Human Internalization, Cognitive Augmentation, Persistence, and Transfer

detail.title: Bidirectional Cognitive Transfer in Human AI Systems: AI to Human Internalization, Cognitive Augmentation, Persistence, and Transfer

The author used OpenAI’s ChatGPT to assist with conceptual development, drafting, revision, and formatting. The author reviewed and approved the final manuscript and accepts responsibility for its content, interpretations, and references.

detail.abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence can either reduce the amount of cognition performed by a human user or become a scaffold through which new cognitive capability develops. Existing research on cognitive offloading, AI-assisted learning, metacognition, human-AI co-adaptation, and hybrid intelligence increasingly shows that these outcomes should not be treated as equivalent. Some forms of AI use improve immediate performance while producing little evidence of durable unaided capability; other forms of interaction are associated with deeper processing, independent judgment, creativity, transfer, or reconstructive learning. This paper proposes Bidirectional Cognitive Transfer (BCT) as a framework for identifying one mechanism through which AI-assisted cognition may become durable human capability. 

AI-to-human cognitive transfer is defined here as the persistent incorporation into human cognition of a cognitive structure that originated in, or was materially transformed through interaction with, an artificial intelligence system, such that the structure remains independently available and can influence reasoning, language, judgment, problem framing, or behavior in materially novel contexts. Four criteria are proposed for identifying strong transfer: provenance, persistence, independent availability, and generalization. A taxonomy is developed encompassing semantic, procedural, framing, metacognitive, narrative, and prospective transfer, together with an assessment of spontaneous operability in the human when AI is absent. These criteria distinguish durable transfer from temporary assistance, retrieval, or dependence. 

The paper distinguishes cognitive substitution from cognitive augmentation while treating transfer as normatively neutral. Substitution delegates cognitive work without establishing durable independent human capability; augmentation increases independently deployable capability. Transfer can contribute to augmentation, but it can also preserve errors or harmful habits. The central hypothesis is that outcomes depend partly on how interaction is organized. Active evaluation, reconstruction, and independent reuse may promote durable capability, but this proposed relationship requires controlled testing.

detail.abstract: Conventional state-failure indices treat the country as the unit of analysis and sovereignty as a binary or a rank, obscuring the everyday experience of those who live under thinning authority. Building on the Trinity of Sovereignty Decay (TSD) theory, this paper proposes the Decoupling Sovereignty Index (DSI), a zone-level instrument designed to measure the gap between a state's formal legal authority and its effective, lived reach; the DSI was first outlined publicly in a syndicated column. Using documentary evidence from three zones-Port-au-Prince (Haiti), Catatumbo (Colombia), and Zamfara (Nigeria)-it identifies three configurations of decoupling: contested, competing, and negotiated sovereignty. Across these cases, the paper traces three disappearances-protection, legibility, and representation-through which individuals remain legally recognised but become institutionally invisible, a condition termed "becoming nobody." Rather than waiting for the language of collapse, the DSI enables earlier detection of decoupling by focusing on where, how, and to what degree sovereignty reaches the individual. The paper argues that the zone, not the state, is the more revealing unit for understanding contemporary sovereignty decay, and it sets out the conceptual anatomy that later operational work will formalise. The DSI's technical specification is documented separately.

detail.abstract:
Education initiatives led by the state in resource-constrained environments often prioritise physical inputs over the quality of material learnt. This creates an implementation gap: increased enrollment does not translate into basic literacy and numeracy. Drawing on the 'supply side' and 'demand side' explanations popularised in Poor Economics, along with institutional theory from Why Nations Fail, this paper investigates how grassroots community initiatives adopted by NGOs resolve these internal voids. 

Using primary observational research and qualitative interviews across four learning centres operated by the Kishalay Foundation in the Sundarbans, India, this study analyses how decentralised accountability works. Observations have revealed that the physical presence of parents in classrooms creates a lateral incentive for performance; this points to a scalable mechanism to counter teacher absenteeism, which frequently troubles marginalised regions. Additionally, locally recruited teachers represent a form of human capital whose community proximity builds trust and a more responsive approach to teaching. These primary reflections are supplemented by a comparative perspective, informed by volunteering in UK state schools, to consider how educational inequalities persist across different environments. Python-based analysis of attendance and learning records further explores the effectiveness of bottom-up learning initiatives.  

These findings suggest that community-driven models can respond to local needs in ways that centralised provision might struggle to achieve. This paper argues that such initiatives should complement, rather than replace, state education, with systematic tracking to help local successes influence wider institutional improvement in India.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Investment Management and Financial Innovations, volume 23, issue 1, 2026[10.21511/imfi.23(1).2026.31]

detail.abstract: The growing importance of renewables in the global push towards low-carbon economies has led to rising investor interest in clean energy stocks; however, their performance remains sensitive to macroeconomic and financial conditions. This study aims to examine the dynamic short-run and long-run impacts of macroeconomic and financial stress factors on clean energy stock returns, proxied by the Clean Edge Green Energy Index. Monthly data covering the period from January 2008 to June 2025 are employed. An autoregressive distributed lag modeling framework is used to capture both short-run dynamics and long-run equilibrium relationships between clean energy stock returns, crude oil prices, exchange-rate, interest rate, and the volatility index. The results confirm the existence of a stable long-run relationship among the variables, as evidenced by the bounds testing approach. In the short run, increases in volatility, exchange-rate appreciation, and rising interest rates exert statistically significant negative effects on clean energy stock returns, while the adjustment toward long-run equilibrium is rapid, with approximately 74% of short-run deviations corrected within one month. In the long run, exchange-rate movements and interest rates continue to impose persistent and economically meaningful adverse effects, whereas crude oil price changes remain statistically insignificant. These findings underscore the importance of macro-financial conditions in shaping clean energy stock performance beyond commodity price dynamics and highlight the role of stable financial environments in supporting long-term investment in renewable energy markets.

detail.abstract: The paper examined the validation of the environmental Kuznets curve hypothesis on the relationship between economic growth on environmental sustainability in African low-income economies, with a focus on the influence of financial system development and the speed of urbanization in the classification, using data from the World Development Indicator on panel ARDL-AMG techniques. The results of the unit root tests indicate that the variables are of mixed integration order, while the cross-sectional dependency test established the existence of cross-sectional dependence among the cross sections. The results of the cointegration test revealed the presence of a longrun relationship in the overall model, which further justifies the adoption of the panel second-generation unit root test, which also showed a consistent conclusion with the first generation. Following this mixed integration order and the treatment of cross-sectional dependence problem, the results of the adopted AMG technique adopted to analyze these relationships showed that environmental Kuznets curve was validated by the significant positive and negative values of GDPpc and GDPpc squared respectively suggesting an inverted U-shape nonlinear connection between economic growth and environmental sustainability, with negligible positive and negative contributions from urbanization and financial development respectively in lowincome Africa economies.

detail.title: Measurement Breaks in Bridge Condition Classifications:State-level Evidence from FHWA Good, Fair and Poor Counts, 2015-2025

detail.abstract: Bridge condition shares underpin federal performance measures, funding formulas and deterioration models, yet little is known about whether the classification of bridges as good, fair or poor is stable over time. This study assembles FHWA's published good, fair and poor bridge counts for 51 jurisdictions and eleven years (2015-2025), verified so that every year's columns sum exactly to FHWA's published national totals, and asks whether classification shows measurement breaks at documented schema dates and at the state level. Pooled step tests with state-specific trends find no common shift at the 2018 or 2022 dates that stands out from placebo dates. State-level discontinuities are common and heavy-tailed, however: 3.5% of state-year changes in the poor share, 5.7% in the good share and 7.3% in the fair share are more than four robust standard deviations from the cross-state norm, and the typical year-to-year noise in the good/fair shares is two to three times that in the poor share (0.84 and 0.71 versus 0.31 percentage points). The largest breaks are a 16.5-point jump in Georgia's share of good bridges in a single year (2019→2020) and a 13.4-point jump in California's (2015→2016). Breaks are most frequent in 2019-2020, the interval before the 31 December 2020 snapshot used by the Bridge Formula Program, and fewer after 2022. Bridges FHWA leaves unclassified fall from 50-110 to zero from 2019. Using the 2016 table, which I could not retrieve earlier, a transient count spike in Ohio (+1,180 bridges in 2016,-939 in 2017) is visible; excluding Ohio the earlier finding of no serial signature of record churn holds. Classification boundaries differ in stability, and the good/fair boundary needs closer screening than the poor boundary.

title: From Rubble to Regulation: Disaster-Risk Law and Tourism Recovery in North Lombok after the 2018 Earthquakes

detail.title: From Rubble to Regulation: Disaster-Risk Law and Tourism Recovery in North Lombok after the 2018 Earthquakes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No potential conflict between authors
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding received

detail.abstract: The 2018 earthquakes in Lombok, Indonesia, killed more than 560 people, displaced over 440,000 and struck hardest in North Lombok Regency, home to the Gili Islands and the gateway to Mount Rinjani, two of the province's main tourism assets. This paper examines how Indonesia's disaster-management law framed the recovery of tourism in North Lombok and what the case reveals about integrating tourism into disaster-risk governance. Using a qualitative case study based on secondary data, we analyse the national disaster-management law and its implementing regulation, the presidential instruction on post-earthquake rehabilitation and reconstruction, the tourism law, official disaster statistics, the international disaster-risk-reduction framework, and published research on Lombok's recovery. Drawing on regulatory impact analysis and the tourism disaster-management literature, we identify four governance gaps: tourism is treated as an economic sector to be restored rather than as a risk-bearing system to be governed; the recovery framework prioritised housing and public infrastructure, leaving tourism businesses and workers to recover through private and community means; tourist safety and evacuation obligations are dispersed across sectoral rules without a destination-level plan; and community and gendered dimensions of recovery are weakly reflected in formal instruments. The paper proposes a destination disaster-risk regulation framework that links regency disaster plans with tourism business licensing, tourist safety standards and community financial resilience. The findings are relevant to other hazard-exposed island destinations.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops an integrated framework linking predictive fundamental market timing, discounted cash-flow valuation, sector
rotation, market structure, and commercialization of financial knowledge. The research record spans approximately thirty years and
includes DCF valuation, CAN SLIM, free-cash-flow-to-enterprise-value, book-to-market, moving-average, momentum, and
volume-price approaches. The central empirical question is whether fundamental information identifies economically meaningful
differences among securities and whether technical confirmation adds incremental value.
The business proposition is that a documented version of this research architecture can become a differentiated financial-information
product. The commercial case therefore depends on four connected layers: market structure, research evidence, operating
economics, and enterprise valuation. The proposed $208 monthly subscription price and 30% affiliate commission are illustrative
planning assumptions rather than verified commercial terms.
The supplied empirical evidence includes a quarterly Russell 1000 FCF/EV-plus-dividend-growth exhibit reporting displayed
cumulative/total return of 4,124.43 versus 2,136.58 for the benchmark over the displayed 1995–2025 period, and a
low-book-to-market/MA10 exhibit reporting displayed total return of 5,720.69, mean return of 17.39%, Sharpe ratio of 0.65, and
Jensen alpha of 4.12. The sector extension supplies 30-year VPCI MA10 exhibits for ten sectors. These results are promising but
remain subject to source verification, robustness testing, and out-of-sample validation.

detail.abstract: Do stock returns follow a schedule, or does each day depend on the days before it? This paper treats these as two separate questions and tests both on the Nifty 500, using 4,955 daily returns from July 2006 to July 2026. We test seasonality, a pattern tied to position in a repeating cycle of trading days, across 25 cycle lengths using a generalised seasonality test that pools p-values to avoid false discoveries. Sequential dependence, where today's return depends on past returns, is tested with variance-ratio and Chow–Denning tests, with a runs test and an ARCH-LM test as supplementary checks. No seasonality is found at any cycle length, in the full sample or in any of the four five-year sub-periods. Sequential dependence is significant in 2006–16, consistent with momentum, but the variance-ratio tests no longer detect it in 2016–26, a change that coincides with the growth of algorithmic trading on the National Stock Exchange but cannot be attributed to it. Volatility clustering persists throughout and offers no directional signal. The results are consistent with weak-form efficiency in the later period but not the earlier one.

title: Explainability-driven False Positive Reduction in Intrusion Detection Systems using SHAP
affiliations: Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University, Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University, Nile University of Nigeria and Durban University of Technology

detail.title: Explainability-driven False Positive Reduction in Intrusion Detection Systems using SHAP
detail.abstract: This study presents an explainability-driven framework for reducing false positive rates (FPR) in deep learning-based intrusion detection systems (IDS). While deep learning has improved detection accuracy, the lack of model transparency and persistent high false positive rates remain critical challenges, causing alert fatigue and eroding trust in deployed systems. We proposed a deep neural network (DNN) train on UNSW-NB15 dataset, integrated with SHapley Additive ExPlanation (SHAP) to identify systematic patterns in misclassifications. Our key contribution is using SHAP insights to guide decision threshold optimization, transforming explainability from a purely interpretive tool into an active performance enhancement mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework reduces the false positive rate by 94.5% (from 0.0156 to 0.0009) with negligible accuracy loss (0.03%), achieving near-Pareto improvement in IDS performance. Statistical significance is confirmed by McNemar’s test (p < 0. 000001). This work establishes that explainable AI can serve a dual purpose: providing interpretability and actively improving IDS performance, leading to more reliable and trustworthy cybersecurity solution.

detail.abstract: I test whether large language models exhibit the disposition effect, the tendency to sell assets that have risen in value since purchase more readily than assets that have fallen. Four frontier models answered 7,200 prompts asking which of two positions to sell, where the positions differ in purchase price and, in some trials, slightly in recent returns, which a stated momentum rule makes decisive. Under a plain description of the account, all four models sell the losing position more often than the winning one, which is the reverse of the pattern documented for individual investors. A single sentence naming the disposition effect, however, leads three of the four models to sell winners more often than losers, and one of them often does so even when the momentum rule favors selling the loser. When the purchase price is omitted, every model follows the rule. The direction in which these models use the purchase price thus changes with the wording of the prompt.

title: Analysis of Energy Performance Benchmarks in Tea Industry using Multiple Predictor Variables

detail.title: Analysis of Energy Performance Benchmarks in Tea Industry using Multiple Predictor Variables

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: Energy performance benchmarks have emerged as vital guiding targets used by the governments and private sector to set energy efficiency performance goals for energy consuming facilities. For tea sector, in Kenya, the benchmarks set currently rely solely on production-based metrics. This benchmark uses only one model for all the facilities across the country, using a simple regression model, which uses production of tea as the only predictor variable of energy use. This model overlooks localized climatic variables like the temperature and relative humidity, limiting its effectiveness in accurately predicting energy consumption. It may also disadvantage some factories, for they are distributed in different climatic zones in the country. This work introduces the use of a benchmarking model that considers the effects of production, temperature and relative humidity, setting targets for facilities that only share the same climatic zone. The possible energy savings from the proposed model is then compared to those from the existing model. To achieve this, the study used one year data covering electricity consumption, firewood consumption, and tea production data from 69 tea factories in Kenya. Climate-related data was obtained from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Power (NASA Power) website. Two benchmarking approaches were developed and compared: a conventional production-based regression model (Model 1) and a climate-adjusted regression model incorporating production and air-enthalpy derived from temperature and relative humidity (Model 2). To test the applicability of Model 2 for energy benchmarking purposes, statistical significance of the predictor variables (enthalpy and production) was analysed using confidence interval of 95% (α=0.05). Next, the possible savings that could be achieved by setting targets using the two models were determined and compared. The statistical significance results indicated Production output was statistically significant in all zones for both electricity and firewood, having a p-value < 0.05. The enthalpy variable, however, revealed mixed results. In zones 1-4 the enthalpy variable was statistically significant in predicting electricity consumption and insignificant in predicting firewood consumption. Conversely, the variable was found to be a statistically significant predictor of firewood consumption in zones 4, 5 and 7. It failed the test for prediction of electricity in zones 5 and 7. For zone 6, the enthalpy variable failed the test for prediction of both energy sources. Comparison of the targets using the two models suggests differences of up to 6% in electricity savings and 26% difference in firewood savings. These results imply that the use of a single predictor regression model for benchmarking tools oversimplifies the conditions that affect energy consumption in tea processing facilities. Adoption of the improved model will lead to setting more pragmatic energy consumption targets and improvement of energy efficiency in the country.

title: Explainable Bidirectional LSTM with Bayesian Optimization for Stock Price Prediction on the Casablanca Stock Exchange: A SHAP and LIME Analysis

detail.abstract: The stock price prediction task in the relatively under-researched arena of emerging African financial markets is especially noteworthy. In that regard, the Casablanca Stock Exchange (CSE), the leading exchange in Morocco included within the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, provides an interesting context for the forecasting task, characterized by serial correlations of lagged prices exceeding 0.99, established behavioral biases on the part of investors, and distinct sectoral responses to geopolitical events from 2022 to 2024. This paper proposes an explainable Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) network with per-stock Bayesian hyperparameter optimization via Optuna, applied to next-day closing price prediction for five CSE stocks — Maroc Telecom (IAM), Bank of Africa (BOA), Banque Centrale Populaire (BCP), Auto Hall, and STR — over a ten-year period spanning May 2016 to May 2026. A geopolitical resilience stock selection criterion explicitly excludes commodity-sensitive sectors whose price dynamics require external sentiment modeling, thereby isolating the intrinsic predictive capacity of technically-driven sequential architectures. Fourteen technical indicators spanning trend, momentum, volatility, and volume dimensions constitute the feature space. The proposed Bi-LSTM achieves a mean R² of 0.9210 on normalized predictions and a mean MAPE of 2.97% on real MAD prices, outperforming the one-directional LSTM on four of five stocks. To our knowledge, this is the first study to apply combined SHAP and LIME explainability to individual stock price prediction on the CSE. According to SHAP attribution, SMA_20 is the main predictor variable (|SHAP| = 0.1404), whereas EMA_12 represents the key trend follower indicator (|SHAP| = 0.0679). This study adds value to the body of research in deep learning in the African emerging stock markets context, providing useful insights into the functioning of the Moroccan capital market environment.

detail.abstract: Human oversight is increasingly positioned as a central safeguard for artificial intelligence (AI), and recent literature has specified what makes oversight effective rather than nominal. Almost all of that work, together with classic human-factors research on automation, examines the competence, situation awareness and authority of the human who is currently interacting with the system. This paper adds a complementary, longitudinal and organisational question: after AI reallocates the developmental work through which expertise was historically acquired, how does an organisation reproduce the expert overseers it will need in future? It argues that AI governance can become temporally self-undermining. Organisations may retain enough expert stock to satisfy present oversight requirements while degrading the expertise flow needed to satisfy those same requirements later, so the governance deficit lags adoption and is missed by metrics focused only on current performance. The paper formalises a stock-and-flow account of oversight capacity in which AI both slows expertise generation and accelerates its depreciation, distinguishing maintenance risk to current experts from regeneration risk to future ones. Its central contribution is this temporal decoupling. It develops three linked ideas: developmental task value, which separates a task's contribution to expertise formation from its economic value; Expertise-in-the-Loop, defined as whether a work system can keep producing humans able to intervene meaningfully; and a Sustainable Human Expertise Framework mapped onto the stock-and-flow model. The central claim is that sustainable oversight requires not only a human in the loop but a renewable pipeline of human expertise.

detail.abstract: Bankruptcy systems differ in whether distressed firms are typically reorganized or liquidated. We study how these institutions shape firm growth, capital allocation, and aggregate productivity through firms' debt choices. Across countries, bankruptcy regimes favoring reorganization are associated with greater use of cash-flow-based debt. Where such debt is more prevalent, firms are larger on average and small firms grow faster relative to large firms. We develop a heterogeneous-firm general equilibrium model with endogenous debt composition, in which borrowing capacity depends on creditor recoveries in liquidation and reorganization. In a calibration to Europe, improving reorganization efficiency to match the U.S. mean cash-flow-based debt share raises aggregate output by 1.9 percent and TFP by 0.3 percent. The gains arise because cash-flow-based debt enables small firms with limited internal funds and productive firms with high going-concern value to finance growth beyond collateral while preserving the option to reorganize in distress. We show such effects are missing in standard asset-based debt models, when endogenous composition choice is muted, and during liquidation-based financial reforms.

detail.abstract: Institutional economics theory predicts that multinational enterprises operate in foreign countries with high institutional quality, which is known as the institutional profile effect. Nevertheless, the predictions of this theory seem to diverge from the international presence of certain multinational enterprises, raising questions about the broader applicability of the institutional profile effect. We posit that the phenomenon of learning by multinational enterprises offers an explanation for the occasional ineffectiveness of the institutional profile effect in specific contexts. Thus, we seek to answer the following research question: What types of learning reduce the probability of multinational enterprises operating in countries with high institutional quality? To address this question, we investigate the role of experiential and vicarious learning as boundary conditions for the institutional profile effect and compare their respective effects. Through our empirical analysis of a sample comprising 60 telecommunications multinational enterprises, 39 home countries and 145 host countries, we find that both experiential and vicarious learning have a negative moderating effect on the institutional profile effect. Furthermore, our findings indicate the existence of a cumulative effect resulting from the combination of different types of learning.

title: Exploiting Weight Clustering in Stochastic Computing CNN Accelerators

detail.title: Exploiting Weight Clustering in Stochastic Computing CNN Accelerators

detail.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) demand extensive computational resources, particularly within convolutional layers where a vast number of multiply-and-accumulate (MAC) operations dominate execution time and hardware cost. Stochastic computing (SC) has emerged as a compelling low-cost alternative to conventional binary arithmetic for CNN acceleration, offering substantially reduced hardware footprint and power consumption. However, SC-based accelerators continue to face challenges related to long processing times imposed by bit-stream operations. In this work, we propose a weight consolidation methodology that applies K-means clustering to the filter channel weights of convolutional layers, strategically reducing the number of distinct weight values. When deployed on differential SC-based architectures that store weight differences in sorted order, this consolidation dramatically increases the occurrence of zero-valued entries in the weight buffer. We further introduce a run-length encoding (RLE) scheme for the weight buffer that exploits this increased sparsity, yielding simultaneous reductions in both computation cycles and hardware area. Comprehensive evaluations on LeNet-5 (MNIST) and AlexNet (CIFAR-10) demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves speedups of up to 4.27× and 13.02× over state-of-the-art differential and non-differential architectures, respectively, on LeNet-5, with hardware area reductions of 18%–25%. On AlexNet, speedups of 1.32× and 1.67× are attained alongside area reductions of 23%–25%, all while preserving competitive classification accuracy. Energy is reduced by 41%–83% on LeNet-5 and by 34%–48% on AlexNet relative to the differential and non-differential baselines.

detail.abstract: American multinationals split their technical work across countries, building models at home and testing and running software abroad. I follow about 4,500 U.S. multinationals across the United States, India, the United Kingdom, Mexico and the Philippines, read each job posting into one of seven kinds of technical work, and interpret placements through a multidestination model of trade in tasks. Destinations do not rank tasks alike: India specializes in technical application and testing, the United Kingdom and the Philippines in business-facing application and governance, and the most doctoral-intensive jobs are 30 to 81 percent less likely to be placed abroad. Over a decade India gained every kind of work, yet its gap in model building never closed. Generative AI did not shift this division of labor; it changed hiring at home, where junior software-developer postings fell 19 percent relative to senior ones in 2023 and recovered by 2024.

detail.abstract: Student migration from Kerala to foreign countries has increased significantly in recent years due to educational aspirations, better career opportunities, and global exposure. This study examines the major factors influencing students' decisions to pursue higher education abroad. The research highlights the role of quality education, availability of advanced courses, employment prospects, scholarships, migration networks, and socioeconomic conditions in shaping migration decisions. Push factors such as limited educational opportunities, unemployment, and intense competition within the state are also considered. In addition, the study explores the influence of parental expectations, peer groups, and the growing trend of internationalization in education. The findings reveal that economic advancement and the desire for improved living standards are among the primary motivations for student migration. The study contributes to understanding the changing educational and migration patterns among Kerala students and provides insights for policymakers and educational institutions regarding international student mobility.

detail.abstract: We turn each 1-minute bar into a word built from four parts: its shape, its intensity, its range-to-volume balance and its relation to the previous bar. We then ask whether these words improve 15-minute volatility forecasts beyond the standard public intraday models: HAR, HAR with signed semivariances and jumps (HAR-RS-J), multiplicative component GARCH and Realized GARCH. We call the model with the words added HAR-W. The tests use QQQ, TSLA and US small caps on data the models never saw. They were registered in advance and judged against the best benchmark chosen after the fact, on two losses (MSE of log volatility and QLIKE). The words pass 10 of 12 tests. After volatility spikes they add 1.7 to 3.7 points of out-of-sample R² and cut QLIKE by 4% to 9%. At every minute the gain is smaller but consistent: 0.5 to 1.3 points and 1.6% to 4.2%. In every model confidence set, a model with the words survives. On daily bars the words add nothing beyond HAR, so the effect is an intraday phenomenon. Against Kronos, a pre-trained foundation model for candles, the words still add to the best benchmark after spikes on QQQ and TSLA; on small caps they add to it but miss the registered R² bar by a hair (4 of 6 tests pass). The spike bar and the three bars after it carry most of the gain (+0.74 R² points on the hold-out year). The words do not predict direction.

detail.abstract: Employers and economic development plans across Southside Virginia and northeastern North Carolina tell the same story about work: there are not enough workers, and the ones there are lack the credentials that new jobs require. This paper tests that account against federal data for 39 rural counties and independent cities. Adults in the region are far less likely than residents of their states to hold a bachelor's degree. The median locality's share is 18.6 percent, against 42.2 percent in Virginia and 35.7 percent in North Carolina, and in the median locality about 14 percent of adults 25 and older have not finished high school. Attainment tracks labor force participation closely (r = 0.66 for bachelor's attainment), so the region's low schooling is bound up with how many adults are working at all. Attainment tracks wages far less closely (r = 0.19). Localities with similar schooling pay very different weekly wages, and the paper argues that employer mix explains more of that variation than residents' education does, although industry data needed to test the claim are not yet available. The region's skills pipeline cannot be measured from adult attainment alone. Enrollment, completion, and transfer flows are the missing evidence, and the paper identifies them as the next data task. Recent vacancy reports point to real shortages in credentialed health care and corrections work, which suggests that the regional shortage is concentrated in occupations that require training many residents do not have. The paper closes with policy options the evidence supports and with the questions it leaves open.

detail.abstract: This paper examines when central bank asset operations affect equilibrium determinacy and fiscal transmission. In a New Keynesian model, we characterize when debt and tax adjustments absorb financing differences between government-bond purchases and central bank lending. Asset operations generally become relevant when policy restricts a public financial position. Under money financing, asset operations change determinacy conditions, and their fiscal multiplier ranking can reverse with spending persistence. The reversal reflects how endogenous money demand affects fiscal financing and the required inflation adjustment. Using fiscal feedback estimated from pre-crisis U.S. data, the calibrated model exhibits broad determinacy regions and substantial multiplier differences.

detail.abstract: Public debate about artificial intelligence often jumps from a technology label to a moral harm label—“displacement,” “bias,” “surveillance,” “inequality”—without stating what unit was observed, what contrast was estimated, or what statistic would falsify the claim. This working paper proposes a three-field estimand protocol for AI labor and scoring research: (i) population unit, (ii) contrast, and (iii) reportable statistic. We apply the protocol to four common claim families—task-exposure forecasts, employment and wage effects, hiring or credit error gaps, and workplace monitoring intensity—and show when each family can legitimately support a harm sentence and when it only supports a proxy. Drawing on labor economics, algorithmic fairness, privacy scholarship, and development writing, we treat integrative reviews of linked AI disadvantages as one background map among many sources rather than as a single data spine. The contribution is operational: a reusable checklist and worked examples that force authors and referees to name the outcome before they name the harm. No new survey or administrative dataset is collected here.

detail.abstract:
Entrepreneurship programs continue to reproduce growth-driven capitalist models, neglecting alternative socioeconomic models that could enable socially just and ecologically sustainable societies. Through a reflective case study on the establishment and development of a postgrowth enterprise-a Tool Library in Australia-by a then-student-founder, this chapter illustrates enablers and barriers across contemporary 'innovation' systems. 

The chapter argues for moving beyond a single growth-driven model of innovation and entrepreneurship to embrace multiple narratives and related business approaches. Entrepreneurship programs can represent important prefiguration and imagination infrastructures which can nourish ideas, values and possibilities that make alternative societal trajectories possible. By supporting more diverse innovation approaches, such post-growth models, educational and entrepreneurship programs could also foster socio-political innovation alongside technological change. Government and universities play an important role in fostering the broader social and economic conditions that shape and direct innovation. The chapter concludes by emphasising that the direction of innovation systems can become a barrier or a facilitator of imagination, hope and the capacity to build post-growth futures.

title: Remittances and Poverty in Afghanistan

detail.title: Remittances and Poverty in Afghanistan

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest.

detail.abstract:
This study provides micro-level evidence on how remittances shape household income and poverty outcomes in Afghanistan, offering insights for achieving Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 1: No Poverty. Remittances have demonstrated significant poverty reduction effects across countries (IFAD, 2025). Additionally, the study connects to SDG 10.c, which targets reducing remittance transaction costs to less than 3% (UNSD, 2022)—a pressing issue in Afghanistan, where informal channels like Hawala systems dominate due to banking sector collapse and international sanctions (Cook et al., 2024). 

The analysis draws on primary data collected through a household survey conducted in Balkh and Samangan provinces between September 2023 and January 2024, capturing insights from 553 households (300 in Balkh, 253 in Samangan) selected via convenience sampling. The study employed the Foster-Greer-Thorbecke (FGT) poverty measures to quantify poverty indices, supplemented by logistic regression analysis and robustness checks using probit and linear probability models. 

The data demonstrate that remittances constitute 46% of total household income in Balkh and 36% in Samangan. However, for households that receive remittances, this dependence becomes even more acute—nearly 67% of their total income derives from these transfers. The vast majority of remittance transfers (over 90%) are processed through the hawala system, cementing its position as the cornerstone of Afghanistan's financial infrastructure. Remittance receipt reduces a household's probability of falling below the poverty line by 25 percentage points—a protective effect 2.5 times stronger than the 10-percentage point reduction from salary income.

title: Greece's Sovereign Debt Crisis (2009-2018): Fiscal Imbalances, Restructuring Mechanisms, Macroeconomic Effects

detail.title: Greece's Sovereign Debt Crisis (2009-2018): Fiscal Imbalances, Restructuring Mechanisms, Macroeconomic Effects

detail.abstract: Greece's sovereign debt was notably one of the most important fiscal and financial crises in the history of the euro zone. The crisis emerged from a compound of inordinate public borrowing, repeatedly fiscal deficits, sluggish economic growth, and systemic inefficiencies in public management and labour markets. By 2009, public debt had surpassed €300 billion, corresponding to about 130% of GDP, while modifications to official deficit data revealed years of fiscal misrepresentation and acutely impaired investor confidence. As sovereign bond yields surged and access to capital markets eroded, Greece needed consecutive international rescue schemes financed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), European Union, European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF), and later, the European Stability Mechanism (ESM). The report uses analytical frameworks of sovereign-debt, which include debt-to-GDP ratios, fundamental balances, debt-drivers models, conditions of debt sustainability, net present value (NPV) analysis, as well as sovereign-bond spreads to assess the evolution of Greek debt level between 2009 and 2018. The analysis shows that Greece's debt distress stayed remarkably high through the period of crisis despite immense policy interventions. Public debt rose from nearly £300 billion in 2009 to more than €330 billion by 2018; in the same period, the debt-to-GDP leaped from 130% to nearly 181%, manifesting the joint impacts of falling output, recession, and sustained financing prerequisites. The defining occurrence of the crisis was notably the 2012 Private Sector Involvement (PSI) adjustment, which involved roughly €206 billion of sovereign bonds and sanctioned 53.5% nominal haircut on private investors, with evaluated NPV losses of approximately 75%. Despite the adjustment decreased the face value of debt, the benefits were partially neutralised by economic contraction and declining GDP. During the same period, Greece in piecemeal upgraded its fiscal level, shifting from deficits prior to 2013 to maintained primary surpluses beyond 2016. Debt negotiations centred progressively on maturity prolongations, concessional financing, including interest-rate cuts, resulting in a deep positive change in the ownership structure of Greece's debt, with authorised institutions becoming major creditors. The crisis had extensive effects for both Greece and the broader euro zone. Greece witnessed a cumulative GDP contraction surpassing 25%, unemployment went up to roughly 27% at its highest level, and the banking sector underwent acute losses that needed recapitalisation.

title: Foreign Policy Similarity Index: A Multidimensional Approach To Comparing Foreign Policy

detail.title: Foreign Policy Similarity Index: A Multidimensional Approach To Comparing Foreign Policy

detail.abstract: Foreign policy similarity is widely used in International Relations, yet the dominant measures rest on a single type of data, usually alliance portfolios (the S-score) or United Nations voting. A country pair can look highly similar on one indicator and very different on another, and no transparent, validated composite exists that combines several dimensions of foreign policy. This study constructs and tests a Foreign Policy Similarity Index (FPSI). The research question is: to what extent can a multidimensional index that combines diplomatic, security, economic, and multilateral indicators validly measure the similarity of foreign policy between pairs of countries? The unit of analysis is the country pair in a given year. The case set is eight countries (India, the United States, China, Russia, Japan, France, Brazil, and South Africa), giving 28 pairs, observed over 2000-2014 (420 pair-years). The full design has four dimensions, but the empirical analysis uses secondary data that could be obtained in machine-readable form: Alliance Treaty Obligations and Provisions (ATOP) defence pledges for the security dimension, and UN General Assembly voting records and Correlates of War (COW) intergovernmental organisation (IGO) membership for the multilateral dimension. The resulting two-dimension index (FPSI-core) ranks the United States-Japan, United States-France, and France-Japan pairs highest and the United States' pairs with China, Russia, India, and South Africa lowest. It correlates moderately to strongly with established portfolio measures (Spearman rho = 0.53 to 0.75), is not reducible to any single indicator (rho = 0.33 to 0.70), and separates pre-specified allied pairs from rival pairs (mean 0.74 vs 0.26). It is stable to dimension weights and aggregation rules but not to data-driven (principal-component) weights. UN voting alone ranks BRICS pairs as the most similar (mean agreement 0.77) while the composite does not, which shows why single-indicator measures can mislead. The diplomatic and economic dimensions remain untested and are the first priority for extending the index.

title: Axiomatic Characterization of the Owen Index without Efficiency

detail.abstract: We provide an axiomatic characterization of the Owen index on voting games with coalition structures without imposing efficiency. Our characterization uses the gain-loss property, the dummy player property, the component equal treatment property, the restricted equal treatment property, and the transfer axiom. We interpret efficiency as imposing global scaling and implicitly inducing competition among players across games. In our characterization, the dummy player property imposes only local scaling, while the gain-loss property explicitly captures the competition induced by efficiency. We also show that, unlike for general games, the gain-loss property and the dummy player property do not imply efficiency on voting games, both with and without coalition structures.

detail.abstract: Central banks open settlement accounts to payment firms, market infrastructures and, prospectively, stablecoin issuers, granting access, standing credit and interest separately. This paper asks how they allocate interest among non-bank holders. It shows that the fiscal incidence of remuneration depends on whether the balance would be held anyway: payment transfers income from the treasury mainly on required or inelastic balances, whereas payment on voluntary balances mainly shifts income from banks to holders and the central bank. A documentary comparison of 54 account classes at seven central banks and 27 decisions in Britain, the United States and the European Union finds that the four central banks with role-based rules pay private non-banks only on balances assigned to their operations or to systems they oversee, at or below the rate on bank reserves, and leave the backing of new private money unpaid or capped. Where one schedule covers all account holders, as in Switzerland and Australia, admission carries income. Predictions recorded in advance for four further central banks hold in Denmark and Norway and fail in Japan, which pays securities firms by statutory category; a conjecture on admission gates fails in New Zealand. Why central banks adopt one rule type remains open.

detail.title: Intellectual Property (IP) Data Analytics for Innovation, Research and Development, and Strategic Management

detail.abstract: Intellectual property (IP) data analytics has emerged as an important instrument for evidencebased decision-making in innovation, research and development (R&D), technology transfer, and strategic management. Intellectual property databases contain valuable information concerning patents, trademarks, industrial designs, copyright-related records, geographical indications, plant varieties, and other forms of legally protected knowledge. When systematically collected, classified, and analysed, this information can reveal emerging technological trends, identify research gaps, assess competitors' innovation strategies, support investment decisions, and improve the commercial exploitation of intellectual assets. This article examines the conceptual foundations, principal methods, practical applications, and strategic significance of IP data analytics, with particular reference to the Indian intellectual property framework and international developments. It discusses patent landscaping, bibliometric analysis, technology forecasting, citation analysis, competitive intelligence, portfolio valuation, freedom-to-operate assessment, and artificial intelligence-assisted analytics. The article also considers the limitations associated with incomplete datasets, publication delays, inconsistent classifications, legal uncertainty, algorithmic bias, and the difficulty of translating patent activity into actual innovation performance. It argues that IP data analytics should not be treated merely as a technical exercise in searching intellectual property databases, but as an integrated management process connecting legal information, scientific knowledge, market intelligence, and organisational strategy. The article concludes that the responsible use of IP analytics can strengthen research planning, reduce unnecessary expenditure, facilitate technology commercialisation, and improve the competitiveness of enterprises, universities, startups, and public research institutions.

title: From Actuarial Assessments to Claims Forecasts: A Calibrated Credibility Framework
affiliations: Monash University - Department of Econometrics & Business Statistics

detail.abstract: We develop the Assessment-Calibrated Generalised Link-Ratio model (AC-GLR), a Bayesian framework that learns how much weight to assign to an actuarial factor assessment relative to local claims experience. Historical assessments paired with subsequent claims development inform assessment calibration, while local claims update this calibration jointly with process dispersion and a continuous variance power governing claims-size weighting. The resulting credibility forecast makes the assessment and local-experience contributions explicit. Analytical factor integration and joint posterior averaging yield predictive distributions for positive cumulative claims at the next development age. We establish conditions for identifying assessment calibration and derive risk comparisons that distinguish weighting and borrowing gains from the costs of learning model parameters. As the local sample grows under the stated Gamma claims model and replicated exposure design, AC-GLR matches the leading-order integrated factor-estimation risk of a predictor using the true power, dispersion and calibration, even with a fixed historical calibration sample. Matched simulations show lower estimated mean prediction risk from incorporating the assessment in all twelve settings, while the benefit of learning power depends on its generating value. A retrospective claims application demonstrates how learned assessment reliability enters credibility contributions and predictive uncertainty. In the reported 40-record comparison, AC-GLR has lower mean squared ratio error and monetary root mean squared error than chain-ladder, local generalised link-ratio and equally informed gamma-gamma forecasts, and lower mean continuous ranked probability score than gamma-gamma.

detail.abstract: This paper asks who bears the cost of a tariff cut once the government must replace the revenue it loses. We treat that replacement as an equilibrium choice of the government among a lump-sum tax and taxes on formal consumption and formal labour income whose bases informality narrows, in a two-country New Keynesian model with imported inputs and hand-to-mouth households, calibrated to African microdata and solved member by member for the 49 members of the African Continental Free Trade Area with data. Our main ndings are: First, removing intra-African tariff raises welfare by 0.56% of consumption on population-weighted average, yet nine members lose. Second, under a uniform lump-sum replacement hand-to-mouth households lose in 23 members, which hold 40% of the population, and in the representative member they gain less than other households. Third, the replacement tax decides who gains, since a tax on formal labour income makes them gain in 46 of the 49 members. Fourth, the monetary regime shifts the gain between household types but barely changes its total. Finally, pairing each member with the rest of the continent overstates its gain.

title: AI-Enhanced Workforce Development Systems for Emerging U.S. Industries

detail.title: AI-Enhanced Workforce Development Systems for Emerging U.S. Industries

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am the sole author of this research paper and declare that I have no known financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the research or its conclusions.

detail.abstract: Background: Federal investment in semiconductors, clean energy, advanced manufacturing, and artificial intelligence is creating occupations faster than the workforce system can train people for them. Workforce boards, community colleges, and employers increasingly adopt AI tools for skills matching, pathway recommendation, and tutoring, yet little evidence compares such tools with counselor-led practice under realistic constraints: limited training seats, lagging labor-market data, noisy skill assessments, and hiring screens that may disadvantage some learners. Objective: To develop a conceptual framework for AI-enhanced workforce development, to state it as four testable propositions, and to examine them in a transparent, fully synthetic proof-of-concept. Methods: We synthesized literature (1997-2026) on skills and tasks, occupational mobility, training evaluations, AI at work, algorithmic fairness, and U.S. workforce policy, then built a fictional regional system in which 800 learners per cohort choose among 16 occupations in four emerging industries over AI-Enhanced Workforce Development Systems for Emerging U.S. Industries 2 ten quarters, with binding training seats, lagged vacancy data, a mid-horizon demand shock, and a hiringscreen penalty for a barrier group. Four planners were compared in 40 replicate worlds: counselor practice (A), a static demand-weighted recommender (B), a coordinated, capacity-aware planner with replanning (C), and a gradient-boosting placement model trained on historical cohorts (D), with fairness-aware orderings (+F). Seat-matched, ablation, capacity, sensitivity, misspecification, horizon, exploration, and counterfactual group-gap experiments followed (3,665 planner-world runs). Results: At baseline capacity the coordinated planner raised placement by 5.1 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval 2.8 to 7.5) and wage gain by 0.202 (0.184 to 0.222) over counselor practice, but used 58% more training seat-quarters. At matched seat use its placement was 1.6 to 3.3 points below counselors while its wage advantage persisted (+0.13 to +0.15); counselors who simply added training did worse. The placement advantage vanished at half capacity and when employers hired on a different shortfall rule, but held under noisier data and a longer horizon. The learned model raised wages (+0.157) but not placement (+1.5 points;-1.0 to +4.1), did not improve with more history or exploration, and was overconfident (mean predicted 0.60 versus observed 0.42). Simple demand estimates beat trend extrapolation. Optimizing planners widened the group wage gap (0.034 to 0.100), driven by group differences in skills, hiring screens, and adherence; a fairness-aware ordering raised the parity ratio by 0.035 to 0.051 at no measurable placement cost. Because demand, screens, and group barriers were built into the data-generating process, all results are illustrative only. Conclusions: AI value in workforce development here came from allocation and coordination, not prediction, and depended on capacity, data quality, and hiring rules. The proof-of-concept offers no evidence that any real system would perform as simulated; it supplies an evaluation protocol, falsifiable propositions, and the conditions under which expected gains erode.

title: Developing AI-Enabled Early Detection Systems for Supply Chain Failure to Strengthen U.S. Critical Infrastructure Security and National Resilience

detail.title: Developing AI-Enabled Early Detection Systems for Supply Chain Failure to Strengthen U.S. Critical Infrastructure Security and National Resilience

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am the sole author of this research paper and declare that I have no known financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the research or its conclusions.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this research because it did not involve human participants, patients, or the collection of personal or sensitive data.
