detail.abstract: Background:  Sex (biological attributes) and gender (sociocultural roles, identities and behaviours) are distinct, non-interchangeable variables that can influence drug exposure, efficacy and toxicity. The 2019 ESMO consensus recommends considering both in trial design and analysis, and the SAGER guidelines address their reporting; however, neither is binding. Previous studies assessed their integration in publications rather than prespecified protocol design. We assessed sex and gender integration in oncology trial protocols before and after this consensus.Methods: This retrospective cross-sectional study analysed 333 solid tumour trial protocols, excluding breast and reproductive-system tumours, activated at a tertiary cancer centre in 2015-2025. Indicators included mention outside reproductive contexts, terminological accuracy, ascertainment, sex- or gender-specific dosing, stratified randomisation and planned statistical analysis. Indicators were compared between periods, across phases, between first-in-human and other phase I protocols, and, for sex, according to inclusion of drugs with documented sex-related pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic variability.​Results: Sex was mentioned outside reproductive contexts in 212 protocols (63.7%) and gender in 134 (40.2%). Terminology was correct in 88/212 (41.5%) and 1/134 (0.7%), respectively. Only six protocols specified ascertainment; none justified terminology. Randomisation was stratified by sex in 8/256 randomised trials (3.1%), including 7/140 phase III trials (5.0%). One protocol specified sex-specific dosing; subgroup analyses were prespecified in 63 protocols (18.9%) for sex and 34 (10.2%) for gender; none prespecified sex-/gender-related differences as an endpoint. No integration indicator differed significantly between periods after Benjamini-Hochberg correction.Conclusion: Sex and gender were frequently mentioned but rarely translated into methodological integration, without significant improvement after the consensus. Policy Summary: Non-binding recommendations have not translated into trial design. Protocol templates and review by research ethics committees and regulatory authorities should require clear definitions of sex and gender, ascertainment methods and justification of the presence/absence of planned analyses by sex and, where relevant, gender, as expected for other baseline characteristics.

title: Governing the Unmeasurable: Rules, Discretion, and the Actuarial Convention

detail.abstract: Actuaries certify numbers that no measurement technology delivers: a one-in-two-hundred annual standard no claims record could support, premium risk factors held constant across the underwriting cycle, and, as machine-learned components enter pricing and reserving, outputs whose basis the certifier cannot reconstruct. This paper treats such numbers as conventions in Keynes's sense and asks how they should be governed. A convention is formalized as a published mapping from a verifiable signal to a binding standard, and rule, discretion and the frozen parameter are compared on time consistency, resistance to capture and auditability. Discretionary revision relaxes the standard where the signal indicates most risk and leaves no record, because the number is the record. Rules trade the frequency of capture for its persistence, so a bound on the mapping's output limits distortion, and the bound's optimal width is where the stop-loss premium of the unbounded adjustment equals the capture-weighted bound. Applied to Solvency II, the framework sorts the symmetric adjustment, the 99.5 per cent standard and the premium risk factors into three cells; EIOPA's daily series since 1991 shows the ±10 corridor binding at three published month-ends in a decade, and widths of 10, 13 and 17 points imply revision-survival probabilities of 0.87, 0.94 and 0.98. A closing section applies the criteria to certifying model outputs that cannot be validated.

detail.abstract: I study the effects of racial classification on economic outcomes and racial inequality using data from 37 million newly digitized World War II draft registration cards. I estimate the rule that maps a man's physical and contextual attributes—complexion, eye and hair color, height, weight and name—to the probability of being classified as Black, and find that it required different amounts of evidence across counties and commuting zones in the United States. A man with the same description carried odds of being classified as Black 5.7 times higher in a locality one standard deviation readier to record a man as Black, and 3.8 times higher in the South than in the rest of the country. Conditional on a man's description, the locality's evidence threshold serves as an instrument for his race category. Men beyond the reach of every threshold, whose category is the same everywhere, identify the threshold's direct effect on employment, and the excess response of the men near the threshold is the effect of the category itself. Being classified as Black lowered employment a decade later by 4.55 percentage points, three-fifths of the Black–White employment gap among men with the same description. The threshold of each locality also decided the racial group membership of men on the margin, and I show that the recorded Black–White schooling gap understates the gap that one national threshold applied in all localities would produce, holding the population and its outcomes fixed. In large non-Southern cities the understatement reaches 3 to 12 percent. Finally, I provide preliminary results from a registrar design that exploits men's assignment to registrars within a local board on a registration day.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how exposure to communal violence shapes long-run educational attainment in India. I focus on the 2002 Gujarat violence, widely considered one of the most severe episodes of communal conflict in post-independence India. Beginning on February 28, three days of intense violence resulted in large-scale deaths and displacement, followed by further outbreaks of violence in the following months. To estimate the causal effects of this conflict, I use data from the 2019-21 National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5) and a difference-indifferences design that exploits variation in exposure across regions and birth cohorts. I compare individuals who were of school-going age during the violence to individuals who were old enough to have already completed their schooling, in Gujarat, relative to the rest of India. I find that Grade 12 completion declined by 6 percentage points (23%), and total years of schooling fell by 0.5 years (7%). Consistent with the violence disproportionately targeting women and children, I find that the declines were more concentrated among the youngest cohorts at the time of violence. Moreover, heterogeneity analyses show that the education losses were larger among females than among males, with Muslim females experiencing the largest declines. In India, where school completion rates are relatively low, these findings highlight how communal conflict can impose persistent educational costs and exacerbate existing inequalities.

title: The Compendium of Unrecognised States: A Taxonomy of Attempted and Contested Self-Governance, 1492 to the Present

detail.title: The Compendium of Unrecognised States: A Taxonomy of Attempted and Contested Self-Governance, 1492 to the Present

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founding director of the Startup States Society (Geneva).
declarations.funderStatement: The author has self-funded 100% of this.

detail.abstract:
The Compendium of Unrecognised States is a reference work on attempted and contested self-governance from 1492 to the present. It records 628 cases in which a community, government or individual presented itself as a country, or as the seed of one, and the surrounding international order declined to acknowledge the claim in full. The entries cover unilateral secessions and breakaway governments in the Americas, Africa, Asia, the Middle East, the Pacific, Europe and Eurasia; settler republics, de facto states and client states; internationally administered zones and free cities; colonisation settlements and chartered dominions; filibuster republics, self-proclaimed monarchs and maritime outlaw polities; offshore ventures and micronations; and the network states, seasteading ventures and digital-nation programmes of the twenty-first century. A small number of earlier comparative cases are admitted as flagged exceptions.

The work is arranged in twelve parts. Parts I to XI hold the entries, grouped by region and by kind of case. Each entry is written from the sources named in its notes, with primary documents, court and tribunal records, archival collections, newspapers of record and peer-reviewed scholarship preferred. Where sources disagree, the entry gives both accounts with attribution; where a case rests on a single source or on a project's own statements, the notes say so. Part XII contains no entries. It reads the record as a whole and asks which claims reached recognition by other states or membership of the United Nations, by which routes, and what separates them from those that did not, through eight matched pairs, a comparison of Montenegro and Kosovo, and lessons for founders.

Appendices provide a register of limited and contested recognition, a glossary, a geographical index of entries and a guide to directories and resources, followed by a select bibliography and indexes of persons and entries. Four atlas plates locate the entries. The interactive Atlas of Unrecognised States, a component of this work, is published at https://startupstates.swiss/unrecognised/.

The word "unrecognised" is used in a broad sense, as shorthand for the want of general, complete or lasting recognition, and carries no judgement on the merits of any claim. Published by the Startup States Society, Geneva.

detail.abstract: We study how political beliefs shape firms' price-setting. Linking retail scanner data to convenience store managers' voter registrations, we find that politically misaligned managers raise prices more in response to inflation for identical products sold on the same street; relative to Democrats, Republican managers' pass-through rises 21% under Biden versus Trump. This mirrors partisan divergence in inflation expectations and intensifies after pessimistic local inflation news. Market forces discipline the pricing gap: it concentrates in less competitive markets, is stronger for less elastic products, and fades as customers substitute and revenues fall. Overall, political beliefs meaningfully shape prices despite market discipline.

detail.abstract: Standard analyses of retirement adequacy focus on financial metrics such as contribution rates and replacement ratios, while climate scenario studies typically emphasize broad macroeconomic outcomes. Neither approach, however, directly addresses what matters most to individuals: the quality of life in retirement. Retirement security under climate change is inherently multidimensional, shaped not only by financial wealth but also by health systems, infrastructure, environmental conditions, and social resilience. We develop an integrated framework that combines qualitative climate scenario narratives with quantitative macro-financial modelling to assess retirement outcomes in the United Kingdom through 2050. We construct three internally consistent SSP-RCP-based scenarios and translate them into indicators of retirees' lived experience alongside climate-damage-adjusted macroeconomic trajectories, which inform long-term asset return assumptions and retirement income projections. The results show that financial adequacy metrics alone can misrepresent retirement resilience. Relatively small differences in expected investment returns can coexist with large divergences in longevity, health, service reliability, and everyday living conditions. By linking narratives with numbers, the framework clarifies how socioeconomic environments and financial outcomes interact, providing a more decision-relevant assessment of climate-related retirement risks for pension funds, long-horizon investors, and policymakers.

title: Recognition at the Margins: States with Limited Recognition, Diplomatic Reversal and the Practice of International Recognition, 1945–2026

detail.title: Recognition at the Margins: States with Limited Recognition, Diplomatic Reversal and the Practice of International Recognition, 1945–2026

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founding director of the Startup States Society (Geneva).
declarations.funderStatement: The author has self-funded 100% of this.

detail.abstract:
Recognition at the Margins examines the recognition by members of the United Nations of eight entities that stand outside the Organization: the State of Palestine, the Republic of Kosovo, the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, the Republic of China (Taiwan), Abkhazia, South Ossetia, the Republic of Somaliland and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus. It asks which members recognise which entities, how that pattern has changed since 1945, and what the pattern reveals about the conditions under which recognition is granted, held and lost.

The study rests on a dataset built for it and published with it: a matrix of the 193 members of the United Nations against the eight entities, each cell coded from documented events and graded by the quality of its evidence, together with an event register of more than five hundred dated acts, registers of comparative, historical and excluded cases, a source ledger and a codebook. Every count in the text can be reconstructed from the dataset. All statements of current status speak as of 10 October 2026.

Five findings emerge. Entities gain recognition in waves tied to moments and lose it singly, through negotiated reversals. Portfolios of recognition are small because the coalitions that recognise each entity are separate. A determined opposing state can reverse recognition at scale, as the Hallstein Doctrine and the campaigns of Beijing, Belgrade and Rabat show. Recognition is not membership: the gate to the United Nations is article 4(2) of the Charter, and the permanent members of the Security Council hold its keys. For a new entrant, recognition follows the consent of a parent state and stalls, fragments or reverses in its absence, while the territorial alternatives of unclaimed land, Antarctica, the high seas and outer space are closed by treaty and by the law of territory.

Further chapters treat presence without membership, recognitions that ended, non-territorial claims, and the claims of the Free Republic of Liberland and the Free Republic of Verdis. The interactive Atlas of Recognition, a component of this work, sets each recognition and its dates on a map at https://startupstates.swiss/recognition/. The book, its dataset and the Atlas are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence. detail.abstract: This study assesses the association between finance ministers' educational attainment and economic growth using a hand-collected dataset covering 437 unique finance ministers across 33 countries over the period 1960-2015. A finance minister holding a PhD in economics is used as a proxy for advanced economic training, and its association with GDP per capita growth is examined across advanced and emerging and developing economies. Although finance ministers with PhDs in economics are more prevalent in emergin g and developing economies, a statistically significant positive average association is identified only in advanced economies, where GDP per capita growth is estimated to be approximately 0.8-1.5 percentage points higher than in countries whose finance min isters hold a bachelor's or master's degree or a PhD in another discipline. In emerging and developing economies, no statistically significant average association is observed. However, interaction and marginaleffects analyses reveal that this average result masks substantial institutional heterogeneity. A positive association is present in relatively low-corruption environments but gradually disappears as political corruption increases. The findings remain robust across alternative model specifications, quantile regressions, and placebo tests.

title: AI Chaos: When Intelligence becomes Ubiquitous but Governance does not

detail.title: AI Chaos: When Intelligence becomes Ubiquitous but Governance does not

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal relationships that could have influenced, or be perceived to have influenced, the work presented in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The research and manuscript were prepared independently.

detail.abstract:
An AI assistant that drafts a wrong answer produces an error. A network of AI agents that acts on that answer, passes it to another agent and acts again produces a consequence that no one decided. This conceptual paper examines that problem. It belongs to The Symbiotic Intelligence Programme but is written to stand alone.

Artificial intelligence is moving from tools that people use to agents that act, and to agents that act on one another. In 2025, 88% of surveyed organisations used AI in at least one business function, and 62% of organisations in McKinsey's survey were at least experimenting with AI agents, although only 23% were scaling them. Governance has not moved with this change. The EU AI Act, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001 govern individual systems and the organisations that deploy them, and they address dependencies along the value chain. None of them specifies a declaration of validity conditions with each output, checked by the receiving agent at the point of use and revalidated when a condition changes. Risk now travels along the handoffs between systems and builds up between validation and action. Agent-to-agent protocols, learning in operation, shrinking decision time and deployment at scale will widen this gap. The stages of diffusion accumulate, and a simple structural model shows why the risk compounds: once each output is used by more than one agent and the checks on receipt stop too few invalid outputs, exposure grows exponentially with the depth of the chain. Governance also stands outside the process and acts at intervals, while risk moves inside it continuously; sandboxes, risk tiers and soft law narrow the gap in time but do not change that position.

The paper calls the resulting systemic instability AI Chaos and traces it to a family of related failures. Epistemic Stripping removes the conditions of validity from an output as it travels. AI Laziness, introduced here as the machine form of epistemic inertia, is the behaviour of an agent that keeps acting under conditions that have expired because it does not re-examine its conditions or its ecosystem; a four-part diagnostic rule makes it testable. Entrainment Failure leaves the assumptions built on a changed assumption unexamined. A hidden learned pattern, which updating the declared conditions does not reach, lets optimisation intensify on an old objective while results under the new conditions decline. Rigidity is not confined to machines, so the paper proposes mutual correction, in which human and machine notify each other of rigidity while final authority stays with a human. A Five-Factor Lens (capability, autonomy, connectivity, delegated authority and consequence) shows why an agent's embedding can matter more than its capability. Small failures of validity can be amplified, and made unpredictable, at machine speed: a governance analogue of the butterfly effect, not mathematical chaos. Impact is traced across five layers, with effects moving in both directions.

The solution rests on Unified Symbiotic Intelligence Science (USIS). Its Law of Epistemic Conditional Validity holds that every output is valid only within a declared domain D_M = (A, M, S, E) of assumptions, methods, scope and environment, a minimum open to further dimensions. From the USIS papers on Epistemic Conditionality and Recursive Scientific Domain Addressing the paper derives a nine-step guideline. Each agent declares its validity address and carries it with every output; validity is judged before value at two gates; the gates reopen when conditions change, and the reopening reaches every dependent assumption; and the learned pattern is checked through a Standing Pattern Review. When an output enters a consequential decision, its address persists in a Decision Object. Human arbitration is graded by reversibility and consequence so that it can work at machine speed, and the guideline is placed in the SDOF spiral of Decision-Making Driven Design, where the VIVO validity gate controls each transition.

The contribution is the systematic treatment of validity conditions as information that must be declared, transmitted, inherited and re-examined as outputs move between agents. The paper states eight testable propositions, specifies a factorial test of an AI Chaos Threshold and outlines six research streams. It reports no empirical test.

detail.abstract: Contemporary on-chain artificial intelligence (AI) encounters an intractable Von Neumann memory and latency wall. Storing static floatingpoint neural weight matrices inside Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) storage costs millions of gas, rendering direct on-chain inference impossible. While Zero-Knowledge Machine Learning (ZK-ML) offloads matrix tensor multiplications to offchain provers, it introduces fatal constraints: 10 to 300 seconds of SNARK proving latency and 250,000 to 500,000 gas per proof verification. Because decentralized finance (DeFi) exploits-such as uncollateralized flash-loan attacks, predatory sandwich MEV, and toxic loss-versus-rebalancing (LVR) flow-occur atomically inside a single block, ZK-ML oracles cannot react in time. Here, we present Werracle, a production-grade, zero-storage on-chain AI decision oracle fitting inside a single 32-byte EVM storage slot (bytes32). Leveraging foundational procedural Mandelbrot escape dynamics (z n+1 = z 2 n + c) established by Daglı et al. (arXiv:2609.25498), Werracle derives continuous non-linear decision hyperplanes from a 24byte coordinate triplet Θ = (c x , c y , zoom). Implemented in pure Solidity bytecode using fixed-point Q16.16 arithmetic (WerrMath.sol), Werracle evaluates a 16-point Pareto micro-grid in only 21,438 gas (under $0.0005 on Layer-2 rollups like Base and Arbitrum) with sub-millisecond execution latency. We demonstrate real-world DeFi efficacy via WerracleFeeHook.sol, a Uniswap v4 dynamic swap fee governor that measures orderbook turbulence on-the-fly and atomically adjusts liquidity provider fees between 0.05% and 0.50%. The protocol is formally verified against a 1,000-test cryptographically sealed deterministic verification suite (100.0% pass rate) with telemetry permanently disabled, operating live on a dedicated EVM devnet sandbox (Chain ID 4242).

detail.abstract: Delivery platforms use estimated delivery times to manage customer expectations, but the behavioral and operational consequences of varying these estimates after checkout remain unclear. We examine how post-checkout delivery estimates influence purchasing behavior, customer communication, and fulfillment performance using a customer-level randomized field experiment on Careem’s grocery delivery platform. Customers were assigned to either a fixed 10-minute estimate or an order-dependent estimate of 10, 15, or 20 minutes, while fulfillment policies and courier assignment remained unchanged. Difference-in-differences estimates from a matched sample of 208,079 transactions involving 15,810 customers indicate no statistically significant changes in order value, basket size, or time to the next order. Longer displayed estimates are associated with a 1.16-minute reduction in realized delivery time and an increase in delay-related customer calls within the displayed delivery window. Because couriers did not observe the treatment, this pattern is consistent with an indirect behavioral channel through which customer inquiries influence delivery execution. These findings suggest that post-checkout delivery information has operational implications beyond short-term purchasing responses, with customer communication providing a potential link between information design and service performance. The study contributes to research on delivery-time communication and behavioral operations by examining how information presented after purchase relates to customer intervention during fulfillment.

title: OptScientist: Automated Discovery of Optimization Laws
affiliations: Xiamen University - School of Economics, Eberhard-Karls University Tübingen and Princeton University

detail.title: OptScientist: Automated Discovery of Optimization Laws

declarations.funderStatement: The research was conceptualized and initiated by Ma ZhenYao, with the primary computational resources provided by Yue Liang.

detail.abstract: Many scientific phenomena are best understood as outcomes of underlying optimization problems, yet automated scientific discovery has largely focused on recovering equations that describe observed input–output patterns. We introduce OptScientist, a novel automated framework for discovering compact symbolic optimization laws directly from data. OptScientist comprises (i) a model that infers symbolic optimization problems by first learning to represent data as an optimization problem and then extracting its symbolic form, and (ii) an LLM agentic system embedding the model in a discovery process that integrates theoretical priors from scientific literature, discovers candidate laws, abstracts their underlying mechanisms, and suggests new data to collect. We first evaluate OptScientist on OptFeynman, a novel benchmark of 99 physics-derived optimization problems, where OptScientist recovers ground-truth laws for over 80% of the problems and remains robust to noisy contextual information, while substantially outperforming machine-learning, symbolic, and LLM-based model-discovery baselines. On human risky choice and central-bank monetary policy, OptScientist discovers compact symbolic optimization laws that achieve held-out predictive performance competitive with leading baselines, while using few parameters and substantially fewer tokens than LLM baselines. Overall, OptScientist extends automated scientific discovery to uncovering optimization laws that generate observed phenomena, enabling automated theory building across the physical, biological, behavioral, and social sciences.

title: Who Acted? Attribution as a Control Point for Distributed Applied AI

detail.title: Who Acted? Attribution as a Control Point for Distributed Applied AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that could have influenced, or be perceived to have influenced, this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is an analytic paper. It involves no human participants, personal data, or experiments on live systems, so ethics approval and consent were not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific funding from any public, commercial, or not-for-profit organization. It was self-funded.

detail.abstract: Oversight of advanced AI has concentrated on developers. A small number of developers host their models, log usage, apply safeguards, and can revoke access, and developers of open-weight models set safeguards once at release. This paper examines why that arrangement is not enough. Safeguards can fail at every tier: hosted models can be bypassed, fine-tuned, or stolen, and open-weight models can be modified by whoever later holds them, so any sufficiently capable model may end up operating under reduced safeguards. Capability is also spreading to smaller models that run on local hardware and devices, which makes the timing relevant for technical and policy readers now. Many of the systems society depends on, including vehicles, radio and satellite links, rail, social platforms, and logistics networks, rely on authentication and attribution practices designed for a world without inexpensive autonomous actors. We argue that risk depends less on the model, its size, or its developer than on three factors: the capability and access of the actor, the weakness of the target in authentication, integrity, or availability, and the time defenders need to detect, attribute, and respond. We define two failure modes. Loss of control is a case in which an agent acts outside the intent or authority of its principal and cannot be halted in time. Targeted remote control is a case in which an adversary takes over a legitimate system or agent, or deploys its own agents, against a target. We give a threat model with five attacker classes, a timing model of containment, and a population model showing how the spread of capability raises aggregate risk even when per-actor intent is rare. We analyze six domains (vehicles, rail and radio, satellites, platforms, records, and supply chains) and distinguish, for each, what has been demonstrated from what is plausible or speculative. We give probability estimates for eight incident scenarios over three horizons, produced by a Monte Carlo simulation over author-specified inputs, together with a judged estimate for one policy scenario. Software-mediated scenarios, such as hijack of deployed agents and manipulation of ranking systems, are the most probable. The physical and radio scenarios are less probable and more severe. As a response, we examine a positive-authentication design for privileged actions. Agent traffic carries a verifiable signed origin credential tied to an accountable principal, humans use privacy-preserving personhood credentials, and unidentified traffic is confined to a low-privilege lane. The design authenticates the privileged and does not depend on detecting who is human. We analyze what it does and does not stop. It shortens attribution and response time for software-mediated attacks, but it does little against radio interference and physical attacks, which need authenticated safety protocols and sensing. We compare governance options for issuing identity, including a multi-issuer, pseudonymous approach with escrowed linking, and we state the commitments that a middle ground between private and state control would have to meet. The paper closes with separate recommendations for technical security practitioners and policymakers, and lists limitations and open questions. One topic is deliberately omitted: biological threat vectors, for reasons given in Section 5.7. The simulation inputs are the author's own judgments, so the simulation propagates uncertainty and is not independent evidence. The inputs are provided so that they can be challenged and replaced.

detail.abstract:
Objectives: This research aims to explore the effects of AI personalization and AI anthropomorphism on the two contrasting outcomes i.e. financial wellbeing through consumer spending self-control and materialistic consumption through compulsive buying, that follow from consumer trust in the AI. It tackles the “AI consumption paradox” that is currently emerging by incorporating both paths.

Methodology: The study employed purposive sampling and hybrid data-collection methods to gather data from 300 consumers aged 18–40 in major cities of Pakistan who are exposed to AI products/services. Data were analyzed by PLS-SEM of SmartPLS 4, based on measurement and structural model assessment.

Results: AI anthropomorphism was significantly more predictive of AI trust than was AI personalization. AI trust significantly predicted both consumer spending self-control and compulsive buying. Financial wellbeing was positively predicted by spending self-control and materialism was strongly predicted by compulsive buying. The mediation analysis indicated that the effects of AI anthropomorphism on both pathways were more stronger than AI personalization mediated by AI trust.

Originality/value: The study proposes a novel AI trust concept, treating it as a psychological process that branches from AI marketing antecedents to financial wellbeing and materialism consumption in an under-researched South Asian context.

Research limitations/implications: The design is cross sectional/non-probability, so it has limited generalizability and causal inferences. Longitudinal or experimental designs would be advantageous for future studies and could look at other boundary conditions.

Practical implications: Integrate aspects of responsible spending alongside anthropomorphic interfaces in an inviting way to promote responsible consumption amongst AI developers and marketers. The findings underscore the importance of consumer education and responsible use of AI-driven marketing in emerging digital markets, like Pakistan

detail.abstract: Since April 2024 Indonesia has offered a dedicated remote worker visa (E33G), joining a growing group of countries that use immigration policy to attract location-independent workers. Whether a destination benefits from such a policy depends not only on the visa itself but on how the destination communicates what the visa allows, what the place offers, and what is expected of visitors. This paper examines the alignment between Indonesia's remote worker visa and the digital communication of Lombok, with particular attention to Kuta Mandalika, which has been promoted as an emerging digital nomad destination. Using a qualitative case study based on secondary data, we analyse the published visa requirements, immigration law, research on digital nomadism and smart destinations, and prior studies of Lombok's digital tourism communication. The analysis identifies four alignment gaps: an eligibility gap between the visa's income threshold and the freelance profile often depicted in destination imagery; a legal-message gap between "work from paradise" promotion and the prohibition on working for Indonesian employers; an information gap created by fragmented digital channels; and a community gap in which the benefits and costs of remote-worker presence are not communicated to residents. We propose a communication framework that links visa rules, place infrastructure, digital information and community integration, and derive implications for destination marketing organisations and immigration authorities. The study contributes to the emerging literature on digital nomad visa policy by showing that policy effectiveness at the destination level is mediated by communication.

detail.abstract: As enterprise data topologies decentralize into federated data meshes, autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly consume distributed Data Products directly via application-layer protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agentto-Agent (A2A) frameworks. However, existing data catalogs and static data contract specifications-including the Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS) and Open Data Product Standard (ODPS)-are designed for asynchronous human governance and batch CI/CD validation rather than synchronous, runtime agent consumption. While preliminary runtime architectures have introduced a three-vector structural Context Quality Index (CQI) coupled with in-kernel Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) socket interception, all three baseline metrics are query-invariant table properties that could be pre-calculated periodically in a database, failing to detect query-conditioned subspace corruption, latent semantic drift, or adversarial retrieval rank hijacking. This paper introduces the Dynamic Context Quality Index (d-CQI), a mathematically bounded, five-dimensional semantic verification functional embedded within self-describing decentralized data products. The d-CQI couples a decoupled two-phase evaluation pipelinewhich pre-materializes query-invariant dataset priors (load-keyed freshness watermarks, topological DAG lineage trust, and Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD 2 u) and 1-Wasserstein (W 1) drift stability) at 5-minute database intervals while synchronously evaluating intra-interval clock attenuation, query-conditioned column completeness, and top-k latent query-neighborhood asymmetry (S poison) at runtime-with a non-linear multiplicative hazard gate. Furthermore, this research formalizes Autonomous Data Contracts (ADC) and Metric First-Order Temporal Logic (MFOTL) Policy-as-Code extensions to Cedar and Open Policy Agent (OPA). Empirical evaluations across 5, 000 synthetic data product mutations and 2, 500 adversarial injection traces on a 128-core baremetal testbed demonstrate that two-phase d-CQI reduces silent semantic and intra-interval corruption bypasses from 20.78% (under 5-minute pre-computed database CQI) to 0.08% at a 0.48 ms runtime evaluation overhead, while maintaining 0.12 ms transport enforcement via HSM-signed Context Tokens and eBPF TCP RST circuit breaking.

detail.abstract: AI systems now draft clinical records, interpret organisational data, recommend operational interventions and act through delegated permissions. Technical governance can establish which system acted, what it was permitted to do and what it recorded. It cannot, by itself, establish whether an organisation was justified in relying on the proposition the system produced. This paper examines that gap as a question of organisational epistemic warrant: the context-specific, revisable justification an organisation can demonstrate for adopting or acting on a proposition generated or materially transformed by an AI system. I compare the question against meaningful human control, organisational epistemology, sociotechnical safety, professional responsibility, calibrated reliance and assurance-case methods, and against four constructs from my own research programme: the Digital Transformation Resilience Model (DTRM), Decomposition-Induced Governance Blindness (DIGB), Structural Decision Intelligence (SDI) and proposition-relative governance of digital benefit claims. Most of the problem is already addressed in that body of work. The candidate residual is narrower: the moment at which an AI-mediated proposition becomes an organisational basis for action, the justification required at that moment, and the conditions under which continued reliance should be challenged. The paper proposes the proposition-action episode as a unit for comparing governance methods, four candidate conditions of warrant (evidential support, interpretative adequacy, adoption authority and practical challengeability) and a model that records adoption status and warrant status as separate variables, so that adoption without adequate justification stays visible. Four falsifiable propositions and a staged research programme follow, with explicit abandonment criteria. The construct earns independent standing only if explicit warrant assessment improves the detection or treatment of unsupported reliance beyond competent existing practice, at acceptable cost. If it does not, its distinctions belong inside the traditions it draws on. AI disclosure: Generative AI tools were used in drafting, revision and copy-editing. detail.abstract:
Background: Cultural heritage can inform contemporary enterprise, but commercial differentiation does not by itself establish cultural stewardship. Organizations that draw on historical knowledge must translate cultural inspiration into contemporary offerings while maintaining authenticity, quality, accountability, and economic viability. Existing frameworks address these requirements separately rather than as one organizational system. 

Objective: This paper introduces the PERSEPOLIS Beauty of Civilization Business Model (PBCBM), a multidisciplinary conceptual framework integrating cultural heritage, contemporary innovation, institutional governance, brand identity, and sustainable enterprise. Framework: PBCBM specifies a six-level institutional hierarchy, from the PERSEPOLIS official master brand, the Beauty of Civilization guiding philosophy, and House of PERSEPOLIS as institutional and creative home to the ten-pillar framework, the implementation ecosystem, and evaluation. It defines six strategic dimensions and ten operational pillars structured around the letters of PERSEPOLIS: Preservation, Excellence, Research, Stewardship, Enterprise, Prestige, Originality, Learning, Integration, and Sustainability. The pillars are justified by organizational function and grouped into four complementary clusters. A proposed dual-value flywheel describes how cultural knowledge, contemporary innovation, commercial activity, and recorded reinvestment may reinforce one another, with cultural and economic outcomes reported in separate ledgers subject to noncompensable constraints. Methods: The framework is developed through problem-driven conceptual synthesis of scholarship on corporate heritage, brand authenticity, business-model innovation, organizational learning, dynamic capabilities, institutional legitimacy, and mixed-methods research. Ten research propositions and an implementation and evaluation algorithm are specified. A prospective 18-month longitudinal mixed-methods pilot is proposed, combining embedded project cases, a randomized communication experiment, interviews, independent documentation review, and operational accounting. Implementation setting: PERSEPOLIS, developed within House of PERSEPOLIS and guided by the Beauty of Civilization philosophy (https://houseofpersepolis.com), provides the proposed implementation setting for PBCBM. Its multidisciplinary ecosystem encompasses beauty, fragrance, fashion, jewelry, watches, sunglasses, leather goods, home and living, gastronomy, cultural experiences, education, and publishing. Conclusion: PBCBM contributes an identifiable and testable configuration of established management concepts that distinguishes perceived authenticity from documented cultural integrity. The framework remains conceptual pending prospective evaluation; no empirical effectiveness findings are reported.

detail.abstract: Digital publishers are rapidly adopting AI-generated article summaries, yet their economic consequences for display advertising-supported media remain unclear. We study this question using a large-scale randomized field experiment in which 31,253 articles on a major sports media site were randomly assigned to display an AI-generated summary or not, generating around 8.1 million page views and 56 million filled ad impressions. For newly published articles, which account for 97% of the publisher's ad revenue during the experimental period, AI summaries reduce article views by 24.7% while increasing the average viewer's engagement time by 7.5% and marginally reducing exit rates by 3.9%. As a result, AI summaries reduce the advertising revenue from newly published articles by 23.8%. For pre-existing articles, effects are substantially smaller, with a 4.3% increase in the average engagement time, a 4.3% decline in exit rate, and a negative but statistically insignificant effect on page views and ad revenue. Our mechanism analyses show that traffic losses for newly published articles are concentrated early in the article lifecycle and primarily reflect reduced organic search traffic resulting from lower search exposure. Ad-slot diagnostics further show that the increase in user engagement leads to more filled impressions per view for the ad slots that appear at the top or side of the page, but this increase is offset by fewer in-content filled impressions. These findings reveal a trade-off between audience reach and engagement quality in deploying AI summaries on publisher websites.

detail.abstract: There have been studies on cross-situational within-person variability in personality and some research on personality mindset (beliefs about malleability of personality). Nonetheless, there has been no study on both. This study aims to confirm if there is within-person variability in personality and to explore if it has any relationship with personality mindset. To do this, two phases were conducted. Phase 1 measured personality mindset measured an 8-item implicit theory scale. Phase 2 involved experience sampling (ESM), measuring big five traits four times a day for one week. This study found that personality mindset did not significantly predict within-person variability in all personality traits. Likewise, except for its weak effect on extraversion (b= .25), mindset did not significantly predict between-person variability in personality (average trait levels). Finally, within-person variability existed but was significantly less than between-person variability on average in the original sample. However, they became similar in magnitude in a sample subset excluding participants who did not respond properly or adequately enough to capture within-person variability. Consistent with past findings (e.g. Pruneddu, 2013; Spinath et al, 2003), the results of this study were not in favor of personality mindset. This questioned the extent to which the personality mindset is related to real personality variability within and between individuals. Overall, the present findings cast doubt on the predictive validity of the personality mindset theory, at least for short-term variability across situations.

detail.abstract: Digital payment systems have become a leading way of paying in several of the world's largest economies, with China's Alipay and WeChat Pay and India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI) as two prominent cases. University students, as digitally native and increasingly financially independent consumers, are a key group for understanding what sustains adoption. This paper combines a literature synthesis, grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT and UTAUT2) and Innovation Resistance Theory, with an exploratory survey of university students. The review shows that performance expectancy is a consistent predictor of adoption intention in both countries, while the roles of effort expectancy, social influence and facilitating conditions differ across studies. To examine these patterns directly, an anonymous online questionnaire was completed by 100 students, of whom 88 gave valid, complete responses (54 studying in China and 32 in India). Perceived usefulness (r = .80), ease of use (r = .80), social influence (r = .73) and trust (r = .72) were strongly associated with intention to continue using digital payments, whereas perceived risk showed a weak negative association (r =-.30). In a multiple regression, only usefulness and ease of use were unique predictors (R² = .73). Mean levels did not differ significantly between students in China and India, and the stronger associations seen in the Indian subsample did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. Because the sample is small and non-probability, the findings are exploratory. The paper closes with implications for fintech design and a plan for a larger multi-group study.

detail.abstract: University tuition and fees impact student engagement and school enrollment. Thus, it is important that students be satisfied with what they are paying. This research incorporates social comparisons in communications to students and examines the impact that these comparisons have on student satisfaction with their cost of attendance and overall university experience. In particular, this work employs an experimental design with two conditions. In the Increase condition, participants learned that a counterpart university planned to increase its tuition and fees, while their own university kept the cost of attendance constant; in the Constant condition, participants learned that both the counterpart university and their own kept tuition and fees constant. The dependent variables were participants’ satisfaction with their own university’s tuition and fees, as well as their overall satisfaction with their university experience. In addition, this research examined relative value as a potential mediating variable influencing these outcomes. The results demonstrate that students become relatively more satisfied when their tuition and fees remain constant, but a counterpart university increases its tuition and fees (the Increase condition) versus keeps these costs constant (the Constant condition). In other words, simply knowing that another university has raised prices (vs. kept them constant) but theirs has not, enhances student satisfaction with tuition and fees, which leads to greater satisfaction with their overall university experience. These findings emerge because students perceive the price they pay for their cost of attendance to be of higher relative value when another university raises prices (vs. keeps them constant). Notably, whereas most research demonstrates how consumer satisfaction can be helped by an organization spending money, this research identifies a cost-free method that universities can use to enhance student satisfaction.

detail.abstract: The increasing use of internet-enabled technologies in the workplace has made non-work-related internet use during working hours a growing concern because of its potential effects on employee performance and organizational effectiveness. This study examined the association between non-work-related internet use during working hours and employees' self-reported work effectiveness in a medical equipment importation company in the Philippines. Guided by Effort-Recovery Theory and Conservation of Resources Theory, the study employed a quantitative, descriptivecorrelational, cross-sectional research design. The study collected data from 60 employees using a validated, researcherdeveloped questionnaire. The study used descriptive statistics and Spearman's rank-order correlation coefficient to analyze the data and determine the relationship between non-work-related internet use and work effectiveness. The findings revealed that employees sometimes engaged in non-work-related internet activities during working hours, with personal messaging being the most frequent activity and communication with family during emergencies serving as the primary reason for such behavior. Respondents reported high self-rated work effectiveness, particularly in teamwork, engagement, and quality of work, while productivity and task completion received moderate ratings. Non-work-related internet use was significantly and negatively associated with work effectiveness. Employees also reported neutral work-related challenges associated with personal internet use. Based on these findings, the study proposes company policies on non-work-related internet use to further improve employees' work effectiveness. The findings support Effort-Recovery Theory and Conservation of Resources Theory and highlight the importance of responsible internet-use practices, digital selfregulation, and clear workplace policies in promoting employee effectiveness and organizational performance.

detail.abstract: Online retailers now decide what a shopper sees before the shopper has typed a single word. Recommendation engines, tailored offers and personalised messages sit behind most large ecommerce platforms, and they are probably the most visible use of artificial intelligence in marketing today. This paper looks at one narrow question within that field: how AI-driven personalisation affects consumer trust and purchase behaviour, with particular attention to India. The study rests on secondary research, drawing on recent empirical studies, industry surveys and India's new data protection framework. The evidence reviewed suggests that relevant recommendations raise purchase and repurchase intention, but mostly through intermediate factors such as perceived relevance, satisfaction and trust, although not every study agrees on the route. Indian consumers appear unusually receptive to AI suggestions, yet they remain worried about data breaches and the misuse of personal information, and many still prefer human help when something goes wrong. The paper argues that personalisation works only when it is explained clearly, built on data that customers have agreed to share, and kept within limits they find acceptable. It closes with practical suggestions for marketers and a note on the limits of a desk-based approach.

detail.abstract: The automated classification of retinal pathologies from Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) imaging represents a clinically and methodologically significant challenge for deep learning, necessitated by the morphological subtlety of disease signatures and the substantial clinical burden of sight-threatening conditions including Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV), Diabetic Macular Edema (DME), and Drusen. Despite frequently high benchmark accuracies reported in the literature, CNN-based approaches to OCT classification exhibit structural limitations that constrain crossstudy comparability and translational utility: among them, the absence of rigorously constructed first-principles baselines, inconsistent evaluation protocols, and under-characterized domain transfer from ImageNet-pretrained backbones to grayscale medical imaging data. This paper presents a structured scoping review of CNN-based OCT and related retinal-imaging research based on a coded corpus of 55 records published between 2017 and 2026. The corpus is organized by architectural family, from purpose-built CNNs through transfer-learning approaches to hybrid, attention-augmented, and Transformer-integrated architectures. Five persistent research gaps are identified: three operational gaps (absence of controlled first-principles baselines, incomplete characterization of ImageNet-to-OCT transfer effectiveness, and the unexplored unification of multi-scale feature fusion, channel-and-spatial attention recalibration, and sequential modeling) and two conceptual gaps (uncharacterized representation geometry distinguishing model capacity limitations from intrinsic Drusen-Normal ambiguity, and crossscanner domain shift and the predominant reliance on indomain evaluation for high-performing benchmark studies). The review further reveals systemic evaluation weaknesses: across the 55-record coded corpus, 74.5% of records report accuracy as the primary evaluation metric, whereas AUC/AUROC and class-sensitive metrics are reported substantially less frequently. The paper concludes with six concrete recommendations for methodological reform, including controlled baselines, per-class metric reporting, crossscanner generalization benchmarking, and geometric characterization of learned embeddings.

detail.abstract: This article advances the hypothesis of inherited affective inequality of logos: the geometric resemblance of a sign to forms repeatedly encountered in everyday experience may transfer to it the previously established affective significance of a referent. This is hypothesized to create unequal initial competitive conditions associated with differences in trust, advertising returns, persistence of preferences, and brands' shares of total market revenue. The paradox of latent reverse reference is also proposed: a familiar referent may unconsciously reactivate a representation of a logo without the sign itself being presented. The primary test compares actual market leaders and lagging brands; a separate experiment is needed to test the proposed unconscious mechanism. Testable implications, alternative explanations, and falsification criteria are presented. All causal propositions are treated as the author's hypotheses rather than established regularities.

detail.abstract: AI provides an unprecedented ability to determine patterns in aggregated data which can produce inferences about people. There are two ways in which AI inferences undermine privacy laws. First, when AI allows inferences to be made, the inferred data is beyond what was disclosed to people in the privacy notice. Second, many privacy laws protect sensitive data differently from regular personal data. With AI inferences, sensitive data can readily be inferred from combining pieces of regular personal data. Determining which data should be classified as sensitive becomes nearly impossible. Whether they recognize inferences or not, privacy laws are in a bind. There is no easy escape from the AI inference problem. The laws must start to reckon with it.

detail.abstract: We develop a method for estimating price elasticities from prices and sales across markets. The method applies under measurement and identification conditions whether conventional price instruments are valid or difficult to justify. Prices from one market group provide information about shared demand conditions; adjusted sales from another measure their demand effects. Because sales also respond to donor-market prices, we reconstruct the sales measurement at each candidate demand parameter and estimate demand and the measurement relationship jointly. For finite-dimensional demand and measurement specifications, we characterize identification with nonlinear price effects, observed heterogeneity, and nonunique measurement coefficients. We give sufficient conditions under general pricing rules and construct asymptotic confidence regions allowing weak demand identification and bounded approximation errors. Feasible calendar-week inference accounts for shared donors and estimated controls. Using benchmarks reconstructed from a retail pricing experiment, our elasticity estimates have about half the mean absolute error of peer-price IV across twelve categories.

detail.abstract: In today's era, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the education sector by enhancing learning outcomes and personalizing educational experiences. This study investigates the effectiveness of AI-based adaptive learning systems in higher education using a quantitative research design involving 300 postgraduate students and 48 faculty members from urban, semi-urban, and rural institutions in Odisha, India. Participants were selected through stratified sampling, and data were gathered through surveys and academic records to compare students using adaptive learning systems with those in traditional classroom environments. Statistical techniques, including independent t-tests and one-way ANOVA, were employed to analyze AI-driven behavioral differences and emerging trends in the higher education sector. The primary goal is to assess the impact of these systems on academic performance, student engagement, and retention rates. The results indicate that students, being more digitally adaptive, actively engage with AI tools for personalized learning, real-time feedback, and independent exploration. Conversely, teachers exhibit a more reserved adoption pattern, shaped by concerns regarding digital literacy, pedagogical integration, and the need for adequate training. Furthermore, students utilizing adaptive technologies reported increased participation, motivation, and higher retention rates. Despite these positive outcomes, the study identifies key challenges, including technical barriers, initial implementation costs, and resistance to change among educators. The findings underscore that successful AI implementation depends heavily on institutional readiness and robust infrastructure. The study recommends targeted teacher training, equitable access to technology, and the development of inclusive, context-sensitive AI tools to ensure effective and equitable integration across diverse educational landscapes. Ultimately, these insights provide a strategic roadmap for educators and policymakers seeking to optimize the integration of AI in higher education.

detail.abstract: Using a continuous measure of task distance between occupations built from O*NET descriptors, this paper estimates the wage cost of involuntary job loss in South Korea with the Korea Labor and Income Panel Study, 2009-2023. Involuntarily separated workers lose 6.8 percent of their wage per unit of task distance; the corresponding estimate for voluntary movers is zero. The penalty is substantially steeper for workers separated from the manufacturing sector, from jobs held for ten years or longer, and from union jobs: three markers of standing accumulated in the origin job. Workers separated from manufacturing and from long-tenured jobs lose even when they move to higher-paying or more skill-intensive occupations and controlling for destination union status leaves the penalty unchanged: the cost of involuntary separation is neither an occupational downgrade nor the exit from a protected segment, but the destruction of standing, the value of which transfers only to similar work. Reemployment policy should therefore target support by the origin-job characteristics that predict large losses and weigh task proximity in judging placements.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that the artificial-intelligence systems now being procured at scale across the Atlantic Alliance are configured for the analytic task at which they are structurally weakest: the recognition of the consequential outliers — novel attacks, abandoned hypotheses, cross-domain recombinations — that have historically decided cognitive-security and innovation outcomes. It advances three claims and concedes the limits of each. First, that strategic recognition comprises two distinct failures of the mean — a distributional failure (rare-event detection) and an abductive failure (cross-domain inference) — which share a consequence, strategic surprise, but not a mechanism. Second, that the dominant deployment topology, the sequential analytic pipeline, compoundsthe distributional failure multiplicatively in the depth of the chain, so that fielded systems are more tail-blind than the single-model evidence shows. Third, that the corrective — an inverse-intelligence capability — is therefore not a model to be invented but a verification pipeline to be deployed, and that its near-total absence from Alliance systems is the central capability gap. The paper grounds these claims in a peer-reviewed evidence base, a risk heatmap across seven architecture classes, a verified map of the failure classes onto fielded NATO and ministry-of-defence systems, the historical case of the Ufimtsev–Lockheed stealth asymmetry, and a formal treatment of daisychaining, and it submits the reformed thesis to a structured adversarial review. A closing section extends the diagnosis to a second, normative axis — the freezing of value-alignment into unratified 'constitutions' and the resulting gap in normative interoperability between allied systems — showing it to be the same failure of the mean transposed into the ethical register.

detail.abstract: The United Kingdom's investment rate is commonly understood as being unusually low, having declined by around two percentage points since the 1970s. In this paper we document an apparent mean-shift in gross fixed capital formation in the late 1980s, and present a sectoral shift-share decomposition to explain this phenomenon. We argue that the decline can be accounted for by a secular process of de-industrialisation, which was masked in the 1970s by the North Sea oil boom and in the 1980s by a short-lived real estate boom. We compare the United Kingdom's experience to those of comparable countries, and consider the implications of changes in the types of assets being accumulated, their relative prices, and their depreciation rates, for the evolution of real capital accumulation.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the trade-off between minority shareholder protection and innovation-driven specialization created by South Korea’s regulation of vertical spin-offs (muljeok bunhal) — a wholly-owned daughter firm structure at the center of Commercial Act reforms since 2022, which critics warn may suppress a legitimate channel for technological specialization in the name of shareholder protection. Using 206 spin-offs disclosed on DART between 2016 and 2024, I construct firm-quarter measures of patent-based technological value (following Kogan et al., 2017) and input-output-based industry heterogeneity between parent and daughter (following Antras and Chor, 2013.

An event-study difference-in-differences design shows spin-off announcements are associated with a 4.2 percentage point abnormal decline in parent stock returns — significant only once industry heterogeneity is controlled for. Daughter firms spun off into more dissimilar industries create substantially more technological value (a one-standard-deviation increase in heterogeneity raises it by 36.8 percentage points), and parent firms show a symmetric reversal from technological value destruction to value creation as heterogeneity rises. A cost-benefit simulation combining these estimates finds that expected innovation gains exceed estimated shareholder losses in 201 of 206 cases — a result that depends critically on accounting for industry heterogeneity, and would reverse sharply if heterogeneity were ignored.

detail.abstract:
In the second quarter (Q2) of 2026, most key indices of the Manufacturing Business Survey Index (BSI) rebounded sharply from an unusually weak first quarter, though many indices remained below the baseline of 100. Business conditions climbed from 79 to 90, while the sales index jumped from 79 to 93, the strongest reading since the second quarter of 2024. By sector, most industrial groups reported stronger sales and export sentiment, particularly the semiconductor and ICT sectors, as well as large companies which surpassed the baseline.

Declines were most persistent in the textiles, refined petroleum products, and automobile sectors, where sentiment stayed well below the baseline despite the broader rebound. The outlook for Q3 suggests manufacturers anticipate further improvement, with business conditions projected to reach 97 and sales to reach 99, both edging just under the baseline. Gains are expected to be concentrated in a handful of key sectors, such as wireless communication products, secondary batteries, shipbuilding, and ICT, while the refined petroleum products and textiles sectors are expected to remain the weakest performers.

detail.abstract: GPU-accelerated enterprise servers concentrate computational value and operational risk: a hardware fault can interrupt workloads, while malicious traffic or compromised services can degrade availability, confidentiality, and integrity. Reliability monitoring and cybersecurity detection are often implemented as separate workflows, leaving operators to reconcile signals across hardware telemetry, workload behavior, and network events. This paper proposes an AI-driven framework that places a cybersecurity classifier and a future GPU-reliability predictor within a shared risk and response architecture. The empirical component evaluates binary intrusion detection using the public UNSW-NB15 training and testing files supplied for this study. The combined dataset contains 257,673 records: 175,341 training records and 82,332 held-out test records. The modeling pipeline excludes the record identifier and the attack-category field from predictors to avoid direct target leakage, imputes numeric missing values, one-hot encodes protocol, service, and state, and compares class-weighted Logistic Regression with a 100tree Random Forest. On the provided test split, Random Forest achieved 88.75% accuracy, 84.11% precision, 98.10% recall, 90.56% F1-score, 0.9835 ROC-AUC, and 0.9877 average precision. Logistic Regression achieved 71.92% accuracy, 69.08% precision, 88.72% recall, 77.68% F1-score, 0.8168 ROC-AUC, and 0.8098 average precision. These results support the feasibility of the cybersecurity branch on this benchmark, not a claim of validated GPU-failure prediction. GPU reliability prediction, cross-domain risk fusion, deployment overhead, and real-world lead time remain proposed components because the available records do not contain synchronized GPU telemetry or hardware incident labels. The paper contributes a reproducible baseline, an explicit data-boundary statement, and an architecture for future integrated validation.

detail.abstract: This study examines how geopolitical risk, trade war uncertainty, and climate policy uncertainty, used here as a proxy for environmental shocks, relate to the volatility and cross market dependence of United States equities and crude oil, using monthly data from January 1990 to December 2024. We combine a Markov switching GARCH framework augmented with exogenous shock indices, a dynamic conditional correlation model, and a generalized forecast error variance decomposition, and we add a long short term memory network as a predictability check. The baseline specification identifies two weakly separated volatility states for the S&P 500 and a single state for oil. In the extended specification, the response of equity volatility to all three shocks is larger in the crisis state, with climate policy uncertainty carrying the largest coefficient, whereas the mean response of equity returns to trade war uncertainty changes from positive in the stable state to negative in the crisis state. The conditional correlation between equity and oil returns averages 0.058 and peaks at 0.231 around 2020, and equities are net transmitters of spillovers to oil, at 2.60 percentage points, with the rolling spillover index rising during the Global Financial Crisis and the pandemic. The neural network yields negative out of sample R squared values, which is consistent with weak return predictability. The findings support regime aware hedging and macroprudential monitoring, subject to the estimation caveats discussed in the paper.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how firms’ emphasis on different areas of marketing strategy contributes to firm value in the face of increasing product market similarity. We argue that tangible and intangible strategic differentiators of marketing play asymmetrical roles. Intangible differentiators (i.e., promotion and customer relationship management (CRM) features) are primarily non-transactional and more difficult for rivals to replicate. In contrast, tangible differentiators (i.e., product, price, and place features) are largely transactional and may not provide a sustainable competitive advantage in markets with high product similarity. To test these predictions, we develop and validate textual measures of each marketing strategy area. Consistent with the predictions of the contingency framework, the results show that greater emphasis on promotion and CRM has a stronger value-enhancing effect when the firm’s product space is characterized by high versus low similarity, whereas no such effect is observed for product, price, and place features. However, an important boundary condition exists: the stronger value-enhancing effect of intangible differentiation in high-similarity industries is attenuated when firms face high financial distress, which tends to increase uncertainty about the future benefits of these differentiators. Our findings provide new insights into the complex and dynamic nature of investors’ valuation of firms’ marketing strategies amid accelerating commoditization.

detail.abstract: Background and Objective: Evaluations of lifestyle prescriptions for chronic kidneydisease (CKD) typically assume perfect patient compliance, yet real-world adherence isdynamic, partially observed, and decays over time. We develop a publicly reproducibleadherence-aware world model to screen sequential prescriptions under this uncertainty.Methods: The model couples a four-state hidden Markov model of latent adherence (ad-herent, partial, lapsed, dropout), noisy adherence scores, and a stochastic kidney kerneladvancing eGFR and albuminuria. Simulated patients are survey-weighted NHANES re-samples (1999–2023); seven parameters spanning adherence and CKD progression are cal-ibrated by differential evolution to published anchors. A belief-state planner, which neverobserves the latent adherence state, selects prescription intensity every three months viaMonte Carlo rollouts. Using common random numbers, we compared it against a full-adherence ablation of the same planner across 100 patients over five 60-month episodes;annual eGFR slope was the primary endpoint.Results: The adherence-aware planner favored lower-intensity prescriptions (mean 0.22vs. 0.71), improving mean adherence (0.34 vs. 0.22) and lowering dropout (91% vs.96%). The paired eGFR slope difference was small (-0.014 mL/min/1.73m2/year; 95%CI-0.044 to 0.016) and included zero. High dropout in both arms may explain the smalldifference. A forced-adherence sweep showed the kidney kernel responds to adherence(slope -2.46 to -1.69 mL/min/1.73m2/year, adherence score 0 to 1).Conclusions: This simulation framework enables the evaluation of adherence-awaredecisions before prospective study; it is not a clinical recommendation and lacks longitu-dinal validation. Although CKD is the demonstration domain, this simulation frameworkapplies to sequential interventions dependent on latent, evolving adherence.

detail.abstract:
A venture can pass a stage gate while important questions about its development remain unresolved. Drawing on SHAKE, this paper examines how entrepreneurial support organisations keep that continuing inquiry connected to decisions about further support, including when the evidence needed for a decision takes longer to obtain than the programme’s review timetable allows.

Programme documents, development matrices and decision records, together with public descriptions and a separately identified practitioner account, inform a process model distinguishing translation from transition. Translation is the developmental work through which venture questions, evidence and assumptions become assessable and actionable. Transition is an authorised change in programme stage or commitment. Continuing mentoring and maintained matrices connect specialist input to collective review. Decisions can authorise support while returning unresolved questions to development, so translation continues across gates.

Three design propositions address continuity in support relationships, the scope of commitments and review as ventures and portfolios mature. Within this wider process, the Venture Commitment Record makes an established commitment process explicit. The practitioner account describes its development and use during Cohort 5. A research specification was developed and checked using the same three commitment episodes; this exercise did not assess usability or organisational effects. The study offers a process model and design propositions for examining how developmental work remains connected to authorised support, and who carries that work forward.

detail.abstract: Purpose Despite known benefits of research in radiotherapy, engagement from radiographers (RTT) is still low. A previous nationwide survey produced by the Scottish Radiographers Research Forum identified areas of improvement with regards to establishing RTT-led research. This study aimed to engage RTTs in the development of national strategies to address these areas and support RTT-led research engagement. MethodsA prospective multi-centre study was conducted through twelve focus groups attended online or in-person. Questions were developed to address the lowest scoring survey scores of the previous national survey, validated and piloted by representatives across Scottish radiotherapy centres. Thematic analysis was conducted with findings reviewed by core research team to develop initiatives which were then validated by a national survey to assess acceptability and prioritisation using a 5 point Likert scale and ranking. Results73/315 (23%) of all Scottish RTTs attended a focus group. Thematic analysis of discussions identified five key themes- barriers, culture, time management and flexibility, communication, and relevance and impact. 118 RTTs completed the survey and ranked initiatives in order of preference. National research modules, research presentations, national Teams channel and a dedicated local research hub were ranked 1st to 4th respectively with over 65% of RTTs positively responding to each.ConclusionScottish RTTs have identified initiatives for implementation nationally to support RTT-led research engagement through the analysis of FG outcomes and a national survey. These initiatives are aimed at ensuring equitable access to time and improve research culture nationally both of which were identified as barriers to research.

detail.abstract: Although diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) have become more prominent in human resource policies, evidence linking DEI practices to organizational culture and employee performance remains uneven across settings and over time. This narrative review synthesizes theoretical and empirical research on diversity management, equity-oriented practices, inclusion climate, organizational culture, and individual and organizational outcomes. It draws on theories of workgroup inclusion (Shore et al., 2011; Randel et al., 2018), organizational culture (Schein, 2010; Cameron & Quinn, 2011), and diversity management (Ely & Thomas, 2001; Thomas & Ely, 1996), alongside meta-analytic and empirical studies and recent scholarship on the backlash against corporate DEI initiatives. The literature suggests that inclusive leadership and psychological safety are more directly associated with employee voice, engagement, and innovation than workforce representation alone. Evidence for a straightforward business case linking demographic diversity to financial performance remains mixed. The review also identifies continuing challenges in distinguishing and measuring diversity, equity, and inclusion; accounting for cultural and regional context; and establishing causal relationships through longitudinal research. A proposed conceptual framework positions organizational culture as a filter through which DEI practices influence employee outcomes via psychological safety, organizational justice, and inclusion climate, including belongingness. The article concludes with implications for human resource practitioners and policymakers and recommendations for contextual, longitudinal, and mixed-methods research in a polarized policy environment.
