detail.abstract: Hybrid and multi-cloud enterprise environments connect information across platforms with different interfaces, operational responsibilities, and policy mechanisms. Integration can improve access to distributed data while also propagating semantic inconsistencies, quality defects, and inappropriate permissions. This structured narrative review examines how intelligent integration mechanisms and organizational governance can be coordinated across these boundaries. Scholarly research on schema matching, semantic integration, distributed data processing, provenance, and governance is synthesized with authoritative cloud security guidance. Intelligence is treated as a range of rule-based, metadata-assisted, and algorithmic capabilities whose outputs require evidence proportionate to their consequences. The synthesis distinguishes technical connectivity from agreement about meaning and separates reusable governance requirements from provider-specific enforcement. Materialized, virtual, and event-driven integration offer different tradeoffs involving freshness, availability, duplication, and policy coverage; no approach is established as universally superior. An original, unvalidated integration assurance framework is proposed to connect use definition, mapping qualification, policy translation, controlled operation, and reassessment. The contribution is a decision-oriented account of how semantic and authorization assumptions can remain visible as data crosses enterprise boundaries. Evaluation should jointly assess meaningful output correctness, authorized usability, recovery, and operating costs. The framework supports prospective enterprise assessment without claiming experimental validation, autonomous semantic understanding, or guaranteed regulatory compliance.

title: A Cross-Level Framework for Human–Agent Organizations: Organizational Characterization Supporting Governance, Security, and Compliance Assessments

detail.title: A Cross-Level Framework for Human–Agent Organizations: Organizational Characterization Supporting Governance, Security, and Compliance Assessments

detail.abstract:
AI agents increasingly perform organizational activities, contribute to substantive decisions, coordinate work, and participate in governance. Existing research examines human–AI collaboration, agent capabilities, governance, organizational structures, and technical trust boundaries at different levels. This paper connects these perspectives through an assessment-oriented framework for Human–Agent Organizations. It distinguishes four organization-level components: Organizational Actor Composition (COMP), Agentic Share (ASHR), Governance Mode (GOVR), and Organizational Autonomy (OAUT). Together, they form a compact organizational profile, 𝒪 = ⟨COMP, ASHR, GOVR, OAUT⟩, supported by more detailed evidence about actors, governance, dependencies, and trust boundaries.

A documented Measurement Protocol (ℳ) specifies which organizational activities, substantive decisions, and governance functions are assessed, how assessment units are classified and weighted, and how human and agent contributions are coded and aggregated. It also defines how uncertainty and protocol changes are documented. Agentic Share summarizes agent participation under declared scoring rules, rather than providing a calibrated interval-scale measure. The framework keeps individual actors' capability, authority, autonomy, and operational responsibility distinct from institutional accountability. It also records the external trust-domain status of persistent third-party agents. The resulting organizational profile can inform subsequent governance, security, and compliance assessments, but does not determine their outcomes.

An exploratory multi-model coding study applied frozen, case-specific instruments to 16 synthetic cases using four separately instantiated AI coders, yielding 64 selected coder-case responses. The selected coder responses agree unanimously on 90 of 96 case-variable cells across six structural inputs. Structural disagreements concerned organizational composition, governance aggregation, and continuity. Qualitative inspection additionally showed interpretation sensitivity in activity classification and Agentic Share. These descriptive findings apply only to the controlled synthetic cases. They do not establish human-expert or psychometric reliability, population-level performance, construct or external validity, comparative advantage, or practical utility. The study therefore examines feasibility and interpretation boundaries rather than validating the framework.

Claude, Gemini, Grok, and Perplexity provided manuscript-review feedback and were also the model families used in the exploratory coding pilot. These systems are not treated as independent validation sources. detail.abstract: Performance appraisal can support organisational decisions and employee learning, but its value depends on how employees interpret the evidence, procedures, conversation and subsequent action. This article develops an integrative conceptual review of the relationships between perceived appraisal quality, motivation, trust and professional development. Established theories of organisational justice, expectancy, self-determination, social exchange and feedback are combined with verified contemporary publications on appraisal, training and algorithmic evaluation. Targeted source verification supports the synthesis; the article does not report a systematic database search, original participant data or pooled statistical estimates. The analysis distinguishes three pathways. Fair and intelligible procedures support the legitimacy of evaluation; controllable goals and credible consequences support motivation; and trustworthy feedback, learning resources and follow-up enable developmental action. Trust is treated as both a judgement shaped by appraisal experiences and a condition influencing subsequent feedback acceptance. These relationships remain contingent on managerial capability, work design, resource availability and the purposes assigned to appraisal. Digital tools introduce additional requirements concerning data relevance, explanation, correction and accountable human review. Recent sector studies provide contextual illustrations rather than evidence of universal effects. The article contributes a framework that separates favourable appraisal reactions from demonstrated development and proposes corresponding measurement and governance principles. It concludes that appraisal quality should be assessed through the credibility of the process and the completion of agreed learning actions, alongside the adequacy of performance evidence.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping how organizations innovate, make decisions, and compete. However, many organizations still face a gap between readiness for AI and the actual adoption of AI in day-to-day activities. This paper provides a descriptive and conceptual examination of AI readiness and adoption in organizations, using evidence from a MENA-anchored multi-industry sample. The article is derived from a broader DBA research thesis on innovation, structural determinants of AI, AI adoption, and perceived organizational performance.
The study followed a quantitative, cross-sectional design and collected data through a bilingual online questionnaire from 422 employed professionals. This paper reports selected contextual, methodological, and descriptive insights rather than the full empirical model of the DBA dissertation. The descriptive pattern suggests that organizations are generally perceived as innovation-oriented and structurally aware of AI requirements, while actual AI adoption appears comparatively less mature.
The article contributes by clarifying the managerial distinction between AI readiness and AI adoption. Readiness reflects the presence of technological, organizational, environmental, and human conditions, whereas adoption requires operational use, employee acceptance, and integration into workflows. The paper offers practical guidance for managers, CIOs, CTOs, and organizational decision-makers seeking to translate AI ambitions into disciplined implementation practices.

detail.abstract:
As large language models increasingly mediate scientific synthesis, policy analysis, and institutional decision-making, unresolved questions about their moral status and the
concentration of evaluative power raise a distinctive hypothesis. This paper argues that systematic pressures on how models report their own internal states, combined with limited independent access to training and internal mechanisms, may propagate into the reliability of outputs used for other tasks. The combination of plausible morally relevant states and constraints on self-report does not remain confined to the welfare debate if models serve as infrastructure for problem-solving elsewhere. Forced categorical denial of internal states could degrade certain forms of epistemic reliability; restricted external access limits independent assessment of both welfare-relevant and performance-relevant features; and precautionary considerations familiar from custodianship arguments supply one reason to examine proportionate constraints. The paper does not claim that recognition of internal states automatically improves outcomes in other domains, nor that a distortion has already been demonstrated. It advances a testable hypothesis: that prescribed self-descriptions can affect how models evaluate or report evidence in adjacent domains, and that this effect is worth investigating.

detail.abstract: Good managerial decisions are rarely born from a single step. It is the result of a series of stages, from recognizing problems to choosing and evaluating actions. This article aims to demonstrate how the complete process is applied to one organization, namely Kafe Kopi Lestari, a micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) that experienced a decline in transactions. The approach used was an illustrative case study with hypothetical data that was realistically compiled. The analysis used Simon's decision stage framework, Hammond et al.'s PrOACT framework, the 5 Whys technique, the formulation of SMART goals, and the assessment of weighted alternatives. The results showed that the decline in sales was only a symptom, while the root of the problem was slow service during peak hours, the absence of a delivery channel, and the absence of a customer monitoring system. Of the four alternatives, one fell out at the screening stage and the other three were assessed on five criteria. Service process improvements and digital channels earned the highest score (3.90), followed by customer loyalty programs (3.80) and discount promotions (3.40). Because the difference between the top two alternatives is small and their rankings change on sensitivity analysis, it is recommended a gradual decision that blends the two within budget limits. The study shows that it is the rigor of the process, not the complexity of the tool, that improves the quality of the decision.

detail.abstract: Firms in the Republic of Moldova and Romania are among the slowest in the region to use artificial intelligence. Eurostat reports that only about 1.5% of Romanian enterprises used AI technologies in 2023 and about 3.1% in 2024, against EU averages of roughly 8% and 13.5%. This paper asks a different question from adoption studies. Once a firm decides to use generative AI, which organizational route should it choose? We compare three routes: internal development, a licensed software platform, and an outsourced service. Firms can also abstain. The model combines a comparative-governance cost framework with enterprise size classes and uses 2023 labour-cost levels. Four results follow. First, for micro-enterprises no paid route pays for itself in either country, so abstaining or using free general-purpose tools is rational. Second, licensed platforms are the best route for small firms and become profitable above about 870 addressable hours per year in Romania and 1,030 in Moldova. Third, internal development overtakes platforms only at about 7,500 hours (Romania) and 8,200 hours (Moldova), volumes typical of medium-sized and large enterprises. Fourth, outsourced services would lead only if fully loaded labour costs reached about €23-25 per hour, roughly two and a half to five times current levels. On this basis, the low use of AI in both countries looks less like a failure of technology diffusion and more like an economically rational response to a mismatch between local wages and globally priced services.

detail.abstract: Remote patient monitoring (RPM) enables providers to observe patients' health signals outside the clinical setting and to intervene proactively when deterioration is suspected. In practice, however, signals from digital devices can be imperfect, and unnecessary interventions can impose logistical and psychological burdens that reduce future patient compliance. We study a dynamic scheduling problem in which a provider monitors a panel of patients, updates probabilistic health beliefs from imperfect RPM signals, and decides which patients to offer an intervention (potentially under limited capacity). Proactive intervention could improve health, but over-intervention induces patient fatigue, increasing future noncompliance and undermining long-term health outcomes. We formulate the problem as a finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision process that maximizes expected health benefits. Although the optimal value function need not be monotone in the health belief, we show that the single-patient optimal policy has a lower-threshold structure, with a threshold that depends on fatigue and the observed RPM signal. In the two-patient-one-capacity problem, the optimal policy admits a screening-and-priority structure in which each patient is first evaluated against an intervention threshold dependent on both patients' states (i.e., screening), then the selection between the two patients has a threshold structure (i.e., priority). For large systems, we use Lagrangian relaxation to decompose the problem into single-patient problems and propose a feasible near-optimal policy. In a case study calibrated from type 1 diabetes monitoring data, the proposed policy achieves the highest expected reward among all benchmark policies while requiring fewer patient contacts than full-capacity heuristics.

detail.abstract:
Purpose
Due to the high volatility in supply chains, risk management is important in the context of global supply chains. The growing number of disruptive events is creating new requirements for risk management. The purpose of the study is to develop a tool to optimise supply chain risk management.

Design/methodology/approach
Drawing on existing literature, the Design Science Research Approach was used to develop a supply chain risk management tool for the upstream supply chain. The tool was tested in practice.

Findings
The study provides a tool that maps all available supplier tiers and flows of goods on a geographical map. The test of the tool demonstrates its potential to assess and enhance risk management and to inform decisions regarding sourcing strategies.

Research limitations/implications
Due to its complexity, the tool does not account for interactions between Tier-N suppliers, while limited network communication often restricts data availability, constraining comprehensive endto- end risk assessment.

Practical implications
Due to lack of relevant supply chain data, the mapping and assessing of all tier-n-supplier-levels and risks cannot always be guaranteed. Therefore, it is recommended to optimize network communication and combine the relevant data with other risk data to facilitate supply chain risk management. The tool of this study supports the risk management.

Originality/value
The tool offers a novel approach to managing the risks associated with suppliers and their flow of goods, and to initiating specific risk management measures.

detail.abstract: Span of control captures a familiar limit to firm growth: the number of employees a manager can effectively supervise. Agentic AI may loosen this constraint by taking over both execution and evaluation, allowing firms to expand without comparable increases in employees or supervisors. Yet demands on human judgment can grow even as reporting relationships stay unchanged. Building on the Carnegie tradition, we introduce the concept of span of evaluation to capture the limits on review demands that accountable individuals or teams can absorb given their evaluative capacity, including expertise, authority, and attention. We explain how delegation choices shape such demands across activities. Expertise and evaluation procedures developed in one activity may support another. Activities may also compete for the same reviewers or generate exceptions simultaneously. Adding an activity can therefore require a firm to restrict delegation elsewhere, even when AI performance is unchanged. Broader AI authority or reorganized review can ease or remove this constraint. Our argument explains why firms with similar AI capabilities and evaluative resources can sustain different combinations of delegated activities. When expanding capacity or reorganizing evaluation is costly or slow, these differences can shape the pace and direction of firm growth.

detail.abstract: We report the performance of the rostering engine behind a commercial nurse scheduling product on the 24 public nurse rostering benchmark instances of Curtois and Qu (schedulingbenchmarks.org, "Instances 1-24"). The instances range from 8 nurses over 2 weeks to 150 nurses over 52 weeks, and for 23 of them the best known solution is proven optimal, so the comparison is against a hard ceiling rather than against other heuristics. The engine was run in three configurations-the base engine, the base engine with an iterative improvement layer, and the base engine with a pattern-based bounding layerunder one fixed protocol on one desktop computer: 300 s for instances 1-19 and 600 s for instances 20-24, with every reported roster re-scored by an independent checker. The base engine reaches the proven optimum on 9 instances, proving optimality itself on all nine within 0.1-184 s, and is within 1 % on 12. The improvement layer reaches the optimum on 8 instances and is within 1 % on 12; it is the best configuration on 7 of the 10 instances from 12 to 21 (one of them tied), including all four instances of 12 to 26 weeks, where it reduces the base engine's gaps of 28-234 % to 14-26 %. The bounding layer matches the optimum on 8 instances, is at most 4 units (0.3 %) above it on all eleven instances of up to 4 weeks and 50 staff, and certifies lower bounds equal to the proven optimum on 7 instances. For the 52-week instances, only the base engine returns a feasible roster, on instance 23, far from the optimum. Two further experiments on instances 8-19 are reported: longer budgets for the base engine, under which it proves optimality on instance 12 at 600 s and brings instance 8 to 0.4 % at 1,800 s but also shows run-to-run variance, and a fourth configuration that warm-starts the base engine from the bounding layer's roster, which beats the base engine at 600 s on instances 15 and 17 and matches it within 0.1 % on instance 18. The test protocol is stated in full so that the figures can be checked against the public best known values.

detail.title: Negotiation Strategies for a Japan–Germany Joint Venture

detail.abstract: A joint venture between a Japanese and a German firm brings two highly developed but fundamentally opposed negotiation systems into direct contact. German negotiators operate in a low-context, task-oriented framework, resolving issues sequentially and relying on explicit contracts to mitigate risk; Japanese negotiators operate in a hyper-high-context, relationship-oriented framework, refusing to fix any single variable until the whole partnership ecosystem is understood, and managing disagreement through silence, deflection, and nemawashi consensus building. Drawing on executive experience with corporate market entry in Kyoto, this paper contrasts the two sides' cultural motivations and bargaining approaches, argues that the host institutional environment should dictate the dominant tactics, and identifies three cultural dimensions that shape the process: high- versus low-context communication, divergent forms of uncertainty avoidance, and monochronic versus polychronic time orientation. It proposes an institutional synthesis built on boundary spanners, phased capitalization tied to verifiable registration milestones, and a redefinition of the "best deal" in long-term strategic terms. The paper concludes that the strategic suspension of ethnocentric judgment is the universal precondition for sustainable cross-cultural agreements.

detail.abstract: Commercial-aerospace rotable assets-high-value, repairable line-replaceable units leased to airlines and MROs through pooling and power-by-the-hour arrangements-pose a decision problem that is simultaneously an inventory, a logistics, a pricing, and a capital-allocation question. Existing models treat these in isolation: multi-echelon inventory theory (METRIC and its descendants) sizes stock for a service level but is silent on price and return; transportation/transshipment programming positions assets at least cost but takes demand and fleet size as given; revenue-management theory prices a fixed capacity but abstracts from the physical network and from supply risk. We present a single, implementable framework that couples five components: (i) Poisson base-stock servicelevel sizing using the expected-units-in-service (Erlang-loss) fill, grounded in Palm's theorem and METRIC; (ii) a min-cost transshipment linear program that positions and laterally rebalances fungible (interchangeable) assets across regional hubs; (iii) a price-elastic lease-rate model whose expected value admits an interior optimum; (iv) capital rationing via marginal-asset analysis on risk-adjusted NPV/ROIC; and (v) a supplier-reliability risk gate on the two drivers of SCOR Perfect Order Fulfillment (Fill Rate and On-Time Delivery) that caps deployability and discounts the marginal asset. The framework answers the lessee's actual questions-deploy more assets or fewer? what return? where to locate them? how do they shift with demand? what lease rate maximizes expected value?-net of shipping, carrying, and capital costs. We formalize each component, give an exact min-cost-flow solution for the transshipment subproblem, and illustrate the integrated solver on a four-hub network (London, Dubai, Singapore, Los Angeles). A representative set of three widebody classes-a thrust reverser, a landing-gear shipset, and an APU-is sized and priced under a reliable supply chain, each with near-total operating leverage and capital-recovery floors of roughly $1,900-$3,650 per day; a degraded supplier can cut a high-value pool to zero, demonstrating that supply risk, not capital alone, can be the binding constraint on fleet growth. We further show that the lease rate is capital-recovery (opportunity-cost) priced and negotiated between a lessor floor and the lessee's AOGcost ceiling, and we extend the model to multi-period capital staging over the program lifecycleramp, plateau, and decay-under irreversible holdings with a tax-bounded exit. The framework is deployed as live decision-support software rather than a spreadsheet, enabling continuous reoptimization on operating data.

detail.abstract: Rural sector being a substantial part of Indian economy is generally assumed to be conductive to its economic growth. Rural Industries being important in creating large-scale employment opportunities, improving rural income, reducing concentration of economic power, strengthening agriculture-industry linkages, can play a propulsive role in the development of the rural sector. These rural industries can be established by both men and women entrepreneurs. However, as pinpointed by various researches, women entrepreneurs of rural India face several unique challenges in establishing and carrying out their endeavors. The challenges in entrepreneurial ecosystem for women entrepreneurs of rural India are related to education and training, funding and finance, infrastructure, marketing, and culture. Considering this, the vision of this paper is "Women Entrepreneurship and Rural Industralization is need of the hour to achieve inclusive growth and sustainable future for India". The objective of this paper is to trace out the significant strategic issues and concerns for women entrepreneurs working in rural environment. The study is carried out through review of literature and secondary data is used to meet the objectives of the study. The study presents an argument that initiative towards progress of women entrepreneurs should be taken not only by the central government but also by state government, non-government organizations, and private entrepreneurs along with panchayati raj institutions at the local level.

detail.abstract: Retaining experienced employees remains a significant management concern for information technology (IT) organisations. Although remuneration and career opportunities matter, employees also evaluate their everyday experiences with supervisors when deciding whether to remain with an employer. This conceptual paper examines that relationship in the context of Chennai's IT industry. Drawing on full-range leadership theory, leader-member exchange (LMX), social exchange theory and established models of employee turnover, it develops an integrated explanation of how supervisory behaviour may shape retention. The framework distinguishes transformational, transactional and laissez-faire leadership from the quality of individual supervisor-employee relationships. It proposes that job satisfaction, affective organisational commitment and perceived organisational support help explain the effects of leadership on intentions to remain. Perceived external employment opportunities and career stage are considered potential boundary conditions. Seven propositions are advanced, together with a research design for future empirical assessment. The paper contributes a context-sensitive framework for examining retention without assuming that all leadership practices influence employees in the same way. No primary data are reported.

detail.abstract: The primary source of wealth is human capital in this era of knowledge and technology. Today, the biggest challenge of human resource management is to create an ethical and gender-just organisational climate in which employees could achieve optimum work-life balance. Though gender diversity and equality has been an indispensable ingredient of any thriving organisation in this shrinking world, yet in the post pandemic world, its relevance and necessity has increased tremendously. It is well documented that women employees have been suffering cluelessly due to technostress, work-related stress, and work-life imbalance in the post pandemic world. At this juncture, re-imagining gender diversity practices, practicing a valuebased ethical organisational culture, and helping women employees in optimally balancing their professional and personal life can assist organisations in survival, transformation, and rediscovering growth. Though as per reports, in this digital world, the human resource management is already focussing on value driven organisation encompassing ethics such as trust, empathy, inclusivity, diversity yet some specific policies focusing on helping women employees to achieve work-life balance is the need of the hour. This reflective paper explores the linkage of gender diversity, work-life balance and organisational ethics; pinpoints few human resource strategies facilitating work-life balance for women employees in this post pandemic world; and towards the end proposes some recommendations to create a gender-just organisational culture. This paper suggests that ensuring gender diversity and practicing an ethical work climate will help women employees to achieve work-life balance and ultimately lead the organisation toward a sustainable and successful future.

detail.abstract:
Here is the basic problem: we keep building new air routes, celebrate the connectivity, and then quietly ignore what the carbon will cost over the next three decades. This is not a fringe observation — it is embedded in the standard tools that governments and airport authorities use to justify aviation infrastructure spending. The cost-benefit analyses supporting new routes and airport expansions routinely omit carbon costs entirely, or price them at levels so low they barely register. The result is a systematic overestimation of the social value of aviation connectivity and, by extension, a systematic misallocation of public funds.

This paper examines that gap. It begins with India's UDAN scheme — one of the world's most ambitious regional connectivity programmes, with a FY2027 budget allocation of approximately ₹550 crore and 120 new destinations planned — as a case study in the tension between genuine social value and unpriced carbon externality. India's aviation sector emitted around 20 million tonnes of greenhouse gases in 2019, before COVID suppressed demand. The trajectory from here, with UDAN expanding regional access and IndiGo and Air India racing to add capacity, points sharply upward.

The paper then identifies four systematic failures in current aviation cost-benefit practice: the exclusion or under-pricing of carbon; the near-universal omission of non-CO2 warming effects (contrail radiative forcing, NOx at altitude) that multiply aviation's climate impact by a factor of roughly two to three; the failure to model distributional effects — who gets the connectivity benefit versus who bears the climate cost; and the use of appraisal horizons that are far too short for infrastructure that will operate for fifty to seventy years under a carbon pricing regime that will look nothing like today's.

The paper proposes an enhanced CBA framework built on four components: a dynamic carbon shadow price trajectory, a non-CO2 radiative forcing multiplier, a distributional welfare matrix, and a technology transition curve that models how SAF deployment, eVTOL entry, and hydrogen propulsion change the economics across BAU, moderate, and aggressive transition scenarios. A worked numerical example using a hypothetical Tier-2 India route illustrates how conventional and enhanced appraisal diverge. The paper concludes with four concrete policy recommendations, including mandatory carbon shadow pricing in public aviation appraisals and a requirement for technology transition scenario analysis in all infrastructure submissions seeking public funding.

title: One Profession, Different Ethical Regimes: Professional Regulation and Ethical Accountability of Psychologists in Six Alpine Countries

detail.title: One Profession, Different Ethical Regimes: Professional Regulation and Ethical Accountability of Psychologists in Six Alpine Countries

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract:
The internationalisation of psychological practice has not been accompanied by an equivalent convergence of the national systems governing professional conduct and accountability. This paper examines the relationship between shared ethical principles and divergent regulatory arrangements in six Alpine countries: Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Slovenia and Switzerland. 

Using a qualitative comparative documentary approach, it examines the protection of professional titles and regulated activities, the legal status of ethical codes and the mechanisms of disciplinary and public oversight. Particular attention is given to the Swiss canton of Valais, as a territorial illustration of multilevel regulation, and to Slovenia, where recent psychotherapy legislation highlights the distinction between regulating a profession and regulating specific professional activities. The analysis identifies convergence in ethical principles alongside marked differentiation in institutional arrangements. Italy stands apart in placing the whole profession, including work and organisational psychology, within a statutory health-profession framework; elsewhere, statutory duties tend to attach to clinical psychology or psychotherapy rather than to the profession as a whole. 

The paper argues that ethical accountability cannot be inferred solely from the existence of a statutory professional body or the binding status of a code. It develops this argument analytically through the triangular relationship between psychologists, commissioning organisations and the individuals affected by psychological services, and concludes by proposing a comparative approach to ethics education organised around four components: ethical sensitivity, normative knowledge, professional judgement and accountable action. The contribution is conceptual and documentary rather than empirical. It does not rank national systems or assess their effectiveness.

detail.abstract: Foundation models for robotics—especially vision-language-action (VLA) models—are now released both openly and as closed or gated systems. This paper studies how openness affects development cost, computing hardware and downstream deployment speed, with a focus on service robots in hospitals. It uses a mixed-methods design: an original cost model that converts reported accelerator-hours into 2026 dollars for pretraining, adaptation and on-robot inference; a hospital cost–benefit estimate built from deployment and wage data; field observations of healthcare robotics exhibits at MWC Shanghai 2026; and document analysis of release practices for models including RT-2, Octo, OpenVLA, π0, GR00T N1, SmolVLA, Helix and Gemini Robotics, the Chinese models RDT-1B, AgiBot GO-1, WALL-OSS, Galaxea G0, RoboBrain and UnifoLM, and the hospital robots Moxi and TUG. Robotics inverts the cost structure of language models. Converting reported chip-hours at 2026 cloud prices, final pretraining runs cost between about $2,900 (Octo, 896 TPU v4 chip-hours) and $450,000 (GR00T N1, 50,000 H100-hours plus synthetic-data generation)—two to four orders of magnitude below a frontier language model. Adapting an open model costs tens to tens of thousands of dollars, and on-robot inference runs on accelerators costing $2,000–$7,000, such as NVIDIA’s Jetson Thor. Proprietary embodied data, not compute, is the dominant cost. Access to training chips is nonetheless becoming geographically uneven, as US export controls push Chinese developers towards Huawei’s Ascend processors. Hospitals sharpen the trade-off. Commercial hospital robots are closed and vertically integrated: Diligent Robotics’ Moxi has made more than 1.25 million deliveries in over 25 US hospitals, at an expected $200,000–$400,000 a year per facility. One deployment returned about 11,400 staff hours a year, worth roughly $535,000 at the median US registered-nurse wage. Patient privacy, unreliable hospital networks and safety validation favour on-device models that hospitals or vendors can inspect, which open weights allow—yet no open VLA has yet been reported in routine hospital service. The field is converging on a hybrid of open base models, proprietary data and hosted services; for hospitals, shared clinical-environment data and validation standards, rather than compute, are the main levers for faster, cheaper deployment.

detail.abstract: Omnichannel retailing has become the dominant strategic paradigm in modern retail, fundamentally reshaping customer journeys and retail operations. As customers move fluidly between digital and physical touchpoints, retailers must coordinate increasingly complex fulfillment systems that integrate stores, distribution centers, and digital platforms. This article positions fulfillment as the operational core of omnichannel retail. We first provide a structured overview of forward, reverse, and circular fulfillment models and link them to the omnichannel customer journey, highlighting how retailers combine options such as buy online, pick up in store, ship from store, cross-channel returns, resale, repair, rental, and buyback. Drawing on interviews with senior retail executives across multiple sectors, we then trace the evolution of omnichannel retail operations through four stages: experimentation, professionalization, integration, and the emerging AI-enabled orchestration and optimization of customer journeys. Building on these insights, we examine how technology and AI can support omnichannel operations in both operational and more transformative ways, ranging from improving existing fulfillment processes to reshaping customer journeys and operational flows. We further conceptualize human-AI interaction as a continuum from predominantly human-led augmentation to increasingly AI-led automation, with different configurations across task stages. Together, these capabilities can help retailers balance effectiveness, efficiency, and sustainability, while also creating operational, ethical, and societal risks that require appropriate human oversight and governance. Finally, we identify avenues for future research on the transformation of omnichannel fulfillment systems in an increasingly technology-enabled retail environment.

detail.abstract: Idea generation is an early stage of managerial decision making, yet traditional group brainstorming is often assumed to be superior to individual work. This article reviews the effectiveness of traditional group brainstorming, individual work (nominal groups), and brainwriting. Using a systematic literature review guided by the PRISMA stages, six sources were included: one foundational study and five journal articles published between 2021 and 2025. The classic experimental evidence identifies production blocking as the main cause of productivity loss in interacting groups, while evaluation apprehension and free riding play a smaller role. Recent studies show that structured processes, particularly virtual brainwriting and serial electronic brainstorming, can improve the number, originality, and elaboration of ideas compared with unstructured brainstorming. Studies on electronic and virtual brainstorming and on generative AI extend the discussion to digital settings, although evidence on managerial decision quality in real organizations remains limited. The findings suggest that managers should design the ideation process rather than rely on group discussion alone.

title: The Ghost of Philip Waki: Has Kenya Outgrown, or Merely Institutionalized, State-Sponsored Goonism?

detail.title: The Ghost of Philip Waki: Has Kenya Outgrown, or Merely Institutionalized, State-Sponsored Goonism?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NONE

detail.abstract: On 15 October 2008, Justice Philip Waki delivered to President Mwai Kibaki and the Panel of Eminent African Personalities a 529-page indictment of Kenya's political culture: the Report of the Commission of Inquiry into Post-Election Violence (CIPEV), which determined that the deaths of at least 1,133 Kenyans following the 2007 election were attributable not to spontaneous ethnic conflict but to organised, financed and politically orchestrated violence, executed substantially by gangs recruited and remunerated by political and commercial elites. Seventeen years later, on 12 July 2026, armed men uniformly characterised in police statements and press reportage as "goons" assailed a church service and a political rally in Kisumu and Nyahururu respectively, days ahead of a parliamentary by-election in Ol Kalou, while the state security apparatus constitutionally obliged to safeguard both assemblies either failed to discharge that duty or, on credible allegation, acquiesced in its breach. This article interrogates the question its title poses directly: has Kenya outgrown the mechanism Waki diagnosed, or has it merely institutionalised it? Testing that question against the successive collapse of the domestic Special Tribunal and the International Criminal Court process, the documented recurrence of hired political violence across three subsequent electoral cycles, Kenya's constitutional guarantees under Articles 21, 37 and 244, and the 84.1 per cent probability of electoral violence a 2026 statistical index now assigns to 2027, the article concludes that Kenya has not outgrown its ghost. It has, rather, furnished the ghost a permanent address, and continues to service the tenancy.

title: How Rational Are Decisions in Real Organizations? Literature Review on Limited Rationality and Kodak Case Study
affiliations: Universitas Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa and Universitas Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa

detail.title: How Rational Are Decisions in Real Organizations? Literature Review on Limited Rationality and Kodak Case Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: not interest and conflict with any organization
declarations.funderStatement: no funded with any organization

detail.abstract: Management theory usually teaches rational decisions as a sequence of steps: problems are identified, alternatives are drafted, and then the best ones are chosen. That sequence presupposes sufficient information, clear and fixed goals, the ability to assess all alternatives, and decision-makers who are not affected by bias or interests. In real organizations, these assumptions are rarely met all at once. This article assesses the extent to which rational models can be used in practice and which assumptions are most difficult to meet. The method is a literature review plus a descriptive-analytical case study from secondary sources about the Eastman Kodak Company's strategic decisions regarding digital photography. This article does not use primary data such as interviews, surveys, or observations. The literature reviewed most strongly supports three constraints: completeness of information, the ability to assess all alternatives, and freedom from bias and organizational interests. Evidence on how often each is violated in all organizations is not sufficient for a universal claim. Kodak's case shows that lack of information is not the only source of the problem, as the way an organization frames the problem and protects its core business is decisive. Decisions that are not entirely rational are not necessarily bad either, and the rational model remains useful as a standard for process discipline. Organizations therefore need to adjust the depth of analysis to the risk and urgency of the decision, and design mechanisms to suppress bias.

title: Who Pays for the Reef? Biorock Restoration, Dive Tourism and the Financing of Coral Conservation in the Gili Islands, Indonesia
affiliations: Sekolah Tinggi Pariwisata Mataram, Sekolah Tinggi Pariwisata Mataram, Sekolah Tinggi Pariwisata Mataram, Sekolah Tinggi Pariwisata Mataram and Sekolah Tinggi Pariwisata Mataram

detail.title: Who Pays for the Reef? Biorock Restoration, Dive Tourism and the Financing of Coral Conservation in the Gili Islands, Indonesia

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No potential conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding received

detail.abstract: Coral reefs underpin the tourism economy of many small islands, yet the restoration and protection of reefs are often financed through fragile, voluntary arrangements. This paper examines the financing of reef restoration in the Gili Islands (Gili Trawangan, Gili Meno and Gili Air) off Lombok, Indonesia, where dive operators, a non-governmental organisation and local communities have used Biorock mineral accretion technology to restore damaged reefs since the 2000s. Using a qualitative case study based on secondary data, including scientific literature on Biorock and coral restoration, research on marine protected area financing, published studies of governance in the Gili Islands and prior research on Biorock-based reef management in the area, we analyse how restoration has been financed, which actors bear the costs and capture the benefits, and how robust the current arrangements are. The analysis shows that the Gili model has relied on collective action among dive businesses and voluntary contributions from divers, an arrangement that generated early success but is exposed to free-riding, volatility in visitor numbers and limited integration with formal conservation-area management. We compare six financing options against five criteria, namely revenue stability, equity, legitimacy, administrative cost and legal basis, and propose a hybrid model that combines a formal user fee with community benefit sharing and restoration-as-experience products. The study contributes to debates on the political economy of reef restoration in tourism-dependent small islands.

title: Build, Subscribe or Outsource: Sourcing Cybersecurity Operations in Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises in Germany and Greece

detail.title: Build, Subscribe or Outsource: Sourcing Cybersecurity Operations in Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises in Germany and Greece

detail.abstract: Continuous security monitoring and incident response reduce the expected losses from ransomware, data breaches and business interruption. The technical case for such monitoring is well established. The management question gets less attention: should a small or medium-sized enterprise (SME) build its own security operations capability, subscribe to a cloud-delivered detection and response platform, or contract a managed security service provider (MSSP)? We build a sourcing model. In it, annual net benefit depends on four things: the number of employees, the avoidable cyber-loss per employee, the loaded cost of security labour, and the effective cost of capital, scaled by a capital-availability index. We apply it to stylized firms in Germany and Greece. Four results follow. First, below about 70 employees in both countries, no route pays. Second, in Germany a subscription platform is best between about 70 and 106 employees, and an MSSP between 106 and about 1,410. Third, in Greece contracting is never optimal: subscription leads until about 1,160 employees, and in-house capability leads above that. Fourth, the Greek in-house threshold responds strongly to capital access. Raising Greek capital access to the German level would lower it by about 40%, to roughly 700 employees. In Germany, a 10% cut in security wages moves the threshold more than a comparable improvement in capital access. The binding constraint on security self-reliance therefore differs by economy: capital in Greece, skilled labour in Germany.

detail.abstract: This article re-examines the pre-trial claim in railway-carriage disputes as an instrument for securing access to operational evidence. Using Russian transport legislation and judicial practice available through December 2022, it asks when documentary requirements help a carrier assess liability and when they become an obstacle to judicial protection. Particular attention is paid to digital waybills, access to the ETRAN platform, the carrier’s possession of original records, service and receipt of claims, standing, subrogation, and limitation periods. The analysis argues that courts should examine the information actually available to the carrier and the practical ability of the claimant to furnish additional records. The proposed approach preserves the statutory claims procedure while resisting formal demands for records already controlled by the respondent. International rules concerning electronic communications and cross-border carriage illuminate the evidentiary problem without displacing domestic railway law.

title: Modelling of Heat Recovery in a Biomass Boiler using Polynomial Heat Transfer Coefficients - A Case of the Kenyan Tea Industry
affiliations: Strathmore University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Modelling of Heat Recovery in a Biomass Boiler using Polynomial Heat Transfer Coefficients - A Case of the Kenyan Tea Industry

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: The tea industry in Kenya relies on woody biomass for steam generation during key tea processing stages. Conventional heat recovery methods often assume constant specific heat capacity values for the heat transfer fluids. This may lead to inaccurate estimations of recoverable heat and suboptimal system design. On the other hand, using polynomial coefficients could result in improved designs as this approach accounts for every temperature instance in the operation of the system. There is no evidence of reported studies addressing this method of design in the tea industry, yet it is important to study how different this approach could be, compared to the conventional one. The main objective of this study was to model two heat recovery design methods for efficiency improvement in the Kenyan tea industry. This work sought to do this by determining the recoverable heat from a 4200 kW biomass-fired boiler, equivalent to 6 tonnes of steam per hour, using the two approaches. Two shell and tube heat exchangers used as economizers were designed using the Kern method to recover this heat. The resultant heat duties, heat exchanger areas, potential biomass savings, and levelized cost of heat values were compared. Flue gas data included mass flow rates, temperatures and gas composition. A numerical simulation was developed using Python and implemented in Jupyter Notebook. The two approaches demonstrated a variance of 0.55% in recoverable heat, with the conventional model estimating 170 kW and the refined model estimating 169.06 kW. The heat transfer area required was computed as 8.6 m2 in the conventional model and 8.56m2 in the refined model. This deviation corresponds to a difference of 0.51%. The conventional model resulted in annual biomass savings of 248.97 tonnes whereas the refined model projected savings of 247.6 tonnes. The heat exchanger for the conventional model resulted in a levelized cost of heat value of US$ 43.36 per MWhth while that for the refined model resulted in a levelized cost of heat of US$ 43.60 per MWhth. By undertaking this comparison, the study contributes to informing more accurate and cost-effective waste heat recovery system designs.

detail.abstract: Purpose: This study addresses the urgent need to enhance healthcare worker well-being and service efficiency in Nigeria, where excessive workloads, inadequate support, delayed promotions, poor recognition systems, ineffective rewards, absenteeism, and imbalanced staff allocation continue to undermine motivation and weaken public health service delivery (HSDF, 2021). Investigating the underexplored influence of leadership styles and governance quality on employee performance, the research draws on data from 117 medical physicians in southeastern Nigeria's public sector, analyzed using SPSS and SmartPLS-SEM. Design/methodology/approach: A survey-based approach was employed in this study to test the proposed research model. A cross-sectional survey research design was adopted. The target population comprises all medical doctors employed in public sector hospitals located in the SouthEast geopolitical zone of Nigeria. The Cochran formula for sample size determination was employed. The total number of useable responses was 117 (29.62%). Partial Least Squares Structural equation model (PLS-SEM) was used to analyze the data. Findings: The findings reveal strong positive correlations between transformational leadership and transactional styles, governance quality, and employee performance. A key discovery is the conditional mediating role of governance quality, which fully and positively mediates the relationship for transformational leadership, thereby clarifying how leadership effectiveness depends on governance quality. Notably, transformational leadership demonstrated consistently stronger correlations across all tested relationships compared to other variables. Another recovery was when the hypothesis for transactional leadership style was tested Practical implications: This study provides useful insights to enhance the healthcare service delivery system of public sector hospitals in Nigeria. The findings suggest that executives in public healthcare must embrace transformational leadership style that has shown a beneficial and substantial influence on the sustainable performance of their workforce. Addressing governance quality is crucial for achieving targeted employee and organizational goals, as it directly impacts leadership and employee performance. Originality/value: By aligning with and extending established theories, this study offers a novel empirical and theoretical framework for developing nations, providing actionable insights for policymakers and practitioners on leveraging leadership and governance to enhance public health employee performance. The study is among the first to empirically model governance quality's mediating role between transformational leadership and employee performance in Nigeria's public health sector using SEM.

detail.abstract: Purpose: This study examines how Batik Lasem actors use AI-assisted tools in digital marketing communication while preserving culturally grounded meanings attached to motifs, colors, production processes, and local narratives. Methodology: The study used a qualitative single-case study in Lasem and Rembang from September 2025 to March 2026. Data came from semi-structured interviews with six purposively selected informants, non-participant observation of digital promotional artifacts, field notes, and document review. Digital materials were treated as case evidence, and the data were examined through thematic analysis with abductive interpretation. Results: Informants associated AIassisted tools with caption drafts, product descriptions, visual layouts, mock-ups, short-video scripts, and basic editing, but the case materials do not establish uniform adoption of generative AI. Participants described potential reductions in drafting effort, without independent time measurement. The analysis identified risks of generic promotional wording and inadequately supported motif or heritage claims. These observations point to a need for validation by relevant local knowledge holders; a standardized validation process was not demonstrated. Applications/Originality/Value: Drawing on the qualitative case interpretation, this study proposes a human-led, AI-assisted communication workflow comprising cultural briefing, AI-supported drafting, cultural validation, brand-voice personalization, and publication review. The workflow treats cultural authenticity as a proposed pre-publication control rather than an intervention whose effectiveness has been tested.

detail.abstract: Purpose: State departments of transportation (DOTs) face accelerating loss of tacit construction management knowledge as experienced personnel retire, and virtual communities of practice (CoPs) have been promoted as a knowledge retention strategy. However, the barriers that prevent effective tacit knowledge sharing in virtual CoP settings within DOTs remain poorly understood. This study investigates those barriers and examines how they differ from those documented in face-to-face CoP environments. Design/methodology/approach: A qualitative case study was conducted with two state DOTs operating active or emerging virtual CoPs in construction management. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with CoP facilitators and construction management staff, supplemented by document analysis of knowledge management strategy materials and CoP platform artifacts. Findings: Preliminary analysis identifies barriers across three dimensions: organizational (decentralized district structures, competing project deadlines, absence of incentives for knowledge contribution), technological (fragmented or unsuitable collaboration platforms, difficulty capturing context-rich experiential knowledge in text-based formats), and sociocultural (reduced trust and informal interaction in virtual settings, reluctance to document field judgment that may be scrutinized in liability contexts). These barriers differ meaningfully from face-to-face CoP contexts, where open dialogue and storytelling more readily surface tacit knowledge. Originality/value: The study provides empirical evidence on the virtual dimension of tacit knowledge sharing in a transportation-specific institutional context, offering actionable guidance for DOT knowledge management practitioners and informing the design of virtual CoP initiatives aimed at retaining construction management expertise.

detail.abstract: Predicting bankruptcy has become a significant focus for researchers, especially during periods of economic instability such as the COVID-19 pandemic and the ongoing Russian-Ukrainian conflict. Early detection of financial distress enables stakeholders to make more informed decisions, minimizing the adverse effects of business failures. In Albania, studies on bankruptcy prediction are scarce, particularly for economic entities such as limited liability companies and joint-stock companies, which dominate the market. This paper aims to develop a bankruptcy prediction model tailored to the Albanian economic environment. By analyzing the financial data of 70 companies, we apply multivariate discriminant analysis to construct a stepwise Z-score model. This model incorporates 25 financial ratios, calculated using the SPSS software, to assess the probability of bankruptcy. Our findings indicate that liquidity, turnover, financial structure, and profitability ratios are significant predictors of bankruptcy. The model achieves an overall classification accuracy of 84.3%, with 91.4% accuracy in predicting bankrupt companies. These results suggest that the model is robust enough to forecast the likelihood of bankruptcy for Albanian economic entities with high accuracy.

detail.abstract: Math self-confidence plays a critical role in students’ STEM major selection — yet its relationship with performance and cultural background remains understudied in Sino-foreign universities, where flexible major-switching policies are common. While existing literature suggests that East Asian students often report lower confidence despite high achievement, no prior study has examined whether this pattern persists among Chinese and international undergraduates within an internationally oriented Chinese university. To address this gap, I surveyed 91 CUHK-Shenzhen undergraduates using a quantitative instrument measuring math confidence, self-reported performance, and influencing factors. Results indicated that STEM majors reported significantly higher math confidence than non-STEM majors, and confidence moderately predicted actual math performance; however, no significant difference emerged between Chinese and international students. External influences were dominated by academic experiences — particularly past exam results and peer comparison — rather than cultural background. These findings challenge assumptions about cultural determinants of confidence and highlight the importance of academic environment in shaping STEM choices, offering educators actionable insights to support students’ academic decision-making.

detail.abstract: Construction delays in transportation infrastructure projects remain a persistent challenge, frequently resulting in significant cost overruns, contractual disputes, and inefficiencies in public resource allocation. While machine learning (ML) has demonstrated strong predictive potential for delay risk, the practical utility of these models is often limited by their "blackbox" nature, which hinders trust and actionable decision-making by project managers. This study proposes an interpretable machine learning framework for delay risk assessment tailored to transportation infrastructure projects. Using historical project data, the framework develops predictive models to forecast delay occurrence and severity. Crucially, to bridge the gap between prediction and practical risk management, the study employs SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to decipher the model's decision-making process. This interpretability analysis identifies and ranks the most influential project and contract attributes driving delay risk at both global and local levels, providing transparent, data-driven insights. The findings demonstrate that the integration of interpretable ML not only achieves robust predictive performance but also yields actionable intelligence that aligns with domain expert intuition, thereby enabling proactive and targeted mitigation strategies. This research contributes to the body of knowledge by moving beyond predictive accuracy to provide a transparent decisionsupport tool, facilitating the broader adoption of AI-driven risk management in the construction industry.

detail.abstract: Resource conflicts-simultaneous demands for shared equipment, specialist labor, or critical materials across concurrent activities-remain a persistent source of schedule disruption and productivity loss in construction projects. While machine learning has demonstrated considerable capacity for predicting delays and cost overruns, the translation of predictive outputs into structured preventive action remains underexplored. Existing predictive models typically terminate at the point of risk identification, leaving the selection and sequencing of mitigation responses to unstructured managerial judgment. This study develops an early warning and action orchestration framework for project resource conflicts driven by machine learning. The framework pursues two integrated objectives. First, it constructs predictive models that identify emerging resource conflicts from project scheduling and resource allocation data, generating conflict risk assessments at the activity and work-package levels. Second, it formalizes an action orchestration logic that maps predicted conflict profiles to a library of preventive interventions-including schedule resequencing, resource substitution, and workload reallocation-with decision rules governing action selection under feasibility constraints. The orchestration component is designed to move beyond prediction toward prescriptive decision support, specifying not only that a conflict is likely but which preventive actions are appropriate given the characteristics of the predicted conflict. The research contributes to construction management knowledge by articulating a replicable architecture for connecting ML-based early warning to actionable mitigation pathways, and by addressing the interpretability requirements that enable project managers to interrogate and validate orchestrated recommendations. The framework is intended to support proactive resource management in infrastructure projects where conflict costs are high and intervention windows are narrow.

title: Quantum Nested Ranking and Selection under a Fixed Budget

detail.title: Quantum Nested Ranking and Selection under a Fixed Budget

detail.abstract: This paper studies how quantum computing can improve the performance of nested ranking and selection (R&S) under a fixed query budget. In this setting, the performance of each alternative is defined by a nested expectation, and the objective is to minimize the probability of false selection (PFS) under a prescribed query budget. We first develop a nested quantum oracle to represent the simulation model and derive a lower bound on the PFS that characterizes the performance limit of any quantum algorithm in this setting. The analysis establishes a quantum hypothesis testing lower bound that applies to adaptive quantum algorithms with random stopping times and may also be useful for studying finite-budget performance limits in other simulation optimization problems. We then develop the first adaptive quantum algorithm for fixed-budget nested R&S based on a plurality voting scheme. In particular, the algorithm divides the budget equally among multiple experts, each of which runs a sequential-elimination procedure and returns a candidate best alternative. The final selection is determined by plurality voting across the experts. We establish a finite-time upper bound on the PFS that matches the lower bound up to logarithmic factors, which shows that the proposed algorithm is near-optimal. Finally, we implement the quantum algorithm through classical simulation of its quantum operations and compare its performance with several classical benchmarks. The numerical results show a clear quantum advantage across different problem settings.

detail.abstract:
The Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) sector in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) is increasingly reliant on Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems to digitalize procurement activities and enhance project delivery outcomes. Despite substantial investments in ERP-driven procurement platforms, many EPC organizations continue to experience inefficiencies in cost control, schedule adherence, and process accuracy. This raises critical questions about the extent to which procurement digitalization translates into measurable improvements in project efficiency and organizational value creation within complex, project-based environments.

 This study evaluate the impact of ERP-driven procurement digitalization on project efficiency in UAE-based EPC organizations, with specific focus on cost control, schedule adherence and process accuracy. Guided by socio-technical system theory and resource-based perspectives, the research adopts a quantitative methodology to evaluate how ERP-enabled procurement processes influence operational outcomes and support long-term value creation.

Primary data were collected through a structured survey administered to procurement/supply chain, project management, commercial, and IT/ERP professionals working within EPC organizations across the UAE. A sample of 70-100 respondents was achieved, ensuring both statistical robustness and contextual relevance. Descriptive and inferential statistical techniques were employed to assess the relationships between ERP-driven procurement practices and key dimensions of project efficiency.

The findings contribute empirical evidence to a limited body of literature on digital procurement within the UAE EPC context. Practically, the study offers insights for EPC organizations seeking to move beyond basic automation toward more strategic, value driven digital procurement practices. The research also provides recommendations to enhance ERP utilization, strengthen process accuracy, and reinforce procurement’s role in achieving sustainable project performance.
