detail.abstract: Clinical deterioration and disease progression are monitored with condition-specific, threshold-based scores, while machine-learning alternatives are often opaque and poorly calibrated. This study asks whether one transparent probabilistic belief-state framework can deliver accurate, calibrated, and interpretable monitoring across conditions of different physiology and timescale. The framework represents a patient's hidden severity as an ordered chain of regimes, updates the belief over that chain at each time step by recursive Bayesian filtering, maps the resulting risk to a calibrated probability, and explains every risk change through its own log-likelihood-ratio attribution. On MIMIC-IV, the formulation was instantiated for acute respiratory failure (65,363 ICU patients) and acute kidney injury (52,742 stays), and for progression to decompensated cirrhosis (5,597 at-risk patients with repeated laboratory visits). Evaluation was patient-grouped, leakage-aware, and pre-onset. For acute kidney injury, calibrated warning of KDIGO stage 2 or higher reached AUROC 0.81, 0.77, and 0.74 at 12, 24, and 48 hours (median lead 19 hours; Brier 0.060). For cirrhosis, the latent stage at the first modeled admission discriminated one-year decompensation with AUROC 0.71 (95\% CI 0.65 to 0.77), comparably to baseline MELD-Na and better than FIB-4, and was an independent predictor alongside both (hazard ratio 1.18 per SD). For respiratory failure, pre-onset discrimination was modest (AUROC 0.63 to 0.66 from 0 to 24 hours). Explanations agreed with SHAP (Spearman 0.57 to 0.93). The framework provides calibrated, auditable monitoring across acute and chronic conditions, provides an outcome-free prognostic stage, and matches but does not exceed validated scores on single-moment detection.

title: Conflict of Interest and Competition in Decision Making Business: Analysis of Competitors' Reactions and Strategies to Deal with Price Wars Between Digital Platforms in Indonesia
affiliations: Universitas Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa and Universitas Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa

detail.title: Conflict of Interest and Competition in Decision Making Business: Analysis of Competitors' Reactions and Strategies to Deal with Price Wars Between Digital Platforms in Indonesia

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict interest in other organization
declarations.funderStatement: No founder

detail.abstract: Business decisions are rarely made in isolation: the outcome of a pricing move depends on how rivals respond. This study explains how one party's decision is shaped by competitors' reactions under conflicting interests, focuses on price wars between digital platforms, and outlines strategic responses. It applies a narrative literature review of industrial organization, game theory, and platform economics published between 2016 and 2026, supplemented by contextual evidence from Indonesia's ride-hailing and e-commerce markets. The findings indicate that platform price wars follow a prisoner's-dilemma structure that can drift toward tacit cooperation in repeated play; that network effects, multihoming, and capital asymmetry make price cuts more attractive, yet legally and reputationally riskier, for platforms; that conflicts of interest involve platforms, partners, consumers, investors, and regulators, so regulatory reaction is part of rival reaction; and that different decision criteria (expected value, maximin, and minimax regret) can recommend different actions. A staged decision framework combining market diagnosis, value differentiation, credible signaling, selective cooperation, and competition-law compliance is proposed.

title: Robustness Values with Sandwich Standard Errors

detail.title: Robustness Values with Sandwich Standard Errors

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interest to declare
declarations.funderStatement: No funding to declare

detail.abstract: How strong would an omitted variable have to be to overturn a regression finding based on robust standard errors? The usual Cinelli-Hazlett robustness value assumes conventional standard errors. Extending it requires accounting for changes in both the coefficient and its robust standard error. We develop this extension for sandwich covariance rules with fixed weights, retaining the familiar partial-R 2 measure of explanatory strength. Analytical bounds and searches over omitted variables determine the minimum strength needed to remove significance, or an interval containing it. In illustrations based on seven empirical datasets, the unrestricted robust measure often indicates much lower robustness than the conventional measure. We therefore propose two calibrations that use observed controls to benchmark how much an omitted variable may change the ratio of robust to conventional standard errors. One uses the largest change observed when controls are removed and restored; the other also relates the permitted change to explanatory strength. Both calibrations give less conservative assessments that are closer to conventional robustness values. Experiments that temporarily hide observed controls provide empirical support for the benchmarks, although exceptions occur. The calibrated measures are easy and fast to compute; the calibration that accounts for explanatory strength yields a point value in every reference case within numerical tolerance.

title: Attitude Towards Uncertainty in Decisions Startup: Analysis of Optimistic, Pessimistic, and Moderate in Choosing Business Strategies
affiliations: Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa University and Universitas Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa

detail.title: Attitude Towards Uncertainty in Decisions Startup: Analysis of Optimistic, Pessimistic, and Moderate in Choosing Business Strategies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict interest in other organization
declarations.funderStatement: No founder

detail.abstract: Startups operate in dynamic environments and often face decisions when information about the market, customers, technology, competitors, and funding is incomplete. In these circumstances, the decision-maker's attitude is a key factor influencing how opportunities and threats are assessed. This article aims to analyze how optimistic, pessimistic, and moderate attitudes influence startup strategy selection and outline approaches that can help founders make more adaptive decisions. The article was compiled using a descriptive-analytical literature review method, analyzing scientific publications from 2016-2026 that discuss entrepreneurial uncertainty, decision-making logic, effectuation, causation, and business experimentation. The literature suggests that optimism can foster opportunity orientation, but it does not automatically lead to effective action and can lead founders to ignore conflicting evidence. Pessimism helps identify threats and prepare mitigation measures, but if dominant, it can slow down experimentation and lead to missed opportunities. A moderate approach does not always mean choosing the middle path, but rather adjusting the level of courage and caution to the resources, consequences of decisions, and available evidence. Relevant strategies include incremental market testing, establishing acceptable loss limits, scenario development, combining planning with flexibility, and evaluating based on customer feedback. The article concludes that good startup decisions are not determined by a single mindset, but rather by the ability to examine assumptions, learn from actions, and modify strategies in a measured manner.

title: Merged States of an Observer: Discrimination, Reading Cost and Zero-Error Recovery

detail.title: Merged States of an Observer: Discrimination, Reading Cost and Zero-Error Recovery

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no funding.

detail.abstract:
An observer maps states to records. Distinct states with the same record form a merged pair. This paper studies two means of distinguishing such states: side information and repeated noisy readings. A reading assigns an output probability law to each state. A merged pair has three equivalent descriptions: equal records, exchange by a record-preserving permutation, and zero triangular discrimination Δ under every reading whose law depends only on the record. A fourth description uses adaptive protocols. For a fair binary label and an independent initial seed, a pair is merged if and only if every protocol with record-determined conditional readings acquires zero information at every finite horizon and in the limit.

For any binary prior, one reading supplies at most Δ/ln 2 bits. An entropy identity extends this bound to adaptive protocols with stopping and retained initial information. If every conditional reading has discrimination at most Δ > 0 and costs at least one, acquiring c additional bits costs at least c ln 2/Δ in expectation. The bound holds at every horizon and in the information limit. Under stopping with probability one, the limit is the mutual information of the countable stopped-transcript law.

For a fair label, repetition of any finite-output reading with Δ > 0 acquires 1 − h₂(η) bits within 4 ln(1/(2η))/Δ + 1 readings, for 0 < η ≤ 1/2, with h₂ denoting binary entropy. For a fair label under a common discrimination cap Δ, with the fixed reading repeatable at unit cost, the infimum expected cost of a fixed information target between zero and one bit has order Δ⁻¹.

Zero-error recovery depends on the supports of the reading laws, the sets of outputs with positive probability. The least side alphabet of a stochastic reading is the chromatic number of its support-conflict graph. Any positive finite number of repetitions of one hidden input leaves this number unchanged. For fixed reading laws and a prior giving both labels positive probability, zero-error recovery at finite expected cost is possible if and only if neither support contains the other. For a deterministic record, the states sharing a record form a fiber. On a nonempty state set with finite fibers of bounded size, the least side alphabet has the size of the largest fiber. With a separate alphabet of matching size for each fiber, any two resolving coordinates differ by one and only one record-preserving permutation. Applications concern differential privacy, perfect secrecy and local Fisher information. All results are formalized in Lean 4 with proofs that depend only on the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound; the public repository gives the claim-to-code correspondence.

title: Reversal without Restoration: Evidence from Japan's Export Controls on Korea

detail.title: Reversal without Restoration: Evidence from Japan's Export Controls on Korea

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific funding.

detail.abstract: Export controls are increasingly used for economic coercion, yet little is known about what happens once they are lifted. Japan's 2019 restrictions on semiconductor-material exports to Korea, reversed in 2023, provide a complete cycle. Korean customs data show Japan's share of some six hundred never-restricted strategic-list products fell after the lifting, and tends to fall more where exposure to potential control is greater. Among the restricted products, the share returned only in part, where supply was cut. The pattern points to lasting changes in beliefs about the supplier government rather than sunk switching costs: the cost outlasts the control.

title: Information Versus Enforcement Against Greenwashing: Pre-Registered Experiments in a Multi-Agent Artificial Market

detail.title: Information Versus Enforcement Against Greenwashing: Pre-Registered Experiments in a Multi-Agent Artificial Market

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study simulates artificial agents and uses firm-level market and ESG rating data; it involves no human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific funding.

detail.abstract:
Regulators can fight greenwashing by making inflated disclosures easier to see through or by fining them when audits detect them. We compare the two in an agent-based artificial market where 1,000 investors trade the shares of 200 firms. Impact investors value reported ESG scores, and investors switch types by imitation. Every period each firm chooses between costly real improvement, cheap inflation of its report that audits may detect, and doing nothing; a regulator sets transparency, audits and fines. The market is initialised on CSI 300 constituents, investor taste is calibrated to an ESG cost-of-capital slope of about 28 basis points per standard deviation, and the baseline fine is China's statutory maximum of CNY 10 million per case. In a pre-registered experiment of 59 scenarios with 30 paired seeds each: (i) policies work only through investor preference, without which firms neither improve nor inflate; (ii) raising transparency from 0.1 to 0.6 raises the true ESG level more than quadrupling the fine, and both beat the baseline, both without natural decay of the true level and at 0.2 standard deviations (SD) per year; the effect of transparency against the baseline is +0.04 and +0.33 SD at these two uncalibrated rates; (iii) fixed fines lose deterrence quickly because inflation added to an undetected case is not fined again, and they leave large firms, for which CNY 10 million is negligible, inflating in 66% of their decisions. Exploratory supplements designed after these results keep the ordering at three intermediate decay rates, when true levels revert to the mean, when every false report is fined, and when washing costs differ across firms. But the size of the information advantage depends on two assumptions. Under mean reversion at rates bounded by a rating panel, transparency beats the quadrupled fine by only +0.003 to +0.006 SD, because improvements fade while inflation persists. With a fine for every false report, the gap shrinks from +0.205 to +0.058 SD, and the plateau in fine deterrence disappears. With firm-specific washing costs, greenwashing declines gradually with transparency instead of stopping at a threshold. Market feedback strengthens the fixed-fine effect by about 11% and has no identifiable net effect on transparency. A tabular Q-learner trained on realised accounts did not reach a usable policy. A second pre-registered experiment holds the expected number of audits fixed. Auditing in proportion to market value or after jumps in reported scores does worse than random audits when firms know the rule (-0.19 and -0.14 SD): value targeting moves greenwashing from large to small firms, and firms keep new inflation below the jump threshold. With the rule hidden, neither differs from random audits. All results are conditional on the model.
